These definitions explain why a theorem on one region need not control the whole coefficient sum. ### Sharp bounds and boundary arguments The [closed-domain upper theorem](../../notes/research_global_sharp_coefficient_limsup_majorant.md), [full-fiber activation](../../notes/research_full_fiber_sharp_boundary_activation.md) and [stationary classification](../../notes/research_full_fiber_sharp_stationary_classification.md) prove the corresponding boundary and stationary statements. Their arguments establish the directional entropy gains, free-spectrum retuning and protected cap exclusions directly. The [odd main-strand cycle theorem](../../notes/research_stationary_noncross_main_cycle_obstruction.md) uses exact source characters and original face demands; the [flat-cap limitation](../../notes/research_flat_cap_no_local_exponential_angular_gap.md) is an exact alternating-sum inequality. The [seam theorem](../../notes/research_sharp_cross_degree_domination_and_seam_gap.md) concerns the boundary between two degree regions of the original coefficient sum. Its moving cosine-log integral and pointwise tail comparison prove all-spectrum CROSS-degree domination; exact latent-triangle strong concavity gives the explicit gap $\gamma_D=\pi a_D^2/2$. The existing whole-domain integration-by-parts theorem retains all charge currents and gives seam-period negligibility for fixed long fillings. These conclusions are analytical. For this general-plat route, the remaining macroscopic non-CROSS part is not controlled by the seam theorem alone. The four-state and window audits below support the retained finite source factors and indices; they do not establish the analytic majorant, classify its maxima, or prove a global volume comparison. Each linked note states the domain and hypotheses of its proof. ## Exact transfers supporting the phase estimate The analytic phase argument has two focused finite checks: python3 repro/run_research_checks.py phase-transfer The [four-state audit](../../experiments/audit_research_original_four_state_transfer.py) checks 196 recurrence/path comparisons and 85 exact omitted-half scalar identities across ten levels and both parities. The [window audit](../../experiments/audit_research_regular_spectral_window_phase_exclusion.py) checks 402 exact restricted matrix/path identities for half and full rows, including sampled spectral zeros and zero outer weights. Its equality is sign-adjusted on both sides; the common raw sign is established in the source proof. These validate finite indexing and retained factors. The original physical-matrix interface is inherited from the stated original numerator formula. The positive transfer, analytic gauge, strict boundary gaps and shared-torus phase exclusion are proved analytically; these finite checks do not prove their exponential estimates or a global volume bound. The [protected-window and mixed-cycle extensions](../../notes/research_mixed_cross_window_cycle_packing.md) combine local transfer identities with a finite packing of graph cycles. The outer-zero proof specializes the exact transfer; the middle-zero proof retains the actual initial seed and proves its output reflection by finite tilings. The whole-CROSS input uses the central factorization and cofactor angular theorem. Fractional cycle packing is a finite combinatorial argument. Those consequences use no extrapolation of numerical rates; the stated global majorant comparison remains conditional. ## A focused starting set With the dependencies above installed, these four scripts are a smaller entry point into the local recoupling and positive variational calculations: python3 repro/run_research_checks.py local-foundations Read the corresponding result's `scope` field before interpreting its reported outcome. The arbitrary-plat advance has a separate focused set: python3 repro/run_research_checks.py general-plat The root, complex-action and amplitude notes contain their analytical proofs; root finding and large-level comparisons are regressions. The magnetic audit also tests the original finite Casimir equation and the exact joint rational formula, retaining the difference between Gaussian and positive sine binomials. The character and regulator audits check exact rational identities in formal variables. The marked gluing audit uses an actual three-cusp triangulation; the critical-scheme audit checks local inverses and 24 incidence graphs. The reflection and graph audits replay actual finite sources. None of these checks proves the missing general global asymptotic. The joint determinant audit checks the source polynomial before continuation, its three-term recurrence and positive principal minors. The joint amplitude audit compares the literal finite sum with its determinant and asymptotic, including both derivative corrections at folded channels. The framing audit verifies the stated equivalences and local construction; it does not search for or prove a favorable common frame for every plat. The generic-normal audits compare the original generic columns and derivatives, including the exact large-partner collision tail and nonzero extra-pole residues. The right-angled obstruction audit checks reflection signs, polarization identities and exact two-facet examples. Its general conclusion rests on the separate proof of the literal Morse-prefix dictionary and convex incidence, not on extrapolating those examples. ## The exceptional-period checks The matching-edge contour method has focused audits for the generic Casimir polynomial, its root location and positive endpoint convolution, the actual inverse-turn character relation, and the full resolvent with its normal poles. The strict-prefix and Green-action audits check original matrix entries and selected logarithms. The rectangle audit verifies the actual primitive words for all three half-twist cases. Each note links its script and recorded output. The endpoint resolvent proof uses a unitary congruence and exact Schur denominator; it does not claim a Hermitian similarity or a polynomial bound for individual spectral projectors. Numerical rate samples supplement the written asymptotic proofs. None of these local or endpoint checks establishes a contributing contour or the general source asymptotic. ## Rebuilding this guide and its figures The guide is generated from `book/chapters/` and the published notes. Its static HTML uses native MathML and local CSS and JavaScript; reading it requires no account or external math service. ```sh python3 tools/build_book.py python3 tools/check_book.py python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory docs ``` The build requires Pandoc. TikZ sources and their compiled PNG/PDF figures are retained in `book/figures/`. To regenerate the figures, install a TeX distribution with TikZ and the optional Python package PyMuPDF, then run: ```sh python3 tools/render_figures.py python3 tools/build_book.py ``` The guide explains the argument, while the linked technical notes contain the detailed proofs. Existing note paths and audit imports remain stable. The physical paired-normal audit checks the original Casimir entries, weighted Dirichlet identity, double-node reflection and actual generic derivative. Its polynomial estimate is proved on the physical grid; it is not a complex-neighborhood or whole-source theorem. The near-fold complex audit retains the full large generic source and checks the resonant recurrence on a small complex circle. Its subexponential theorem requires shrinking scaled channel windows. The matching-edge audits reconstruct the actual generic matrices on four external representation factors, pivotal signs, root first jets and original row measure. They retain unequal partner derivatives and do not infer a completed positive matrix norm from the scalar formula. The full physical packet audit tests the cone determinant, finite boundary zeros, generic matrix lifts and actual amplitudes outside the old central wedge. The physical generic-jet audit retains both forward and backward q recurrences and nonzero higher divided-pair jets. The localization audit checks the exact low/high flag formulas; its general conclusion is the written continuation and geometric argument. None establishes a contributing global cycle. The completed-projector audit checks the categorical norm, full generic operator identities, actual cyclic turn, paired cluster jets and complete original-measure cancellation. It retains the nilpotent contribution and unequal scalar derivatives. Its finite checks support the written identities; they do not bound the native projectors or establish a global volume limit. The native-energy audit checks the actual generic high-degree adapter, dual measures, residue and completed-projector jets, and exact rank-one norms. The exponential midpoint-energy rate has a written Riemann-sum proof; its numerical sequence only illustrates that proof. The theorem retains the energy rather than asserting polynomial projector norms. The energy-profile audit checks actual Fourier norms, vanished unused nodes, canonical midpoints, both-parity endpoint source formulas and the selected dilogarithm constant. Its even finite full-norm samples concern the nilpotent operator; the completed projector's rate follows from the separate polynomial comparison. The local geometry audit checks original phases, measures, parity factors and all four tetrahedron shapes, without inferring global phase matching. The shrinking-fold audit checks the actual source formula outside complete support as well as its endpoint and measures. The coefficient audit checks log-concavity, tilted modes, literal complex-radius normalization and interior coefficient rates. The shared-cycle audit compares against original Morse contractions, including the first-failure zeros, both-parity carrier cancellation, exact Kirchhoff support and marked charge. The resulting global Cauchy comparison remains an upper bound. The positive-partition audit reconstructs the original endpoint and white scalars, the high-degree Chevalley adapter, and full phase-bearing sums before checking their Cauchy bound. The radial-obstruction audit checks the finite phase derivatives, adapters and cup/mark relation; its general geometric conclusion uses the separately proved common-frame obstruction. Neither audit claims a global rate gap or volume equality. ## The full positive endpoint volume theorem The half-block audit compares the original numerator coefficients, the positive path recurrence, negative roots, exact extreme coefficients, and the finite Lobachevsky formula. Its finite rate profiles remain diagnostics; the uniform closed-domain limit has a written proof. The earlier shared-source audit checks 228 original coefficients, 4590 support patterns, 748302 affine-cut conditions, 118 one-level support certificates and 236 eventual-flow tests. Those tests remain relevant to fixed half-label patterns. The full-kernel theorem instead uses every degree-$N-1$ monomial, continuous entropy on the full simplex, and unrestricted integral flow rounding. A separate transfer audit checks 39599 Laurent coefficient comparisons and the path injection used in the central corridor. The [general endpoint theorem](../../notes/general_fejer_endpoint_source_volume.md) proves the geometric upper bound as well. Its [structural audit](../../experiments/audit_general_fejer_endpoint_source_volume.py) constructs actual Morse faces at widths two, three and four, retains edge identities through genuine identity smoothing, and finds digon disks from the dual graph independently of the Hall subsets. It checks 41 loopless smoothings, 918 hybrid patterns, 121004 Hall cuts, 716 tight sets and 816 independent positive-arc max-flow tests. The general Hall classification, source reduction and volume comparison have separate written proofs. The [signed-chain audit](../../experiments/audit_actual_fejer_hybrid_piece_representation.py) checks 270 signed cyclic fans, four repeated-contact fans, 24 actual circle/line tangencies, eight contact triangles and two oriented strip chains. These validate the volume formulas; the original group pairings, degree-one relative chain and compatible cut-disk collapse are analytical arguments. The [serial audit](../../experiments/audit_actual_fejer_serial_coupon_bound.py) compares 3960 original physical entries, including 1290 illegal-total zeros, and 3120 independent coefficient bounds for literal powers of the same ordered-pair coupon. The [odd regularization audit](../../experiments/audit_actual_fejer_odd_regularized_full_numerator.py) checks the original spectral derivative and the positive comparison used for the odd coupon $V_N(-2)-N^{-2}V_N'(-2)$. The resulting whole-source spectral-jet bound is exact at both parities. These are spectral derivatives at the fixed root, not genuine-$q$ normals. Recorded replays accompany the formulas; finite fixtures do not establish a selected Gaussian cycle, a complementary phase estimate or the general filled-knot asymptotic. ## The full spectral numerator packet The [full packet theorem](../../notes/general_full_spectral_numerator_geometric_packet.md) is an analytical assembly of exact source identities, relative complex cofactor estimates, a global angular gap and the original shared Cauchy coefficient. Its finite tests are scoped to those inputs; samples do not prove the uniform asymptotic or select the later spectral Gaussian contour. The [factorization note](../../notes/actual_cross_cofactor_factorization.md) compares the central formulas with the original unused-row path polynomial and retains both parity endpoints and the odd central-skipping term. The [interior adapter audit](../../notes/actual_cross_cofactor_interior_packet.md) checks 1056 row-replaced determinants, 352 independently constructed original q-Hahn matrix node values, 352 sine-product scalars and 960 tail factorizations at 85 digits. The analytic proof separately supplies the exponential interpolation error and discrete saddle estimate for all physical starting rows. The [protected-middle angular audit](../../notes/actual_cross_cofactor_protected_angular_gap.md) checks 4636 coefficient bounds, 486 complex angular inequalities, 432 actual three-step matrix entries and 16 exact monomer cases. The [marked-action audit](../../notes/actual_cross_cofactor_marked_action.md) compares 24 independent source/cofactor integrals, 17 integral derivatives and 12 literal whole Gauss/collar configurations, together with polarization and Gaussian boundary cancellations. Independent fresh replays reproduce those checks. The protected-middle relative packet, [nodal rigidity](../../notes/actual_cross_cofactor_interpolant_rigidity.md), [global local-angle theorem](../../notes/actual_cross_cofactor_global_angular_gap.md) and the whole-source assembly have analytical proofs. The finite Cauchy--Lagrange and original face-torus arguments carry the asymptotic conclusions. The [direct-power scope](../../notes/fixed_root_direct_power_scope.md) retains all fixed-root spectral derivatives while keeping genuine-$q$ normals separate. Those input audits do not establish global charge dominance or the general filled-knot limit. The later localized contribution is proved by the analytical argument below. ## The localized original filling period The [localized unit-charge theorem](../../notes/general_localized_unit_charge_filling_period.md) retains the original marked prefactor, finite-level action, both determinant branches and every boundary term when the integration cube is translated. Its proof gives a nonzero relative Gaussian coefficient at both level parities. The [charge comparison](../../notes/general_local_charge_critical_monotonicity.md), applied to that same finite action, bounds the other charges in a fixed finite local box. The exact remainder keeps the finitely many selected charges outside the cube and all other charges on their whole original domains; it does not separately sum remote sharp-cube pieces. The proof does not bound this global remainder or establish the general filled-knot volume limit. ## Whole-domain bounds and the balanced full invariant The [large-charge audit](../../notes/actual_whole_domain_large_charge_tail.md) checks original operator entries, both signed Gaussian exponents, and paired endpoint currents. The [diagonal-sector audit](../../notes/actual_global_diagonal_spectral_sector_gap.md) includes removable physical nodes, exact path partitions and sewn polynomial integration-by-parts checks. The [CROSS audit](../../notes/actual_global_cross_spectral_gap.md) checks the start decomposition, rescaled transfer matrices and finite characteristic formulas. Their recorded finite checks support the exact formulas. The uniform bounds are established by the written proofs. The [whole-CROSS period](../../notes/general_all_cross_long_filling_volume.md), [all-angle LEFT envelope](../../notes/actual_global_left_weighted_spectral_envelope.md), and [complete-radius balance theorem](../../notes/general_complete_radius_balance_filling_volume.md) prove the stated conditional full-invariant result. Their arguments retain entire-domain remote charge sums and endpoint currents, including both level parities. The elementary [entropy lemma](../../notes/actual_triangle_entropy_algebraic_balance.md) checks the absolute half-degree normalization and all protected-zero cases. These arguments prove a full invariant theorem under the stated balance hypothesis. Those conditional arguments alone do not prove realization. The uniform family construction below supplies it, without treating numerical experiments as a proof. ## Uniform width and exact bridge number The [family theorem](../../notes/general_one_end_layer_long_filling_volume.md) checks the literal incidences, packing reflection, both recurrence branches and endpoints, then proves the required convex comparison. That proof covers every $k\geq2$; finite packing samples do not justify its coverage. The [zero-middle lemma](../../notes/actual_zero_middle_nine_quarter_balance.md) uses an exact rational lower bound. The [Fox certificate](../../notes/actual_fox_coloring_exact_plat_bridge.md) proves the signed crossing identity, invariance, exact plat count and bridge bound directly. No numerical asymptotic or coverage audit is claimed for these proofs. The two focused family audits supplement these proofs: the reduced-source audit checks 38 literal widths and the rational comparison seed; the one-end-source audit checks 39 literal widths, the changed linear boundary, and all circle contacts and noncontacts in the exact width-two and width-three packings. These finite checks do not replace the uniform convex comparison. ## Shared-radius certificates beyond complete-packing balance The [anchored theorem](../../notes/general_anchored_shared_radius_filling_volume.md) retains common-face Cauchy bounds, both parity partitions, a fixed complex strip and the entire Fourier remainder. Its explicit example uses six stated rational vectors. Arb interval arithmetic evaluates finite Lobachevsky sums with an explicit uniform tail bound; exact algebra checks the original golden-ratio packing. The resulting strict inequalities certify this example, not universal coverage of the criterion. The [fixed-triangle capacity lemma](../../notes/actual_fixed_triangle_boundary_capacity_gap.md) is analytical: closed strong concavity gives the explicit squared-distance loss, and finite convex separation proves the shared dual formula even without attained positive multipliers. It does not assert the same comparison for fractional identity mixtures. ## A structural extension at arbitrary fixed depth The [unit-chain theorem](../../notes/general_marked_unit_chain_filling_volume.md) proves the literal prefix dictionary and an exact extension into the empty marked gap. Its proof preserves every old disk and checks every added crossing-circle block analytically; depth is arbitrary. The focused audit checks 56 original source charts and 12 exact small seed extensions, including 1,084 circle/line support pairs. These finite checks support the source dictionary and geometry, while the proof establishes the unbounded-depth statement. ## Simultaneous insertions at every initial bridge gap The [simultaneous theorem](../../notes/general_simultaneous_bridge_gap_filling_volume.md) has an analytical proof and a finite audit. The audit checks 413 nonuniform-depth source charts, seven exact symbolic transport/ratio identities, and 25 joint small packings with 2,333 support checks. The analytical proof establishes the general source induction, disjoint-gap construction, curvature order and every local block bound. The extended diagram retains its own full normalization; no equality of its framing scalar with the core's scalar is asserted. ## Refined sector covers and a rigorous obstruction The [general finite-cover theorem](../../notes/general_actual_sector_cover_filling_volume.md) partitions the source and transfers the entire Fourier remainder using the original shared face targets and both level parities. The [separation verifier](../../experiments/audit_actual_shared_radius_certificate_separation.py) checks that both certificates use exactly the same original expression with seventeen crossing-circle blocks and the same mark. An 84-variable rational flow rules out one anchored test by more than $0.025$; an 83-variable complete flow and forty rational radius vectors certify the refined cover by more than $0.04$. All face equations are exact, and Arb evaluations include explicit Fourier-series tails. The public scripts contain no numerical optimizer or private diagnostic inputs. The [undivided positive-capacity obstruction](../../notes/actual_complete_source_cauchy_capacity_gap.md) is analytical. Its proof establishes coercivity, rules out escaping level-dependent radii, and distinguishes the bound's exponential loss from the actual coefficient's correct volume rate. The proof retains the finite positive-source normalization and the pure-face entropy values. ## Uniform coefficient energy and rearrangement The [protected-outer audit](../../experiments/audit_actual_protected_outer_spectral_energy.py) constructs the physical coproduct Casimir and extracts coefficients by the original finite Fourier transform. It verifies both parity reference factors and exact spectral sampling nodes. Symbolic identities and fixed integral checks supplement the analytical uniform boundary proof. The [general one-sided audit](../../experiments/audit_actual_one_sided_relative_spectral_energy.py) separately verifies the nonnegative parameter expansion, signed-parameter Cauchy inequalities, interior original coefficients, and the rearrangement identities. The uniform transfer estimate and compact finite-tilt argument are proved analytically, rather than inferred from sampled large levels. The local theorem and its shared-flow consequence have their stated hypotheses; the audit does not establish a stronger global entropy inequality. Four earlier audit consumers now import the physical `Local` class from its defining public module. The lightweight face compiler remains independent of quantum-only imports. Its tensor-contraction helper is now included explicitly and imported by the ten published consumers. The existing small-circle audit replays with results exactly matching its recorded output.

title: Figure gallery
text: # Figure gallery ## The requirements of a volume proof ![An exact decomposition, a nonzero geometric contribution, a strict remainder bound, and an identification of the critical value with hyperbolic volume are separate parts of the proof.](figures/methods-proof-map.svg) Here \(K_N\) is the original invariant, \(G_N\) is the selected contribution, and \(R_N\) is the remaining signed sum. The two analytic estimates determine the growth rate of \(K_N\). The geometric argument identifies that rate with the volume of the actual knot complement. The arrows record logical dependencies; they do not assert that all these steps hold for every knot. The [methods chapter](chapters/methods.md) defines the quantities and proves the elementary implication. [Editable SVG](figures/methods-proof-map.svg) ## Adding terminal tangles on both sides ![One stellar subdivision preserves the old matching edge xy and creates the new matching edge bw. The last panel shows two insertions on each side.](figures/balanced-terminal-fans.png) The vertices in this diagram label white projection regions. They also label circles in the complete packing; the drawing itself records their adjacencies, not their radii. The two triangles beside the blue edge \(xy\) specify the original crossing circle. Insert a new vertex \(w\) in the triangle \(xby\). The new triangles have cyclic orders \(xbw\), \(byw\), and \(yxw\). Pair the first two across the amber edge \(bw\); the old blue edge and its crossing circle remain. In the final panel, \(b_0=b\) and \(c_0=c\) are the original opposite vertices. The vertices \(b_1,b_2\) and \(c_1,c_2\) are the two successively inserted circles on each side. The blue triangles nearest \(xy\) belong to the retained crossing circle, and each amber edge specifies an added crossing circle. The general construction uses any suitable even counts \(j,k\), chosen by the curvature recurrence in the [results chapter](chapters/results.md#decorating-a-planar-diagram). Giving the new tangles odd crossing parity makes an even stack preserve the four outside endpoint connections. [SVG](figures/balanced-terminal-fans.svg) · [PDF](figures/balanced-terminal-fans.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/balanced-terminal-fans.tex) The drawings below explain the constructions used in the guide. Some show actual circle configurations in the boundary plane of hyperbolic space. Others show only incidence, algebraic composition, or the sequence of a proof. Each caption states which kind of drawing it is, defines the important labels, and explains the result for which it is used. The volume theorem applies to the stated ordered Conway compositions with sufficiently long net twists and to several separately certified plat families. A remaining question attached to a local method is not an unresolved step in those theorems. The diagrams below explain the proved constructions and their remaining scope. ## Evaluating one subtree and keeping its attaching variable ![The parent angle u is joined to the current vertex angle t by the complete edge kernel. Child subtrees have already been evaluated as polynomials in t; the crossing trace acts only on t.](figures/tree-boundary-message.png) The triangles stand for child subtrees of the construction tree, not for ideal tetrahedra. Their evaluations are the displayed functions \(M_{w_j,N}(t)\). Multiply these functions by the full kernel on the parent edge, then take the crossing trace at vertex \(v\). This leaves the parent angle \(u\) free and gives \(M_{v,N}(u)\). Only the edge kernel contains \(u\), so the result has trigonometric degree at most \(N-1\), however many vertices lie below \(v\). The [local volume proof](../notes/actual_all_circle_local_message_volume.md) shows that its value at \(u=0\) is nonzero. Dividing by that exact value keeps the child's completed contribution outside the next estimate. The crossing and orientation factors remain in this denominator; they are not discarded. [Vector drawing](figures/tree-boundary-message.svg) · [PDF](figures/tree-boundary-message.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/tree-boundary-message.tex) ## Attaching an octahedron in the original tangle cut ![An octahedron attaches to a projection half along a shaded disk triangle. The parent and child circle vertices are O_v and O_w; the four equatorial vertices are the corresponding strand ends.](figures/octahedral-page-attachment.svg) The blue triangle on the left is a boundary face of the existing projection half. The blue triangle on the right is glued to it with the opposite boundary orientation. Equal labels specify the vertex identifications. The new vertex \(O_w\) belongs to the inserted child crossing circle, while \(O_v\) belongs to its parent. The other three crossing-disk triangles are listed in the [decomposition proof](../notes/actual_all_circle_octahedral_decomposition.md). The same attachment is made in the other projection half. This is the local attachment used in the induction over the tree. The [geometric chapter](chapters/geometry.md#the-geometric-proof-for-the-explicit-degree-and-twist-bound) explains the positive hyperbolic realization and the filling path. Download the [vector PDF](figures/octahedral-page-attachment.pdf) or the [TikZ source](figures/octahedral-page-attachment.tex). ## Established results and remaining scope ![The reduction to long net twists, the full quantum invariant and knot volume, with quantum A-operator formulations and the remaining questions.](figures/research-map.png) Fix an ordered Conway composition with the prescribed cylindrical closure. Reduce it by the explicit twist slides and combinations, excluding an elementary two-strand braid output. Then choose sufficiently long net twists for which the actual closed diagram is a knot. The reduction identifies this knot with one covered by the strict-tree estimates. The three upper boxes describe the proved argument for that knot: reduce the tangle by exact isotopies, control the whole signed quantum sum while keeping a nonzero geometric contribution, and identify its growth with the volume of the actual knot complement. Only the auxiliary crossing-circle cusps are filled; the knot cusp remains unfilled. The lower blue box gives two other exact formulations of the same invariant: a selected period of a quantum difference operator and a positive ratio of Gram determinants. These also have the stated volume limits. The amber box concerns arbitrary short net twists, more general knot families, and extension of the selected geometric-factor theorem beyond trees of crossing circles. The geometric factor is identified for the covered trees; the full recurrence ideal remains a separate question. It does not leave the full-sum estimate open for the covered class. See the [results chapter](chapters/results.md) for the precise hypotheses. [SVG](figures/research-map.svg) · [PDF](figures/research-map.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/research-map.tex) ## Varying the figure-eight meridian near completeness ![The reduced figure-eight invariant approaches a sine profile on the imaginary parameter axis, while its centered regular part approaches one.](figures/figure-eight-meridian-profile.png) Keep the quantum parameter at \(q_N=e^{\pi i/N}\) and write the meridian eigenvalue as \(M=e^{it/(2N)}\). The left panel plots the reduced invariant divided by its complete value at levels \(N=24,47,80\). Its limiting curve is \(2\sin(t/2)/t\), with value one at zero. The right panel shows the error after subtracting the polynomial interpolating the ordinary colors, dividing by \(1+Y+\cdots+Y^{N-1}\), and applying the centering displayed below the axes. Here \(Y=M^2\). At the marked nonzero multiples of \(2\pi\), numerator and denominator both vanish; the dots use the removable derivative values. The logarithmic vertical scale makes the small errors visible. The [profile theorem](../notes/actual_paired_factor_meridian_profile.md) proves convergence on every fixed complex compact set, including these points, and identifies the first correction with the preferred cusp shape \(2\sqrt3\,i\). Its proof uses the positive finite figure-eight sum. A separate criterion states the estimate needed to extend the argument to signed sums for other knots. [Vector figure](figures/figure-eight-meridian-profile.svg) · [PDF](figures/figure-eight-meridian-profile.pdf) · [Reproduction script](../experiments/plot_figure_eight_meridian_profile.py) ## Products of tangle polynomials as the meridian varies ![Two triangles distinguish the Newton products that are nonzero at completeness from those that can become nonzero after changing the meridian.](figures/moving-newton-products.png) A two-strand tangle operator is expressed in the normalized Newton basis \(e_0,\ldots,e_{N-1}\) of its Casimir polynomial algebra. Joining two boxes requires multiplying their polynomials. Here \(i,j\) are the indices of two basis elements; the axes show \(x=i/N\) and \(y=j/N\). At the complete meridian \(s=0\), the product \(e_i e_j\) is zero whenever \(i+j\ge N\). For a generic displacement \(M=q_N^s\), those products become nonzero. The [multiplication theorem](../notes/actual_main_meridian_newton_multiplication.md) gives every coefficient and explains the special displacements where some coefficients vanish again. This is a picture of multiplication in a specified basis. The basis also changes with \(s\); its motion accounts for the nonzero first derivatives of the new coefficients. Keeping the complete basis fixed makes the first derivative of multiplication zero. Neither description by itself estimates the knot invariant, which also requires turns, summation over shared indices, and closure. [Vector figure](figures/moving-newton-products.svg) · [PDF](figures/moving-newton-products.pdf) · [Reproduction script](../experiments/audit_main_meridian_newton_algebra.py) ## Reflecting an index and combining two product junctions ![Three diagrams show a trace-difference bound, its reflected complete pairing, and the fused product junction with all five exterior branches retained.](figures/main-meridian-reflected-turn-fusion.png) The vertices represent multiplication and trace operations on tangle polynomials. In the left panel, a physical quarter-turn joins two equal indices \(h\). The left trace is the difference \(\delta\phi_s=\phi_s-\phi_0\) between its moving-meridian and complete values. The [Fourier estimate](../notes/actual_main_meridian_high_fourier_reflection.md) bounds this difference after replacing \(h\) at that endpoint by \(r=N-1-h\). All other branches, denoted collectively by \(F\) and \(G\), remain attached. The middle panel therefore has complementary labels \(r+h=N-1\). Summing this positive complete pairing gives exactly the single trace \(\phi_0(FG)\), shown on the right. The three branches from the first junction and two from the second give the five displayed branches. Their order is inherited from the original ordered products. The first arrow is an upper estimate; the second is an algebra identity. Deleting the turn in this comparison can change the represented link. The [pressure theorem](../notes/actual_main_meridian_component_pressure.md) proves that the new positive maximum is no larger than the original one, and a strict Fourier estimate controls the case of equal maxima. The invariant and the hyperbolic volume in the final theorem still belong to the original diagram. This comparison is what allows the [general component proof](../notes/actual_main_meridian_general_component_comparison.md) to treat junctions of arbitrary valence. [SVG](figures/main-meridian-reflected-turn-fusion.svg) · [PDF](figures/main-meridian-reflected-turn-fusion.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/main-meridian-reflected-turn-fusion.tex) ## A separated example of the product tree ![Two product junctions are connected through a third junction carrying the original crossing-circle operator p_0. Each connecting edge applies a quarter-turn.](figures/separated-product-junctions.png) The four lower boxes represent the tangle operators \(h_1,\ldots,h_4\). The left junction multiplies \(h_1h_2\), and the right junction multiplies \(h_3h_4\). Apply the indicated quarter-turn \(T\) to each result, multiply them with the original operator \(p_0\), and take the prescribed closing trace. The formulas below the drawing define each leaf and retain its half-twist and auxiliary-circle color. This is a simple instance of the general theorem above. The two outer junctions carry no unturned crossing-circle operator; the central junction does. The [source growth theorem](../notes/actual_main_meridian_source_bounds.md) allows any fixed finite tree with this separation property: whenever two product junctions are adjacent, at least one carries such an original operator. Their degrees and the size of the tree may be arbitrary. The largest source value over the allowed colors and a small neighborhood of the complete main meridian has exponential growth equal to the volume of the augmented complement. The crossing circles remain unfilled in this statement. [Vector figure](figures/separated-product-junctions.svg) · [PDF](figures/separated-product-junctions.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/separated-product-junctions.tex) ## The operations that build the knot diagram ![Three panels show the actual connections for stacking two four-ended tangles, rotating a tangle by a quarter-turn, and taking the cylindrical closure.](../manuscript/build/figures/tangle-construction.png) Each box contains a tangle whose internal strands have been suppressed. The black dots are its four ordered boundary endpoints. In the left panel, the product \(FG\) joins the two upper endpoints of \(F\) to the two lower endpoints of \(G\) in the displayed order. In the middle panel, the entire tangle rotates clockwise, carrying its endpoint labels with it. This is a geometric operation, not a renaming of an internal summation index. The right panel adds the two exterior arcs defining the cylindrical closure \(C(FG)\). These arcs determine the final endpoint pairing and hence whether the result is a knot or a link. The picture introduces the [manuscript's construction](chapters/manuscript.md); the theorem then imposes its explicit recursive and knot-pairing conditions. [PDF](../manuscript/build/figures/tangle-construction.pdf) · [TikZ source](../manuscript/figures/tangle-construction.tex) ## Moving a twist box and combining signed twists ![An integral twist box moves past a tangle with a specified half-turn; adjacent twist boxes then combine by addition.](figures/net-twist-reduction.png) Products are read from bottom to top. In the upper row, moving the integral box $R^a$ past $F$ replaces $F$ by $\rho^a(F)$, where $\rho$ is the half-turn about the stacking axis. An even $a$ leaves $F$ unchanged; an odd $a$ retains that half-turn. The four outside endpoints stay fixed. Rotating the inner tangle and interpolating through the empty end collars gives the isotopy proved in the [net-twist theorem](../notes/actual_conway_net_twist_volume.md). The lower row combines adjacent integral boxes: their signed weights add. Each surviving twist in the general reduction is the sum over a disjoint group of original boxes. The example $(a+2m)+(-2m)=a$ explains why large original magnitudes alone cannot supply the theorem's size condition. The condition is imposed on the final sums. The marked point and any ribbon framing are transported through the moves. [SVG](figures/net-twist-reduction.svg) · [PDF](figures/net-twist-reduction.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/net-twist-reduction.tex) ## Splitting a cap-closed stack ![A sphere around the lower tangle and its bottom cap meets the two interface strands. Cutting produces the cap closures of both boxes, with the summing arcs marked in amber.](figures/conway-cap-splitting.png) The product places $F$ below $G$. The sphere $S$ encloses $F$ and its lower cap; its only intersections with the link are the two marked points. Cutting along $S$ and capping on each side gives $D(F)$ and $D(G)$. The amber arcs specify how to reconstruct the original stack by a connected sum. When a factor is a link with several components, these specified arcs determine which components are joined. The [closure theorem](../notes/actual_conway_arbitrary_closure_volume.md) uses this operation after removing exact zero twist sums and when processing an initial cap closure. For a hyperbolic input with long surviving strict weights, the decomposition contains one strict factor and otherwise only unknots. [Vector figure](figures/conway-cap-splitting.svg) · [PDF](figures/conway-cap-splitting.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/conway-cap-splitting.tex) ## The leaf pyramid and multiplication prism ![An ideal quadrangular pyramid for a leaf and an ideal triangular prism for a product. The blue quadrilaterals are the faces along which cells are glued.](figures/conway-cells.png) A twist-region leaf contributes the pyramid on the left. Its vertices \(O,C_0,C_1,C_2,C_3\) lie at infinity in hyperbolic space. The two amber triangles retain the actual crossing-disk pairing. Its blue quadrilateral is a gluing face, with a specified cyclic order of its four vertices. Multiplying two tangles contributes the prism on the right. Its faces \(F_x,F_y,F_z\) are the two input gluing faces and the output gluing face. The variables \(x,y,z\) are scaled quantum indices. The functions \(g\) and \(m\) are the corresponding limiting logarithmic weights, so the single-cell volumes are \(\pi g(x)\) and \(\pi m(x,y,z)\). Stationarity under the shared-index constraints makes the ordered quadrilateral shapes agree across each attachment. The drawing shows the faces and edges of the two ideal hyperbolic cells. The [geometry chapter](chapters/geometry.md#how-the-cells-and-the-diagram-are-identified) explains how the labeled cells recover the actual complement. ## Constructing the prism in the boundary plane ![Four ordered points on a unit circle and the intersection of two extended chords give five finite ideal vertices of the prism; its sixth ideal vertex is infinity.](../manuscript/build/figures/prism-boundary.png) This is a boundary-plane construction rather than a three-dimensional perspective drawing. The four points \(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3\) lie on the unit circle. The lines through \(v_0v_1\) and \(v_2v_3\) meet at \(P\), outside the circle. Together with infinity, they are the six ideal vertices of the prism. The positive parameters satisfy \(p+q+2r+w=1\); the consecutive half-arc fractions are \(p,r,q,r+w\). The displayed numerical values select a strict cell. The three quadrilateral gluing faces have the ordered vertices printed on the right. Listing the vertices is essential: it specifies the actual face map used to attach two cells. An abstract quadrilateral with the same shape would not determine which corners are joined. The [manuscript](chapters/manuscript.md) derives these shapes and relates them to derivatives of the quantum action. [PDF](../manuscript/build/figures/prism-boundary.pdf) · [TikZ source](../manuscript/figures/prism-boundary.tex) ## A local tetrahedron and its metric ![A truncated hyperideal tetrahedron, with blue polar truncation faces and six labeled original edges.](figures/truncated-tetrahedron.png) The labels \(a,b,c,d,e,f\) distinguish the six original edges. The blue triangles cut off the hyperideal vertices: they are the polar truncation faces. Their appearance in the plane records incidence only. The hyperbolic metric is determined by the Lorentzian Gram matrix of the outward face normals. For an edge carrying integer label \(j_e\), the theorem uses the half-shifted coordinate \(a_e=(j_e+1/2)/N\) and dihedral angle \(\alpha_e=\pi-2\pi a_e\). The normalized local quantum action equals the volume of the tetrahedron with these angles. This is a local geometric theorem. To obtain a knot complement, one must also prove the actual face identifications, edge equations and peripheral conditions. See the [local volume argument](chapters/geometry.md#a-local-tetrahedron-is-a-genuine-geometric-result). ## A change of representation pairing ![Two bases for four fixed external representation labels: the first uses internal label E, and the second uses internal label G.](figures/four-port.png) The four external representation labels \(A,B,C,D\) stay fixed. In the left basis, \(A,B\) are paired first and the intermediate representation has label \(E\). In the right basis, the pairing changes and the intermediate label is \(G\). The coefficient \(L_{G,E}(\zeta)\) is the actual finite change-of-basis entry at generic quantum parameter \(\zeta\). This operation lets one rewrite a quantum contraction in a basis adapted to a different cut of the diagram. Its normalization includes the physical turn and the derivatives needed when spectral labels collide at a root of unity. Bounds for this one matrix entry must still be combined with the shared internal sums. The [mechanism chapter](chapters/mechanism.md#exact-recoupling-exposes-a-local-geometric-scalar) explains that distinction. ## The domain of the local complex formula ![The allowed real parts of two complex wire coordinates, separated into low-degree and high-degree regions by an excluded seam.](figures/joint-kernel-domain.png) The axes are the real parts of two scaled wire coordinates \(x_1,x_2\). Their sum determines the pair degree: \(\tau=x_1+x_2\) below the diagonal seam and \(\tau=2-x_1-x_2\) above it. The internal channel remains an integer. The blue region is the projection of the limiting complex domain; it is not a restriction that the imaginary parts vanish. The dashed outer boundaries and the seam \(\operatorname{Re}(x_1+x_2)=1\) are excluded. At finite level, the zero-free theorem also removes a band of width \(1/(2N)\) on each side of that seam. Thus a fixed compact subset away from the seam is covered for all sufficiently large \(N\). On those compacts, the [local packet theorem](../notes/actual_q_hahn_full_physical_complex_packet.md) gives the selected complex action and a nonzero relative amplitude. It does not by itself select a global integration contour. ## Why two factors can be exceptional ![A planar section of a convex hull of normalized white-face normals. A line through it enters and exits through the two highlighted facets.](figures/two-exceptional-factors.png) The polyhedron here is built from face normals, not from the ideal vertices of the knot complement. Under the stated geometric strip conditions, the two framing flags determine a line through its interior. A generic line crosses exactly two facets. The corresponding two local factors fail the strict physical support inequalities used by the ordinary complex formula. The [localization theorem](../notes/actual_augmented_plat_selected_factor_localization.md) places all the other ordinary factors on that formula's selected branch. The two exceptional facets can be prescribed, including the pair adjacent to a crossing-circle edge. This identifies where a different local treatment is needed; it does not estimate that treatment merely by counting the facets. The complete-color contraction has a separate theorem, and deformed colors and generic derivatives retain their own requirements. ## Removing two redundant framing directions ![A patch of the face graph with two distinguished constant-potential faces and two adjacent physical strand indices that detect their variations.](figures/face-potential-rank.png) Vertices of this graph represent white faces of the original diagram. Edges represent incidences carried by its strands. The amber vertices \(u,v\) are the two constant-prefix faces. After subtracting the common potential on the connected blue part, the remaining free potentials are \(P_u,P_v\). The marked strand \(e_0\) and its neighbor \(e_1\) detect these two variations by the displayed integer matrix. Its determinant has absolute value one. Fixing those two strand indices therefore removes the redundant directions without introducing an unnoticed sublattice factor. The [transverse-rank theorem](../notes/actual_original_boundary_transverse_rank.md) uses this fact to obtain a nondegenerate Hessian on the remaining variables. This is a coordinate statement; the global coefficient saddle and the complete signed contraction have additional proofs. ## The cusp rectangle fixes the Gaussian normalization ![One Euclidean rectangle cut from a cusp and the two rectangles that form its primitive torus fundamental domain.](figures/cusp-gaussian.png) A horosphere cuts one rectangle from each of the two polyhedral copies. Its width is \(W\) and its height is \(H\). In the original tangent-circle coordinates, \(x,y\) are the two outer curvatures and \(b,c\) the two middle curvatures; curvature means reciprocal radius. The formulas under the drawing compute \(W,H\) from those same face variables. Gluing the rectangles gives a primitive meridian of length \(H\) and longitude of length \(2W\), with the orientations shown. This factor of two produces \(C=\pi H/W\). A retained half twist \(\epsilon\) changes the Gaussian parameter to \(Z=C-\pi i\epsilon\), and the primitive cusp shape is \(2\pi i/Z\). The [reflection-and-cusp theorem](../notes/actual_external_circle_reflection_and_cusp.md) matches this geometry to the complete-circle Fourier transform on the scale \(h=z\sqrt N\), where \(h\) is the color deficit. That mesoscopic calculation is one input; estimates for all physical colors and a fixed-color filling neighborhood are separate steps. ## Two marked faces determine one shared strip ![Two finite circles use the same pair of horizontal marked lines. Their selected intersection points separate when the matching tangencies are deformed.](figures/marked-circle-strip.png) The blue lines \(u,v\) are the two marked faces, normalized to heights zero and \(H\). The finite circles have radii \(r_1,r_2\). Their main-strand incidences remain tangent, while the matching incidences open at angles \(\psi_i=2\pi\delta_i\). The points \(p_\pm,q_\pm\) record the selected boundary fixed points; at the complete tangency each pair coincides. The common width \(H\) matters. Solving each crossing region in its own strip would not produce a single geometric representation. The [marked circle-pattern theorem](../notes/actual_marked_deformed_circle_pattern.md) solves all center and radius equations together and proves local uniqueness near the complete pattern. It also retains the selected fixed-point branches through their collision. The drawing illustrates that shared construction, rather than imposing an extra symmetry on all diagrams. ## The actual collar around a crossing disk ![An ordered circle configuration around a crossing disk and its image under a Möbius coordinate in which the side pairing is a dilation.](figures/deformed-circle-collar.png) On the left, \(x,y\) are the outer circles and \(b,c\) the input and output circles. The points \(C_0,C_1,C_2,C_3\) are the ordered contacts used by the original disk pairing. The outer circles intersect at the selected eigenpoints \(P_+,P_-\). Each dashed circle is orthogonal to the three white circles on its side. The coordinate \(w=(z-P_+)/(z-P_-)\) sends them to zero and infinity. In that coordinate, the dashed circles become concentric, with radii \(\rho_b,\rho_c\), and the actual pairing is the dilation \(C(w)=R_0w\), where \(R_0=\rho_c/\rho_b\). It sends \(C_1\) to \(C_0\) and \(C_2\) to \(C_3\). The auxiliary meridian traverses the reverse map, so its holonomy is \(C^{-1}\). This direction and the primitive curve cannot be recovered from an unlabeled cusp shape alone. The [collar proof](../notes/actual_deformed_circle_primitive_collar.md) treats the marked-line limit and the retained half-twist shear as well. [SVG](figures/deformed-circle-collar.svg) · [PDF](figures/deformed-circle-collar.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/deformed-circle-collar.tex) ## A polynomial encoding each crossing-circle factor ![A local operator on two strands becomes a homogeneous polynomial in its four incident face variables; multiplying these polynomials gives one marked coefficient.](figures/homogeneous-face-source.png) The box \(f(\Omega)\) is the actual local operator, written as a function of the pair Casimir matrix \(\Omega\). The surrounding variables \(x,b,c,y\) name its four incident faces. Its polynomial \(H_f\) has total degree \(d=N-1\), with nonnegative exponents. The coefficients may be complex and retain the original repeated-node derivatives. When local polynomials are multiplied, every shared face uses one shared variable. The marked scalar is the coefficient with exponent \(d\) on each ordinary face and zero on the two marked faces \(u,v\). The total available degree is already exhausted by those targets, which excludes spurious Fourier aliases in this extraction. The [homogeneous formula](../notes/actual_homogeneous_casimir_face_source.md) is exact at every level; a volume limit additionally needs geometry and estimates for this coefficient. ## Classifying maxima of a general coefficient bound ![The shared-degree optimization, its central, one-sided and cap configurations, and a four-step phase constraint around two regions and two faces.](figures/sharp-source-boundary-classification.png) A local coefficient has normalized face degrees \(q\) and spectral parameter \(\delta\). Its exponential upper rate is \(H_\delta(q)\). The diagram first joins these rates while keeping every face demand shared; the resulting maximum is \(M_D\). The central cross region, the two one-sided regions, and the marked cap corner are different portions of the same degree constraints. In the small cycle, squares denote crossing regions and circles denote faces. An edge labeled zero asks for equal phases; an edge labeled one asks for phases differing by \(\pi\). An odd sum around the cycle is inconsistent. The [stationary classification](../notes/research_full_fiber_sharp_stationary_classification.md) and [odd-cycle argument](../notes/research_stationary_noncross_main_cycle_obstruction.md) therefore locate a source of cancellation. They do not quantify enough loss to replace an upper rate larger than the geometric rate \(\Phi_D\). The lower box states that remaining problem for this general-plat method; the strict-tree volume theorem is already proved by another argument. ## Following every term through a switch ![An exact transfer with a before state, two active states and an after state, followed by the two boundary terms and residual of an analytic change of basis.](figures/analytic-source-switching.png) The row number is \(r\). Before entering the active recurrence, a path contributes to \(B_r\); while active it uses the pair \((R_r,R_{r-1})\); after leaving it contributes to \(Z_r\). The direct arrow is essential: it represents a path that starts and stops at the same row. The [four-state identity](../notes/research_original_one_sided_four_state_transfer.md) retains that path, all prefix and suffix factors, and the raw sign. On disjoint regular start and stop windows, a carefully chosen analytic change of basis leaves an exponentially small residual. It also leaves the two displayed boundary terms. Those terms and the multiplying transfer products must still be estimated. The [window theorem](../notes/research_regular_spectral_window_phase_exclusion.md) does this on its stated domain and gives a loss when shared phases cannot align. That loss is relative to the same positive envelope; comparing the envelope with the actual geometric volume is a further condition in this route. ## A color neighborhood and its complement ![A schematic two-dimensional slice of color deficits, with a blue neighborhood of complete colors and an amber complement.](figures/external-color-corridor.png) For auxiliary color \(n_i\), put \(h_i=N-n_i\). The axes show \(h_1/N,h_2/N\), so the origin is complete color. The blue square represents a neighborhood of size \(\delta(D)\) for the fixed diagram \(D\), not a universal numerical width. Within the stated untwisted hypotheses, the full quantum sum agrees with its geometric core up to an exponentially small relative error. Shared-radius certificates give signed versions, and the purple axis illustrates a sufficient local test when one color varies. Near the opposite corner, a complete-circle term has an alias that the original small-color term cancels. Estimating only the former would change the problem. The [external-color discussion](chapters/frontier.md#the-external-color-route-and-its-exact-cancellations) explains why this general-plat corridor is not itself a bound on the whole cube. Whole-cube control has already been established for the strict Conway class and the separately certified families. ## A scalar polynomial inside an operator period ![The polynomial zeros, the Casimir spectral interval and the geometric target occur in different parts of the real spectral axis.](figures/exceptional-period.png) The polynomial \(p_a(z)\) has zeros above two. The matrix \(\Omega\) has its physical spectral nodes in \([-2,2]\), while the marked geometric trace lies at \(z\le-2\). The contour \(\Gamma\) in the displayed formula encloses the matrix spectrum. Integrating \(p_a(z)(zI-\Omega)^{-1}\) gives the full operator \(p_a(\Omega)\), including the information at repeated eigenvalues. This is why a large-degree polynomial cannot simply be replaced by its scalar value at a geometric trace inside a network. The resolvent still carries the surrounding contraction and its derivative terms. Local endpoint packets and the entire central cross-sector filling period are proved; finite shared-radius conditions can then control the remainder. The [current scope](chapters/frontier.md#the-external-color-route-and-its-exact-cancellations) concerns extending such full-period estimates to unrestricted plats, not reopening the volume theorems for the covered classes. ## The exact support wall and complex continuation ![The limiting channel coordinate separates a physical integer-support region from the neighborhood of the exceptional complex geometric frame.](figures/support-wall.png) The coordinate is \(\delta=h/N\), with folded channel \(a/N\to1/2\). At each finite level, entries with integer \(h>a\) vanish exactly. The blue interval indicates the domain of the ordinary physical formula. The amber interval indicates where the exceptional geometric calculation requires a different analytic expression; it is not a claim that forbidden physical entries become nonzero. The displayed finite kernel removes apparent poles and retains all lattice zeros. The [deficient-degree packet](../notes/actual_q_hahn_joint_deficient_degree_packet.md) controls its selected continuation near the actual geometric frame, where the magnetic coordinates are complex. The axis is a limiting schematic, not the exact finite cutoff. This local continuation alone does not control a global contour or its boundary residues. Complete-source and covered-family results use the additional global arguments stated in their theorems. ## Twisting as a local dynamical law ![A generic multiplicative spectral coordinate and a singular additive coordinate describe different fibers of the same twist transport.](figures/casimir-twist-transport.png) The outer face variables \(x,y\) are fixed, and the middle variables evolve as twists are added. The combinations \(A=x+y\) and \(P=xy\) enter the displayed recurrence. Generically, adjoining a root \(\lambda\) of \(\lambda^2+\sigma\lambda+1=0\) gives a coordinate \(a\) that changes by \(a\mapsto\lambda^n a\) under \(n\) signed twists. The norm-one condition relates the two conjugate spectral branches. At the parabolic fiber \(\sigma=-2\), the appropriate coordinate is instead \(t=b-z\), which changes additively by \(2nA\). The lower box is the exact quantum counterpart, retaining its scalar factor and repeated-node data. The [crossing theorem](../notes/actual_crossing_casimir_torus.md) specifies the excluded divisors and the other singular fibers. It gives local transport, not an unrestricted global volume estimate obtained by taking absolute values of each factor. [PDF](figures/casimir-twist-transport.pdf) · [SVG](figures/casimir-twist-transport.svg) · [TikZ source](figures/casimir-twist-transport.tex) ## Primitive filling curves and the square-root choice ![A primitive slope on a torus fundamental domain and the two local sheets of a peripheral square-root cover.](figures/peripheral-torsor.png) The left rectangle is a fundamental domain for a torus. Opposite sides are identified. The amber segments then join into one curve in the primitive class \(\mu+2\lambda\), where \(\mu,\lambda\) are the marked meridian and longitude. The drawing records the slope, not a numerical cusp shape. On the right, \(M=e^U\) and \(L=e^V\) are auxiliary peripheral multipliers. Choosing \(\ell=e^{V/2}\) selects one local sheet of \(\ell^2=L\); the other is \(-\ell\). A half twist acts by an integral monomial transformation on this cover and changes the action by the displayed quadratic term. The technical name torsor records that the two choices differ by a sign without a globally prescribed choice in the unmarked data. The original quantum formula selects the branch tending to one. The [marked filling argument](chapters/geometry.md#half-twists-preserve-the-marked-action-through-a-shear) retains that choice and the primitive equation \(U+pV=-2\pi i\). ## What the cube calculation sums ![Four blue rungs connect two orange four-cycles of a cube graph. The blue labels are summed and the orange labels remain fixed.](figures/cube-channels.png) Each edge label is an intermediate representation index in the quantum calculation. The proved odd-level packet sums all four blue rung indices while holding the eight orange cycle indices fixed. Crossings in this planar projection do not specify overcrossings or undercrossings of a link diagram. The distinction matters because a theorem about this projected sum need not survive an additional signed sum over the orange labels. The [cube results](chapters/results.md#cube-sectors-are-kept-separate) retain that restriction. The drawing shows exactly which calculation is established and which further contraction remains to be controlled in that approach. ## From shared-radius tests to the full invariant ![A chain of statements from the complete endpoint through the central filling period and finite sector tests to a full knot-volume theorem.](figures/shared-entropy-frontier.png) The face variables in this method are shared across the original diagram. The complete endpoint has the actual augmented volume, and the entire central cross-sector Fourier period has a nonzero contribution with the correctly filled volume. The remaining terms occupy other degree sectors. For each branch \(B\) in a finite cover of those sectors, one chooses a single positive face-weight vector \(L^B\) and proves the bound \(G_B(L^B)<\Phi_D\), where \(\Phi_D\) is the complete geometric rate. The [sector-cover theorem](../notes/general_actual_sector_cover_filling_volume.md) shows that these finitely many inequalities suppress the full remainder. The twist weights are fixed before \(N\) grows, and the threshold depends on the fixed diagram. Concrete families satisfy the tests at every fixed bridge width. Universal success of this particular certificate is not asserted. The strict Conway-tree theorem supplies a different complete argument for its own class. ## An exact packing seed for larger bridge width ![A symmetric circle packing in a strip of height two, with mirror pairs of blue disks and an orange chain on the symmetry axis.](figures/symmetric-plat-balance-seed.png) The labels in this drawing denote curvatures, meaning reciprocal radii. The distinct mirror disks \(a_1,b_1\) both have curvature one, and the distinct mirror disks \(a_2,b_2\) both have curvature four. The symbol \(a_3=b_3\) denotes one shared axis disk of curvature nine, not two coincident disks. The upper line is \(a_0=b_0\), and the lower line is \(u\); both lines have curvature zero. The orange chain has curvatures \(9/4,45/16,45/4\). The lower panel uses contact heights \(y_j\) and the ratios \(z_j=\sqrt{1-y_j/y_{j-1}}\). Their exact recurrence permits a convex comparison with translated copies of this seed. The [reduced-layer theorem](../notes/general_reduced_layer_long_filling_volume.md) obtains the needed curvature bound for all fixed widths at least four. A [one-end extension](../notes/general_one_end_layer_long_filling_volume.md), with separate small-width packings, covers widths two and three as well. These are specified families satisfying the full-volume certificate; the packing is not a universal model for every plat of that width. ## Adding a chain in an empty marked strip ![New tangent unit disks are inserted to the right of a fixed packing, between the same two marked horizontal lines.](figures/marked-unit-chain-extension.png) The old disk \(a\) and the old core remain fixed. Every amber disk has radius one and is tangent to the same two lines \(u,v\). The shown case has two insertion steps. In the original braid-slot notation, a chain of length \(m\) adds the prefix \((1,2)^m\), hence \(2m\) new twist regions with independent even signed exponents. The [unit-chain theorem](../notes/general_marked_unit_chain_filling_volume.md) proves that the original source identities and the geometric balance survive this insertion under the stated first-cap marking and slot conditions. It permits every fixed chain length; the required twist threshold may depend on that length. The construction uses the indicated empty gap on the first four strands, not arbitrary stacking across the full braid width. [SVG](figures/marked-unit-chain-extension.svg) · [PDF](figures/marked-unit-chain-extension.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/marked-unit-chain-extension.tex) ## Independent chains in the initial bridge gaps ![Two old tangent disks of curvatures one and four bound an empty gap above a line; new disks of curvatures nine and sixteen are inserted inside it.](figures/each-bridge-gap-chain.png) Only part of the old disk of curvature \(A=1\) is visible. The other old disk has curvature \(B=4\), and the blue line \(u\) has curvature zero. A chain inserted into their empty triangular gap obeys the exact rule \(\sqrt{C_n}=\sqrt B+n\sqrt A\), giving the displayed curvatures nine and sixteen. The square-root relation controls every fixed chain length without moving either boundary disk. The [simultaneous construction](../notes/general_simultaneous_bridge_gap_filling_volume.md) performs this operation separately in each original initial bridge gap. The gaps have disjoint interiors, while any shared old boundary disk remains unchanged. The resulting diagram has \(3k-3+2\sum_jm_j\) independently weighted twist regions. Both the bridge width \(k\) and the depths \(m_j\) are fixed before the quantum limit is taken. [SVG](figures/each-bridge-gap-chain.svg) · [PDF](figures/each-bridge-gap-chain.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/each-bridge-gap-chain.tex) ## A finer certificate can succeed on the same diagram ![One fixed marked seventeen-region expression fails a coarse radius test but satisfies a forty-branch refinement of the same degree constraints.](figures/sector-certificate-separation.png) The diagram and invariant do not change between the panels. The first test fixes one right-sided degree sector and estimates every other region without retaining its sector label. An exact feasible flow proves that no choice of radii can make that coarse bound less than the geometric rate \(\Phi_D\). The refinement keeps genuine sector labels at four specified regions. Fifteen nonempty right-sided choices and twenty-five remaining anchors give forty branches covering every unwanted sector string. Each branch has one shared rational radius vector, and explicit interval bounds leave a gap greater than \(0.04\). The [separation theorem](../notes/actual_shared_radius_certificate_separation.md) therefore proves a full filled-volume result for this example while disproving necessity of the simpler test. It neither changes the knot nor proves that every diagram admits such a cover. [SVG](figures/sector-certificate-separation.svg) · [PDF](figures/sector-certificate-separation.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/sector-certificate-separation.tex) ## A local spectral rearrangement and its possible global use ![A tent-shaped folded angle, its uniform distribution, a proved local energy bound, and a separate sufficient inequality for general diagrams.](figures/spectral-energy-rearrangement.png) The horizontal variable \(t\) runs from zero to one half. For the displayed parameter \(\delta=1/4\), the transformed angle \(t'\) rises and falls as a tent map. The shaded interval is the set where \(t'>u\); its length is \(1/2-u\). The [rearrangement proof](../notes/actual_one_sided_relative_spectral_energy.md) establishes the same distribution for every spectral parameter. Together with the exact coefficient Cauchy inequality at the top, it gives the stated local triangle-entropy bound at both level parities. The amber box asks for a further inequality after all local rates have been joined on the original shared face constraints. That displayed minimum-envelope criterion is sufficient, but is not proved for arbitrary diagrams. The bottom box records the logically separate fact that strict Conway trees and the specified certified plat families already have volume equalities under their own hypotheses. Those theorems do not assert that this particular sufficient inequality holds for every diagram they cover. [SVG](figures/spectral-energy-rearrangement.svg) · [PDF](figures/spectral-energy-rearrangement.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/spectral-energy-rearrangement.tex) ## A weighted Conway tree records composition order ![A rooted tree with one integer twist weight at each vertex, quarter-turns along its edges, and an explicit closure formula.](figures/weighted-conway-tree.png) A vertex carries the integer weight \(n_v\) of an actual twist operator \(R^{n_v}\). Its children are turned and multiplied in the displayed order, giving \(W_v=R^{n_v}\prod_wT(W_w)\). A terminal vertex has no children. The diagram allows both branching and chains with one child; it is an algebraic record of the tangle construction, not a projection of the resulting knot. The literal root closure on the right is part of the definition. Writing \(n_v=\epsilon_v-2p_v\) separates the retained half twist from the signed auxiliary filling parameter. The [weighted-tree theorem](../notes/actual_conway_weighted_tree_long_twist_volume.md) fixes the tree and a knot-producing parity choice, then allows all independent weights beyond its long-twist threshold. It retains the original closure even when a different scalar expression is useful for an estimate. [SVG](figures/weighted-conway-tree.svg) · [PDF](figures/weighted-conway-tree.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/weighted-conway-tree.tex) ## A positive probe estimates a mixed composition ![An actual tangle composition on the left and an auxiliary positive comparison for its polynomial norm on the right.](figures/mixed-conway-probe.png) The amber box \(p_0\) is an actual character coupon. The boxes \(L_i\) are polynomial operators supplied by attached subtrees; the multiplication nodes and turns \(T\) retain their composition order. The shaded connected region has no character coupon of its own. Its output is \(Q=T(A)\), with \(A=L_1T(L_2L_3)\) in this example. The norm \(\|Q_N\|_{\mathcal J}\) records values and first derivatives at the spectral nodes, including repeated ones. The comparison replaces boundary coefficient arrays by their absolute values and closes the resulting expression against the positive polynomial \(W_N\). This polynomial is a device for proving an upper bound, not an additional crossing circle in the knot. The [probe theorem](../notes/actual_conway_unflagged_core_probe_bound.md) controls it at the component's actual geometric action, and the subsequent propagation theorem carries the bound through further operations. This supplies the mixed-composition step in the [strict-tree volume proof](../notes/actual_conway_all_strict_tree_long_twist_volume.md). [SVG](figures/mixed-conway-probe.svg) · [PDF](figures/mixed-conway-probe.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/mixed-conway-probe.tex) ## The preferred longitude after filling crossing circles ![Two fundamental parallelograms of the same filled cusp lattice. The meridian is fixed; the preferred longitude differs from the augmented longitude by four meridians in the illustrated case.](figures/main-cusp-longitude-shear.svg) The blue vector is the image of the augmented longitude on the filled knot cusp. To obtain the preferred longitude, add \(\sum_i p_i\ell_i^2\) meridians, where \(p_i\) is the filling coefficient and \(\ell_i\) is the linking number with crossing circle \(i\). The drawing uses one coefficient \(p=1\) and \(|\ell|=2\), so the orange vector differs by four meridians. The [longitude proof](../notes/actual_main_meridian_preferred_cusp.md) derives this correction in the homology of the actual filled complement. [Vector drawing](figures/main-cusp-longitude-shear.svg) · [PDF](figures/main-cusp-longitude-shear.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/main-cusp-longitude-shear.tex) ## Connected trees of trivalent product junctions ![A path and a branching tree, each with degree three at every bare junction and with circle-operator attachments shown.](figures/trivalent-bare-components.svg) The open vertices are product junctions without a crossing-circle operator. Each has three incident branches, counting the attachments to the filled vertices. These graphs record tangle operations: consecutive unturned products have already been grouped, and every displayed edge is a physical quarter-turn. A fixed tree of any size is allowed by the [trivalent meridian theorem](../notes/actual_main_meridian_trivalent_filled_volume.md). This is a retained special case: the [general component theorem](../notes/actual_main_meridian_general_component_comparison.md) now also permits arbitrary higher-valence junctions and arbitrary mixtures of these valences. [Vector drawing](figures/trivalent-bare-components.svg) · [PDF](figures/trivalent-bare-components.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/trivalent-bare-components.tex)

title: A-polynomial volume limits and torsors: current status
text: # A-polynomial volume limits and torsors: current status The [pointed quantum A-period theorem](actual_conway_pointed_quantum_a_volume.md) reconstructs the reduced Kashaev invariant exactly from its genuine all-level recurrence, finite initial values and the derivative data needed at singular steps. For the covered knot families its volume limit follows from the theorem for that same scalar invariant. The proved families now include the long-net-twist Conway constructions and the [quantitative ordered circle trees](actual_all_circle_quantitative_volume.md). The latter satisfy \(\sum_v d_v/(d_v^2+n_v^2)\le2^{-25}\), with the original knot and framing conditions. title: Volume limits constructed from the A-polynomial
text: # Volume limits constructed from the A-polynomial Research note, 26 October 2026. This is an auxiliary classical A-polynomial volume identity. The intended full route starts with Kashaev's own quantum A-module or torsor and uses its structure to prove the invariant's volume growth. This classical construction calibrates the geometric period; it does not replace that actual invariant. Jones is separate. Here is a direct classical construction. It produces marked roots of integer polynomials built from the A-equation by finite-algebra norms, with a proved volume limit on the stated connected geometric class. The remaining choices are a marked curve, path and sampling. No standard quantum A-state is claimed for this construction. It is a discretization of the existing classical regulator, not a claim to have proved the original Kashaev conjecture or to have discovered the regulator identity. ## 1. Conventions and the relative period Use the squared peripheral functions m,l of [the marked regulator note](boundary_regulator_period.md). In SL_2 eigenvalues M,L these are m=M^2,l=L^2, with the recorded orientation of the longitude. Write the corresponding geometric A-equation as A(m,l)=0. It is obtained from the ordinary eigenvalue A-polynomial by its stated finite monomial image, not by renaming M as M^2 without elimination. Let C be a connected marked algebraic curve of representations or a finite augmented cover, containing the geometric and conjugate complete points p_+,p_-. Let beta be its rational crossing or triangulation Bloch class. The already proved boundary identity and complete fundamental-class values are delta beta=-(1/2)m wedge l, D(beta)(p_+)=Vol(X), D(beta)(p_-)=-Vol(X). (1.1) They follow from the actual [boundary-wedge calculation](marked_braid_holonomy.md#8-a-global-boundary-wedge-and-complete-frame-regulator-rigidity) and [fundamental-cycle calculation](crossing_fundamental_cycle.md). No selected quantum state is a premise. Put eta=log|l| darg m-log|m| darg l. The elementary Bloch--Wigner derivative is dD(z)=log|z|darg(1-z)-log|1-z|darg z. Applying it to (1.1) gives dD(beta)=eta/2. Consequently every piecewise C^1 path gamma from p_- to p_+, avoiding the finite shape and coordinate divisors, has integral_gamma eta=4 Vol(X). (1.2) The normalized complete places must be retained: their peripheral coordinate pairs can coincide even though their regulator values differ. This fixes the absolute volume by two specified endpoints, without a zero-volume reference. If C is finite over a normalized A-component, its real primitive descends. Pass to a connected Galois closure. A deck transformation changes the primitive by a constant, since it fixes eta. Its finite order makes that constant zero. Thus the primitive is invariant and descends on the common regular open curve. This is an elementary finite-cover descent argument; it does not concern a quantum state. ## 2. Integer products of A-roots Parametrize gamma on [0,1]. Choose continuous argument lifts theta=arg m, phi=arg l along it. For large N put r=floor(sqrt(N)), h=2pi/N, t_j=j/r. For each interval choose an algebraic point q_(N,j) on C within N^(-2) of gamma((j+1/2)/r), in a fixed finite collection of regular coordinate charts. Such points exist: use a local finite algebraic projection and approximate its regular value by an algebraic number. Avoid its finitely many ramification and coefficient exceptions. Set m_j=m(q_(N,j)), l_j=l(q_(N,j)), a_j=nearest_integer((theta(t_(j+1))-theta(t_j))/h), b_j=nearest_integer((phi(t_(j+1))-phi(t_j))/h), Z_N=product_(j=0)^(r-1) l_j^(a_j) m_j^(-b_j). (2.1) Fix either convention at a rounding tie. These are finite algebraic evaluations with integer exponents; no volume value occurs in their definition. All pairs satisfy the A-equation, with the branch specified by gamma. **Theorem.** Under Section 1's connectedness and marking hypotheses, lim_(N->infinity) [pi/(2N)]log|Z_N|=Vol(X). (2.2) **Proof.** Logs of the moduli are bounded on the compact path. Integer rounding changes h log|Z_N| by O(r/N). Replacing the midpoint values by their algebraic approximants changes it by o(1); the total argument variation is bounded. The remaining sum is the midpoint Riemann sum for integral eta. Its error tends to zero for a piecewise C^1 path. For a C^2 path the total error is O(r^(-1)+r/N+N^(-2)), hence O(N^(-1/2)). Equation (1.2), and h/4=pi/(2N), prove (2.2). The limit is independent of the allowed path, samples and rounding choices because eta has the stated real primitive. The finite values need not be independent of those choices. ## 3. A polynomial defined by norms, not just an informal root product Here is an explicit polynomial containing the marked value Z_N. Let F_N be a number field containing the coefficients of A and the sampled meridians m_j. Require only that the leading and constant l-coefficients at each sample are nonzero; finite exceptional sample points can be avoided. Normalize each A(m_j,L_j) to be monic and form E_N=tensor_(j,F_N) F_N[L_j]/(A(m_j,L_j)). It is a finite algebra. Each L_j is a unit. Let H_N=product_j L_j^(a_j)m_j^(-b_j) in E_N, Q_N(T)=det(T-Mult_(H_N)) in F_N[T], P_N(T)=primitive_integer_multiple of Norm_(F_N/Q)(Q_N(T)).
