For an unflagged component (10), if \(f_{F_i}=g+c_i\), then \[ \Omega_Q=\sum_i c_i+ F_{\mathrm{probe}}\bigl(C(hA(h,\ldots,h))\bigr). \tag{13} \] The quantity \(F_{\mathrm{probe}}\) is the complete positive action of the displayed reference expression. This extra reference leaf is a tool for a variational comparison; it is not a crossing circle inserted into the original knot. The [probe geometry](actual_conway_unflagged_probe_geometry.md) proves (13) from the boundary equations with their signs retained before squaring. At the chosen root, the source and its complete action are \[ Z_N^\epsilon=\phi(P_0\prod_jQ_j). \tag{14} \] and \[ F_0=\sum_j\Omega_{Q_j}. \tag{15} \] Here \(\phi\) is the linear closing functional of the finite tangle algebra. To see the action identity, the corresponding type-\(H\) profile is \(g(1-z)+\sum_j\Omega_{Q_j}\). The coefficient-one closing endpoint is \(z=1\), which gives (15); the complementary root relation gives the same maximum directly. Thus every rate used for a subtree is accounted for in the original \(F_0\), rather than being added to an unrelated upper envelope. ## 4. A positive comparison for an unflagged component Set \(d=N-1\) and \(M=\lfloor d/2\rfloor\). Let \(e_r=\widehat B_r\) be the normalized Newton basis of the repeated-root algebra. Its turn and its closing pairing satisfy the exact identities \[ Te_r=e_{d-r},\qquad \phi(e_re_s)=\mathbf1_{r+s=d}. \tag{16} \] The notation \([e_r]F\) means the coefficient of \(e_r\) in \(F\). The norm \(\|F\|_{\mathcal J}\) records all spectral values and first derivatives at double nodes, and the value at the odd simple node. It therefore controls the full operator data required by the source. Introduce \[ w_{N,r}= \begin{cases}e_r(-2),&r\le M,\\1,&r>M,\end{cases} \qquad W_N=\sum_{r=0}^d w_{N,r}e_r. \tag{17} \] These weights satisfy \(\|e_r\|_{\mathcal J}\le N^Cw_{N,r}\), with low-degree rate \(\log w_{N,r}=Ng(r/N)+O(\log N)\). In this section, “low” means \(r\le M\) and “high” means \(r>M\). These are basis-degree ranges, not yet the physical core and alias terms of a colored leaf. The [positive probe theorem](actual_conway_unflagged_core_probe_bound.md) applies to arbitrary arrays of boundary coefficients satisfying \[ |[e_r]F_i|\le \exp N(c_i+o(1)) \begin{cases}w_{N,r},&r\le M,\\1,&r>M.\end{cases} \tag{18} \] The errors are uniform over the ranges in question. Replace the boundary coefficients by their absolute values and use the same circuit; call the result \(A^{\mathrm{abs}}\). Newton multiplication has nonnegative structure constants. Together with the exact reversal in (16), this gives \[ \|T(A)\|_{\mathcal J} \le N^C\sum_r w_{N,r}|[e_{d-r}]A| \le N^C\phi(W_NA^{\mathrm{abs}}). \tag{19} \] Every high-degree normal direction is included. The final scalar is nonnegative and retains the original support and closing target, so the comparison does not amount to independently maximizing the factors. ![A source component and its separate positive norm comparison. The probe belongs to the estimate and does not add a crossing circle to the knot.](../book/figures/mixed-conway-probe.png) The low input and probe coefficients on the right of (19) have profile \(g\); the high coefficients have profile zero. They are bounded by the profiles \[ \widetilde g(x)=g(\max(x,1/4)),\qquad k(x)=-2J(x/2), \tag{20} \] used in the earlier block estimates. The closed comparison has no flagged junction. It is either the isolated effective three-leaf closure or a regrouping of the completed-root source. The two-leaf and single-attachment inequalities can be applied to these arbitrary arrays because their proofs use only the upper profiles, positive multiplication, the exact support inequalities and cancellation of the supporting tangents at the stationary state. They do not require that the arrays themselves came from a particular physical color. It follows that (19) has upper rate \(\Omega_Q\) from (13). A high boundary index or a high probe index has a strict exponential loss. If all indices are low, the action has the original unique strict maximum, so the complement of any fixed neighborhood also has a loss. The finite \(N-1\) offsets, both parities and the polynomial number of summands are included. No physical alias identity has been asserted for these artificial comparison bands. The [spectral propagation theorem](actual_conway_mixed_core_spectral_propagation.md) strengthens the norm bound to \[ \begin{aligned} \|Q_N\|_{\mathcal J}&\le \exp N(\Omega_Q+o(1)),\\ |Q_N(2\cos(\theta+iy))| &\le \exp N\{\Omega_Q-c(\theta-\pi)^2+Cy^2+o(1)\}. \end{aligned} \tag{21} \] on a fixed small strip in the complex angular variable. The canonical representative is the specified polynomial representative of the finite algebra. The point \(\theta=\pi\) corresponds to spectral value \(-2\); the negative quadratic term measures localization there. Near the all-low maximizing probe index, the Newton polynomial has this strict angular Gaussian. The rest already has a norm gap, which absorbs the Hermite interpolation cost \(\exp(N|y|)\) after shrinking the strip. There is also a loss-transfer statement. Suppose a boundary module has a fixed coefficient deficit on a compact interval around its index in the all-low maximizing state. That deficit gives a strict loss in \(\|Q_N\|_{\mathcal J}\). Outside the interval, the all-low action already has a gap, and high sectors have their separate gap. This is how a physical color deficit can pass through the unflagged component. The argument does not assert a uniform estimate at this smaller rate for an arbitrary turn applied to an arbitrary polynomial. ## 5. Induction over the tree and all physical colors The other induction step is supplied by the [decorated-character theorem](actual_conway_decorated_character_spectral_closure.md). A character is the crossing-circle operator \(L_j\), and “decorated” means that the actual input \(E\) is attached before the turn. If \(E\) has norm upper rate \(c\), then \[ |[e_r]D_j^\epsilon[E]|\le N^C\|E\|_{\mathcal J} \begin{cases}w_{N,r},&r\le M,\\1,&r>M.\end{cases} \tag{22} \] The output norm has rate at most \(c+2G_0\) and its canonical polynomial has the corresponding angular Gaussian. A norm deficit already present in \(E\) passes to every output coefficient. One must also control the color \(j\) of the newly introduced character. The exact root-character Fourier estimate gives, on every fixed compact interval \(I\subset(0,1/2)\), \[ N-j\ge\delta N,\quad r/N\in I \quad\Longrightarrow\quad |[e_r]D_j^\epsilon[E]| \le \exp N\{c+g(r/N)-\eta_{\delta,I}\}, \qquad \eta_{\delta,I}>0, \tag{23} \] when \(E\) has the inherited strip envelope; \(E=1\) is allowed. This estimate keeps the normal terms and the exact cancellation of the folded Fourier frequency. Its validity on every such compact interval, rather than just near \(1/4\), matters because a boundary module of an unflagged component need not have quarter index in the effective maximizing state. We can now proceed from the leaves to the flagged root. Products add the established norm rates and multiply the strip envelopes. A flagged step (9) uses (22)–(23) and the absolute constant in (12). An unflagged step (10) uses (19)–(21) and the intrinsic action (13). A deficit in an older descendant travels by its norm loss. A deficit in the distinguished character of a boundary module travels first by (23), then by the all-low localization from §4. This accounts for each physical color of the original expression. At the root (14), the unturned character has only polynomial cost in the closing functional. A far descendant is handled by its propagated norm loss. If the root color itself is far from \(N\), apply the exact Fourier theorem to the product of the attached representatives, which has the inherited angular envelope. Equation (15) identifies the reference rate with \(F_0\). There are finitely many original colors, so taking the minimum of their positive margins gives one \(\gamma_\delta>0\). This proves (8). The flag-free cases and the strict two-leaf knot case were already covered by the inputs stated in §3. Therefore (8) holds for every presentation in the theorem, including arbitrary mixtures of flagged and unflagged junctions. ## 6. Restoring the selected packet and performing the fillings The comparison bands used in §4 are now replaced by the exact physical identity at each original leaf: \[ h_j^\epsilon=C_j^\epsilon+(-1)^Nh_{N-j}^\epsilon \quad(j>N/2),\qquad h_0^\epsilon=0. \tag{24} \] The term \(C_j^\epsilon\) is the selected core; it is zero for \(j\le N/2\). By multilinearity, the all-core contraction differs from the whole source by finitely many terms with at least one color at most \(N/2\). Estimate (8) with \(\delta=1/2\) makes their total exponentially smaller. This is the [complementary-color principle](actual_conway_weighted_tree_long_twist_volume.md), §4, applied to the physical leaves, not to the auxiliary coefficient bands. The general core theorem consequently gives \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal C_N(\chi) &=N^{3/2}a_\epsilon(\chi)e^{N\Phi_\epsilon(\chi)} (1+O(N^{-1})),\\ a_\epsilon(0)&\ne0,\qquad \Phi_\epsilon(0)=F_0,\\ Z_N^\epsilon(\mathbf N-\mathbf h) &=\eta_N\mathcal C_N(\mathbf h/N) +O\!\left(N^Ce^{N(F_0-\gamma)}\right),\\ \eta_N&=\exp\!\left(\frac{i\pi(N-1)}4\sum_i\epsilon_i\right). \end{aligned} \tag{25} \] A packet is this uniform local asymptotic: a holomorphic exponential action, a nonzero leading amplitude and a controlled error. The action is separately even in the color deficits, and the packet is defined on a fixed complex neighborhood. Its comparison with \(Z_N^\epsilon\) is asserted at the actual integer colors \(\mathbf N-\mathbf h\); the unit phase \(\eta_N\) has not been dropped. The color Hessian is \[ \partial_i\partial_j\Phi_\epsilon(0) =-\frac{2\pi \nu_i}{1-\epsilon_i i \nu_i}\delta_{ij}, \qquad \nu_i=\cot(\pi a_i)>0. \tag{26} \] where \(a_i\) is the complete normalized index of leaf \(i\). Its real part is negative definite. Every such leaf has \(a_i\ge1/4\), so the established high-index and quarter-index packet estimates cover all leaves. For \(H=2\), the both-odd patterns have two main components; the knot patterns contain the pure leaf required by the two-leaf core theorem. The [source long-filling transfer](general_original_source_long_filling_transfer.md) applies to (8) and (25). Its exact Fourier–Hermite circle-basis identity inserts \(R^{\epsilon_i-2p_i}\) in the same leaf frame, giving the rational tangle (2). For each fixed filling tuple the coefficient mass is polynomial in \(N\), so the global exponential error remains negligible. For independently sufficiently long fixed signed slopes, the transfer gives a nonzero leading amplitude with selected exponent \[ S_{\epsilon,\mathbf p}(\chi_*) =\Phi_\epsilon(\chi_*)+ \frac{\pi i}{2}\sum_i\frac{(\chi_{*,i}-1)^2}{p_i}, \qquad dS_{\epsilon,\mathbf p}(\chi_*)=0. \tag{27} \] The point \(\chi_*\) is the critical point of the displayed filling action. The theorem controls the whole transform, including endpoint currents and nonzero Fourier charges; it does not assign a contribution to a formal saddle without checking its contour. ## 7. Identifying the exponent with the knot complement volume The geometric identification uses the original tangle presentation, not a rearranged comparison circuit. The marked geometric theorem constructs its nearby augmented-link representation with primitive peripheral logarithms and the calibrated complex-volume primitive \[ U_i=-2\pi i\chi_i,\qquad V_i=-2\partial_i\Phi_\epsilon,\qquad G=2\pi i\Phi_\epsilon,\qquad \operatorname{Vol}(\rho_\chi)= \Im G-\frac12\sum_i\Re U_i\Im V_i. \tag{28} \] Here \(U_i,V_i\) are the meridian and longitude logarithms in the stated convention. The function \(G\) is the regulator primitive; its imaginary part, with the displayed boundary correction, is the representation volume. The stationary equations in (27) become \[ U_i+p_iV_i=-2\pi i. \tag{29} \] The marked metric completion gives a primitive angular turn of \(2\pi\) and hence a smooth complete finite-volume metric on the exterior obtained by these disk fillings. Every auxiliary crossing-circle cusp is filled to insert its twists. The main knot cusp stays unfilled. At this solution, \[ 2\pi\Re S_{\epsilon,\mathbf p}(\chi_*) =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K_\tau(\mathbf n)). \tag{30} \] There are finitely many auxiliary cusps, so one common neighborhood in the reciprocal filling slopes suffices. Combining its geometric threshold with the analytic transfer threshold proves (4). The [one-cut normalization](actual_complete_augmented_source_normalization.md) contributes its specified polynomial factor and unit framing character, neither of which changes the logarithmic limit. ## 8. Scope of the conclusion The theorem includes the earlier completed-root and weighted-tree families and all strict mixtures of their source junctions. The finite test is (3), equivalently at most one flagged leaf per reduced hub. Branching, valence and depth may be arbitrary finite quantities. The argument does not require a character at every hub. The earlier manuscript retains its stated completed-root theorem. This extension uses the existing exact two-leaf and single-attachment certificates together with the probe and spectral propagation arguments above. It does not replace their proofs by numerical asymptotics. The linked notes provide the detailed local estimates used in the assembly. The [pointed quantum \(A\)-period corollary](actual_conway_pointed_quantum_a_volume.md) combines (4) with the all-level ADO annihilator and finite-pointing theorems. It expresses the same limit through a genuine recurrence operator, its fixed initial data and bounded-order derivatives in the quantum parameter. The result does not classify every arborescent presentation, provide a threshold uniform over growing trees, or establish a short-twist theorem. Identifying the selected classical main-meridian geometric factor and its quantum module with the marked regulator germ is a further problem. The source identities used for estimates do not assert tangle isotopies: the original expression supplies its own packet and marked geometry in §§6–7.

title: Volume limits after reducing a Conway tangle closure
text: # Volume limits after reducing a Conway tangle closure 31 October 2026. The earlier net-twist theorem starts with a cylindrical closure of a product. Here the input may have either of the two usual closures, may begin with a turn, and may contain twist sums that vanish exactly. Cutting along the resulting two-punctured spheres decomposes the knot into factors. When the remaining non-elementary factors have sufficiently large net twists, a hyperbolic input must be isotopic to just one of them. This gives a broader criterion for recognizing covered presentations. Every knot it admits is explicitly isotopic to a long strict knot from the earlier theorem. The argument does not establish a new estimate for short twists or enlarge that previously covered set of knot types. The proof has three distinct inputs. First, actual ordered tangle moves give a componentwise connected-sum decomposition. Second, the established strict-presentation theorem identifies each sufficiently long strict knot factor as hyperbolic and proves its volume limit. Third, an elementary group argument shows that a hyperbolic input knot cannot have two nontrivial factors of these known types. Consequently it is isotopic to one long strict factor. No quantum connected-sum formula is needed. ## 1. The fixed construction and the conclusion A two-string tangle consists of two arcs with four prescribed boundary endpoints in a ball; closed components, if a composition creates them, must also be retained. The endpoints have the original cyclic order. Let \(R^n\) be the integral two-braid with signed crossing number \(n\), let \(T\) rotate the ball through a quarter-turn, and put \(h_i(n_i)=T(R^{n_i})\). Form a finite expression \(E\) from the labelled pieces \(h_i\), quarter-turns, and ordered vertical stacking. Each label occurs once. Allow either cylindrical closure \(C(E)\), joining the upper endpoints to their corresponding lower endpoints, or cap closure \(D(E)=C(TE)\), joining each upper pair and each lower pair. Fix the expression, with \(m\ge1\) labelled pieces, and its closing operation before choosing the integer tuple \(\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_m)\). For a nonempty label set \(B\), write $$ W_B(\mathbf n)=\sum_{i\in B}n_i. \tag{1} $$ Apply the deterministic topological reduction described in Section 2. It returns a tree of componentwise connected sums of: 1. strict literal cylindrical product presentations, with nonzero net weights attached to disjoint label blocks; 2. integral braid closures \(C(R^s)\); 3. unknots \(D(R^s)\). Numerical-zero blocks removed during the reduction are also recorded. Thus surviving and deleted blocks partition the original labels. The strict factors use the finite \(L,H,A\) test of the existing theorem. Each basic piece starts with label \(L\). The labels record intervals of possible normalized output states in the angle calculation: \(L=(0,1/2)\), \(H=(1/2,1)\), and \(A=(0,1)\). They are not twist numbers. A turn \(T\) exchanges \(L,H\) and fixes \(A\); products \(LL,LA,AA\) have type \(A\), products \(HL,HA\) have type \(H\), and \(HH\) is forbidden. A closing product must have types \(AA,AL,AH,LH\), in either order. **Theorem.** There is a finite number \(B_E\), depending only on the fixed expression and the choice \(C\) or \(D\), with the following property. Fix any integer tuple \(\mathbf n\). Suppose: * the literal filled input is a hyperbolic knot \(K\); * every net weight on every surviving strict factor of the specified reduction satisfies \(|W_B(\mathbf n)|>B_E\). Then the reduction has exactly one strict factor. Every other terminal factor is an unknot, and \(K\) is ambient isotopic to that strict factor. In particular, $$ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N}\log|K_N(K)| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K). \tag{2} $$ The invariant is the existing reduced enhanced Kashaev invariant with unknot value one. The limit includes both parities and composite levels. All weights, their zero relations, and the knot are fixed before \(N\) tends to infinity. Their signs and relative sizes are unrestricted. No lower bound is imposed on weights carried only by elementary terminal factors. The hypothesis on the strict factors is not a claim that short surviving strict weights can be ignored. ## 2. The actual reductions and their termination The required topological algorithm is the optional reduction in [the ordered net-twist theorem](actual_conway_net_twist_volume.md), Appendices A and B. Its essential moves are recalled to make clear which topology, rather than scalar source algebra, is used. Write \(\tau=T^2\) for the actual planar half-turn. It reverses the order of a stack and is retained on subexpressions. Rotation about the stacking axis is denoted \(\rho\). The empty-collar isotopy and the original closed pairing give $$ R^aF\simeq \rho^a(F)R^a,\qquad R^aR^b\simeq R^{a+b},\qquad C((TF)G)\simeq C(F(TG)). \tag{3} $$ The first move rotates the intervening tangle; it does not assert that the tangle is invariant under that rotation. The rotation depends only on the parity of \(a\), preserves crossing signs, and is pushed through the ordered syntax by the actual rotation identities. The closed pairing in the last move has its recorded reflection and no extra boundary twist. Cyclically moving the cut in the closed cylinder also gives \(C(FG)\simeq C(GF)\). To expose a selected leaf, follow its path to the root. Associativity and closed cyclicity transfer each sibling into the other factor; the last identity of (3) transfers every encountered turn. This terminates at a form \(C(h_iQ)\), retaining every other leaf exactly once and recording every induced order. If the selected weight is zero, $$ C(h_i(0)Q)\simeq D(Q). \tag{4} $$ This uses \(h_i(0)=T(R^0)\), the cup-cap tangle; it is not the through-identity tangle. At a cap-closed root one has $$ D(TF)=C(\tau F),\qquad D(FG)=D(F)\mathbin{\#}D(G). \tag{5} $$ In the second operation, the upper-cap component of \(D(F)\) is joined to the lower-cap component of \(D(G)\). The horizontal empty collar contains a sphere meeting the link in exactly two points. Cutting it and capping its punctures gives the two stated cap closures. Hence this is an exhibited componentwise connected sum, with its components and marks specified. It is not a four-punctured Conway mutation. ![The sphere around the lower tangle and its bottom cap meets the two connecting strands. Cutting and capping gives the two specified cap closures.](../book/figures/conway-cap-splitting.png) The diagram uses bottom-to-top stacking: \(F\) is below \(G\). The amber arcs are the new upper cap of \(F\) and lower cap of \(G\). Joining along these arcs reconstructs the original stack. This specifies the connected sum even when a cap closure has more than one component. For a cylindrical product, the established ordered normalization gathers direct integral factors using (3), fuses them, and records their disjoint label unions. Any resulting zero weight can be removed by (4). With no remaining zeros, its output is strict or is one integral braid closure. The possible failed \(LL\) closing pair is resolved by $$ C((TU)(TV))\simeq C(U(\tau V)), \tag{6} $$ which exposes two integral factors for a genuine fusion. Root turns switch \(C\) and \(D\), retaining \(\tau\) where (5) requires it. A single box terminates in one of $$ C(R^s),\quad D(R^s),\quad C(h(s))=D(R^s),\quad D(h(s))=C(R^s). \tag{7} $$ Here \(C(R^s)\) is the \((2,s)\) torus braid closure and \(D(R^s)\) is an unknot. The latter isotopy moves successive crossings into the end cap and removes curls. Any ribbon framing is transported and recorded, not silently replaced by a blackboard convention. At \(s=0\), \(C(R^0)\) is the two-component unlink. The one-box rule is applied before a numerical-zero deletion. In particular a last zero box terminates as the appropriate unknot or two-component unlink in (7); it is not removed to create an unspecified empty scalar or an unrecorded component. Fix a rule for selecting the next operation; for example, give the one-box rule priority, process the root closure next, and choose the first eligible leaf or stack in the written order for the remaining steps. Use this same rule for every integer assignment. Every fusion or zero deletion lowers the number of live labelled blocks. Between such events, shortening turn chains, flattening stacks, and processing cap roots removes vertices from the finite expression forest. Exposing a chosen zero follows a finite path without copying its siblings. Thus the process terminates. Connected-sum edges form a tree because each arises by splitting one pending factor into two; rotations and later reductions act within these factors and retain the attaching arcs. ## 3. Finitely many output types and one threshold The algorithm only tests two kinds of integer data: $$ \bigl(n_i\bmod2\bigr)_{i=1}^m,\qquad \bigl(\mathbf 1_{W_B(\mathbf n)=0}\bigr)_{ \varnothing\ne B\subset\{1,\ldots,m\}}. \tag{8} $$ The first determines every \(\rho^{W_B}\) decoration. The second determines every numerical-zero deletion. Rotations preserve the signs of the integral crossings, fusion takes an ordinary sum, and no step copies a label. Every integer expression tested is consequently one of the subset sums (1), not an unbounded new family of linear forms. There are finitely many patterns (8), although some are not realized by integer tuples. On each realized pattern, the chosen schedule, ordered output templates, attaching components, and surviving/deleted label blocks are fixed. Their integer weights remain the displayed linear forms. In particular, approaching another zero wall may change the partition, but there are only finitely many such possibilities. Let \(\mathcal S_E\) be the finite set of strict terminal templates that occur among the realized patterns. For each template \(\sigma\), the existing [strict-tree theorem](actual_conway_all_strict_tree_long_twist_volume.md) supplies a finite threshold \(B(\sigma)\), uniform over its independently signed weights and its knot-producing parity choices. Set $$ B_E=\max\!\left(\{2\}\cup \{B(\sigma):\sigma\in\mathcal S_E\}\right). \tag{9} $$ This maximum is finite. It gives a single threshold for the fixed input, over all input parities and all subset-sum zero patterns. It is an existence and finite-reduction statement; no effective numerical algorithm for the analytic thresholds is added here. ## 4. A knot input makes every terminal factor a knot Retain all closed components throughout the reductions. If \(c_v\ge1\) is the number of components of terminal factor \(v\), and the decomposition tree has \(r\) vertices, componentwise connected sum gives $$ c(K)=\sum_v c_v-(r-1) =1+\sum_v(c_v-1). \tag{10} $$ Thus a one-component input forces \(c_v=1\) for every factor. In particular, no even-\(s\) torus braid closure or two-component zero closure can occur among the terminal factors of the knot. Within a terminal tangle expression, a circle already closed in a subtree cannot reconnect to an outside endpoint. The remaining two arcs still close to at least one other component. Therefore a terminal knot has no such internal circle. Its whole component test, including these circles, satisfies the hypothesis of the strict-tree theorem. By (9) and the assumed longness, every strict terminal factor is a hyperbolic knot with the established volume limit. A terminal elementary knot is either an unknot or a \((2,s)\) torus knot with odd \(|s|\ge3\). No assertion is being made about the primeness of an unknown short strict factor: the longness hypothesis has removed that case. ## 5. The group obstruction to two nontrivial factors Let \(\mu\) denote a knot meridian. Its class generates the infinite cyclic abelianization, so its cyclic subgroup is infinite and injective. Van Kampen applied to the meridional annulus of a connected sum gives $$ \pi_1(X_{K_1\#K_2}) \cong \pi_1(X_{K_1})*_{\langle\mu\rangle}\pi_1(X_{K_2}), \tag{11} $$ where the two meridians are identified, with their orientation carried through the attaching arcs. Iterating over the exhibited sum tree gives the analogous amalgam of all factor groups over the same infinite cyclic subgroup. The usual reduced-word proof for an amalgam injects each factor group. If \(u\) and \(v\) belong to different factor groups and neither belongs to \(\langle\mu\rangle\), the word $$ uvu^{-1}v^{-1} \tag{12} $$ is a reduced word of length four, and is not the identity. Each nontrivial factor in Section 4 has an element outside \(\langle\mu\rangle\) which commutes with \(\mu\). For a long hyperbolic factor, take its preferred longitude. Its complete rank-two cusp injects the peripheral \(\mathbb Z^2\) into the group, so the longitude is not a power of the meridian. For a \((2,s)\) torus knot, odd \(|s|\ge3\), use its central fiber. Here is an argument independent of a longitude sign convention. The two solid tori on either side of the standard torus, joined through the annulus left by the knot neighborhood, give $$ G_s=\langle a,b\mid a^2=b^s\rangle,\qquad z=a^2=b^s. \tag{13} $$ The annulus winds twice around one core and \(s\) times around the other, which gives this relation. The element \(z\) is central. Abelianization is infinite cyclic, with \([a]=s t\), \([b]=2t\), and \([z]=2s t\). A meridian has class \(\pm t\). The quotient by \(\langle z\rangle\) is \(C_2*C_{|s|}\). Its abelianization is cyclic of order \(2|s|\), and the image of any meridian is a generator of that abelianization. A finite-order element in a free product is conjugate into a factor: after cyclic reduction, a word of length at least two has powers of strictly increasing reduced length. Its finite order would therefore divide \(2\) or \(|s|\), incompatible with abelianization order \(2|s|\). The image of \(\mu\) in this quotient has infinite order. It follows that \(z\notin\langle\mu\rangle\). Indeed \(z=\mu^k\) would force \(k=\pm2s\) in abelianization and then force a nonzero power of the infinite-order image of \(\mu\) to vanish in the quotient. More strongly, a relation \(\mu^u z^v=1\) first gives \(u=0\) in the quotient and then \(v=0\) by abelianization. Thus \(\langle\mu,z\rangle\cong\mathbb Z^2\). This proves the precise commuting-element fact needed below without assuming a peripheral injection theorem for torus knots. In conventional oriented torus coordinates the preferred longitude is \(z\mu^{-2s}\), because the torus push-off has linking number \(2s\); that additional identification is not used. Now suppose two terminal factors are nontrivial. Choose the elements just constructed in their two groups. They both commute with the common meridian, while (12) proves that they do not commute with each other. Hence the centralizer of \(\mu\) in the input knot group is nonabelian. This is impossible for the hyperbolic input. Its faithful complete holonomy sends a meridian to a nontrivial parabolic. Conjugate this parabolic to \(z\mapsto z+1\). A Möbius transformation commuting with it must fix its unique point at infinity and have the form \(z\mapsto z+c\). Such transformations commute. Faithfulness therefore makes the meridian centralizer in the knot group abelian. There is at most one nontrivial terminal factor. ## 6. Selecting the strict factor and transporting the conclusion If every factor were an unknot, the input would be an unknot. If its only nontrivial factor were a torus knot, the input would be that torus knot. The first has cyclic group. The second has the nontrivial central element \(z\) of (13), so neither can be a finite-volume hyperbolic knot. For completeness, the center of such a hyperbolic knot group is trivial: a central element commutes with the peripheral parabolic group and is itself a translation fixing that cusp point; centrality would force every group element to commute with this nontrivial translation. The same Möbius calculation then makes every element a translation. A discrete translation group has an infinite-volume quotient of all of hyperbolic three-space, even when its quotient horospheres are compact. It cannot be the complete finite-volume knot group. Consequently the unique nontrivial factor is strict, and all other terminal factors are unknots. Connected sum with each exhibited unknot is removed by straightening the trivial summing arc across its spanning disk. This gives an actual orientation-preserving ambient isotopy from the input knot to the one strict terminal knot \(K_*\). Restricting that isotopy to transported tubular neighborhoods gives a homeomorphism of exteriors carrying the meridian and preferred zero-linking longitude. Pull back the already constructed complete hyperbolic metric of \(S^3\setminus K_*\); this supplies the same complete metric and volume on the input complement. There is no attempt to identify the different augmented exteriors before auxiliary filling. The reduced enhanced Kashaev invariant is the invariant of this same zero-framed knot, so \(K_N(K)=K_N(K_*)\) at every level. If ribbon framings are kept during the moves, their correction is the existing unit complete-color twist; zero-framing removes it, and its modulus would not change the logarithmic rate in any event. The full one-cut modified value retains its single factor $$ \mathcal N_N(K;1)=\frac{i^{N+3}}{N}K_N(K). \tag{14} $$ Apply the inherited strict-tree volume theorem to \(K_*\). These exact identifications prove (2). Neither multiplicativity of \(K_N\) nor additivity of quantum exponential rates over a connected sum is used. ## 7. Scope of the extension The conclusion applies to either closing operation on every fixed finite expression made by the stated actual Conway operations, including initial root turns and all numerical-zero walls. The prescribed reduction and the uniform threshold account for all their finitely many parity and zero patterns. The hypothesis that the original filled link is a hyperbolic knot is essential to this argument. For a composite input, two long strict factors can remain, and (12) correctly detects the obstruction. No new quantum connected-sum theorem has been proved here. Long written twists alone do not imply the hypothesis on surviving strict weights: opposite large twists can cancel. Conversely, original weights or intermediate sums may be zero; only final weights in strict terminal factors must satisfy (9). The theorem does not give a short-twist assertion or a threshold uniform over growing expressions. The topological input is the actual ordered normalization and its two-punctured cap spheres, not the commutativity of the colored source. The analytic and geometric long-filling theorem is inherited for the strict terminal presentation. The new step is the finite all-root reduction together with the group argument forcing a hyperbolic input to equal one of those known strict knots. ## 8. A finite topological criterion and simple conditions on the integers The reduction itself requires no hyperbolic metric. It uses the ordered tangle expression, its endpoint connections, and the integer sums in (1). Under the longness assumption of the theorem, its output also determines whether a knot input is hyperbolic: **Corollary 1.** Suppose the input has one component and every surviving strict-factor weight has magnitude greater than \(B_E\). The input is hyperbolic if and only if its reduction has exactly one strict factor and every other terminal factor is an unknot. Indeed, the forward implication is Sections 4–6. For the reverse implication, straighten the summing arcs of the unknot factors. The resulting knot is the long strict factor, whose complete hyperbolic metric is supplied by the strict-tree theorem. The elementary factors are explicit. A factor \(D(R^s)\) is always an unknot. A factor \(C(R^s)\) is a knot only for odd \(s\), and among those knots it is an unknot exactly when \(s=1\) or \(s=-1\). Consequently the reduction gives a finite topological test once the longness hypotheses have been established. Determining whether an elementary factor is trivial requires these tests for \(s=\pm1\), in addition to the parity and zero tests used to choose the output templates. No numerical values for the inherited analytic thresholds are supplied by this argument. There is also a sufficient condition stated entirely in the original integer parameters. It is stronger than the condition on surviving strict factors, but avoids computing which of their sums will survive. **Corollary 2.** Fix the expression and closure, and suppose that \[ \sum_{i\in B}n_i=0 \quad\text{or}\quad \left|\sum_{i\in B}n_i\right|>B_E \qquad\text{for every nonempty }B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}. \tag{15} \] If the resulting knot is hyperbolic, it satisfies (2). In particular, fix any integer vector \(\mathbf a\) and set \(\mathbf n=t\mathbf a\). For every integer \(t\) with \(|t|>B_E\), every hyperbolic knot obtained in this way satisfies the volume equality. The parameter \(t\) is fixed before the quantum level \(N\) tends to infinity. To prove the corollary, each surviving strict weight is a nonzero subset sum, so (15) implies the theorem's hypothesis. On the integer ray, such a sum is \(t\sum_{i\in B}a_i\); its magnitude is at least \(|t|\) unless it vanishes. This also allows zero entries and exact cancellations in \(\mathbf a\). The corollary does not say that every ray contains hyperbolic knots; Corollary 1 determines the topological alternative under the same longness condition. Another sufficient special case of (15) is that all original integers have the same sign and each has magnitude greater than \(B_E\). ## 9. The operator period and the volume of this complement The [pointed quantum \(A\)-period theorem](actual_conway_pointed_quantum_a_volume.md) applies to the same reduced knot invariant. Fix a genuine annihilator \(P\), its prescribed finite vector of initial ordinary-color polynomials \(c_0(q)\), and the companion row \(r_N(q)\). With \(q_N=e^{\pi i/N}\), its exact reconstruction is \[ \mathscr P_N(P,c_0) =\operatorname{CT}_{u=0} \bigl[r_N(q_N(1+u))c_0(q_N(1+u))\bigr] =K_N(K). \tag{16} \] The product of Laurent germs is formed before its constant term is taken. This retains the derivatives needed at singular recurrence steps. The required number of initial derivatives depends on the fixed operator, not on \(N\). For every knot satisfying the theorem, \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N}\log|\mathscr P_N(P,c_0)| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K). \tag{17} \] The positive Gram determinant ratio of the same pointing theorem has the exact value \(\mathscr G_N=\sum_{j=j_0}^{N}|C_j(q_N)|^2\). Its ordinary-color terms have a polynomial total bound. Therefore \((\pi/N)\log\mathscr G_N\) tends to this same positive volume. These conclusions transfer through the actual knot isotopy of Section 6; they do not compare unrelated recurrence operators or their classical polynomial factors. The classical geometric-factor question remains separate.

title: Arbitrary widths in the actual Conway seed grammar
text: # Arbitrary widths in the actual Conway seed grammar 30 October 2026. The restriction to the seed h^3 is unnecessary. Let A_s=h^s for any fixed integer s>=3, using s separate original complete-circle coupons and their actual stack product. Expressions may use any finite mixture of these seeds, literal turns, and products. Every retained C(FG) with two such expressions has the same strict source geometry and signed mixed-source estimates as the original three-leaf grammar. The proof below checks the changed seed hypotheses; it does not infer them just from an expression name. There is also an extension to the isolated cylinder C(A_s) for s>=4. The isolated C(A_3) remains outside the whole mixed-color gap proved here. All sizes, trees, signs and filling slopes are fixed before the level tends to infinity. No uniform estimate over unbounded diagrams is asserted. ## 1. Full finite support and an interior optimizer The full Newton coefficients of h_N are positive at every index 0<=r<=M=floor((N-1)/2), including its constant coefficient N^2. For N>=3, A_3 already has strictly positive coefficients at EVERY index 0,...,N-1. Since Bhat_r Bhat_0=Bhat_r, multiplication by h preserves that full strict support. Thus A_s=A_3 h^(s-3) has full support for all s>=3 and every N>=3. This is the actual repeated-root algebra identity, including its normal directions. The old N=2 exception is unchanged. Here is the continuous strict-feasibility argument, separately from the finite support. A strict state of a seed has leaves in (0,1/2) and, at every gate (x,y)->z, max(x,y)<z<x+y<1. (1) A_3 admits such a state at every prescribed output b in (0,1). Given this property for A_(s-1), choose 0<c<min(b/2,1-b,1/4), t=b-c/2. Use its strict state at output t and a last leaf c. The gate (t,c)->b obeys (1). This proves feasibility for every A_s. At a macro-product choose both child outputs in (b/2,min(b,1/2)); at a turn use the child output 1-b. Hence every proper expression admits a strict state at every interior output. For C(FG), delete only the forced last gate: its inputs sum to 1 and its exact finite coefficient equals one. Choose both child outputs 1/2 to obtain a strict state of the reduced problem. For C(A_s), s>=4, choose its last leaf c in (0,1/2) and the preceding A_(s-1) output 1-c. Again every retained atom is strict. The boundary barrier is unchanged but is worth making explicit. The leaf atoms are (x,1/2-x,1/2), twice; with p=z-x,q=z-y,r=x+y-z,w=1-x-y the gate atoms are (y,x,w), (p,q,2r+w), (p+q,r,r+w). (2) Every nonvertex-flat atom (0,a,1-a), 0<a<1, has positive infinite directional derivative toward the constructed strict state. A vertex-flat atom has a finite derivative and cannot cancel it. A proper endpoint wire propagates down through turns and products until either a product has interior inputs summing to one, or a leaf equals zero. Both exhibit a nonvertex-flat atom. A leaf at 1/2 does also. With every proper wire interior, any equality in (1) displays such an atom directly in (2). Therefore no boundary state maximizes the action. Each positive tetrahedron is strictly concave in its independent angles. The retained angle maps recover every leaf and product wire; turns then recover their wires too. The removed last gate adds no free tangent direction. Thus the reduced Hessian is negative definite, the optimizer is unique and strict, and every fixed proper-output profile is real analytic on (0,1). This proof uses no special property of the number three after constructing a strict seed state. ## 2. Exact open seed ports for every width For the optimized output b set B=cot(pi b), kappa=exp(-f'(b)), X=sqrt((1+B^2)/(1+kappa)), Y=sqrt(kappa) X. Then X^2+Y^2-B^2=1. The actual product stationarity equations give one common X for its two inputs and output, and B_out=(B_left B_right+X^2-1)/(B_left+B_right), Y_out=Y_left Y_right/(B_left+B_right), B_left+B_right>0. (3) A leaf has B=X=cot(pi a)>0 and Y=1. Consequently every optimized A_s has the SAME a at all its s leaves. Iterating (3), with no restriction placed on the finite source labels, gives B_s=T_s(X)/U_(s-1)(X), Y_s=1/U_(s-1)(X), (4) where T and U are the usual Chebyshev polynomials. These are formulas for the optimizer, not a reduction of the original sum to equal labels. For example the open optimum is on the algebraic branch T_s(X)-cot(pi b) U_(s-1)(X)=0. (5) The output b here is the Newton coordinate, not a renamed physical meridian. The branch and its inequalities follow directly from the positive denominators in (3). If 0<X<1 put alpha=arccos X and h0=sin alpha. Induction gives B_j=h0 cot(j alpha), Y_j=h0 csc(j alpha), 0<j alpha<pi, 1<=j<=s. (6) Indeed B_j+X=h0 sin((j+1)alpha)/(sin(j alpha)sin alpha). Starting at alpha in (0,pi/2), positivity forces the next angle to remain below pi; it cannot skip the entire negative-sine interval. Thus X>cos(pi/s). At X=1 the limit is B_s=Y_s=1/s. For X>1, put beta=arcosh X and h0=sinh beta; then B_s=h0 coth(s beta), Y_s=h0 csch(s beta). (7) In every case, for s>=2, -Y_s<B_s<X. (8) For (6), the upper inequality is strict monotonicity of cotangent and the lower is cot(t)+csc(t)=cot(t/2)>0. For (7), B_s>0 and coth(s beta)<coth beta; X=1 is immediate. This proves the entire seed input needed by the old macro-port argument. ## 3. Closure gives a stronger leaf interval at larger widths The inequality -Y<B<X is preserved by a turn (B,X,Y)->(-B,Y,X) and by every stationary macro-product. For X<1, write its child ports as (B_1,Y_1)=(h0 cot u,h0 csc u), (B_2,Y_2)=(h0 cot v,h0 csc v). The inequalities give u,v>alpha=arccos X and (3) gives u+v<pi. The output has angle u+v, so (8) persists. For X>=1, (8) forces both child B's positive and between sqrt(X^2-1) and X. Therefore 0<X-B_i<1 and B_out-X=[(X-B_1)(X-B_2)-1]/(B_1+B_2)<0; its lower inequality follows from B_out>0. In a closed C(FG) the two root ports are (B,X,Y) and (-B,X,Y). Applying (8) to both gives |B|<min(X,Y), hence X,Y<1. These bounds propagate down every macro-product: its common X<1 is fixed, and Y_out<1 implies u+v<pi-alpha, while u,v>alpha. Hence each child has alpha<u,v<pi-alpha and therefore Y_child<1. Turns exchange X,Y. Stop this induction at a seed, not at its individual leaves, whose Y equals one. At a proper A_s seed, (6) and Y_s<1 say sin(s alpha)>sin alpha, 0<alpha<s alpha<pi. Equivalently (s+1)alpha<pi. Its complete leaf label thus satisfies cos(pi/(s+1))<X<1, 1/4<a<atan(sec(pi/(s+1)))/pi <=atan(sqrt(2))/pi=:a0. (9) In particular every leaf is in the strict high-index source regime, and the old universal alias tangent margin applies. Increasing the seed width strengthens the upper bound; it does not degrade it. The isolated cylinder C(A_s) is explicit. Its final flat relation gives B_(s-1)=-X. Formula (3) excludes X>=1; formula (6) then gives s alpha=pi. Thus X=cos(pi/s), a=atan(sec(pi/s))/pi. (10) For s>=4 this belongs to (1/4,a0], so all required inequalities hold, including the endpoint a=a0 when s=4. For s=3 it is atan(2)/pi>a0; that isolated cylinder is still excluded here. ## 4. The actual source and geometry interfaces extend The extension of the existing signed long-filling proof now follows by its explicit interfaces, rather than by changing its vocabulary. * Exact source: every leaf is still the original T(R^epsilon L_j), epsilon in {0,+1,-1}. Full Newton multiplication, turns, ordinary caps and the exposed mark are unchanged. * Whole-source bounds: at every complete leaf in (9) or (10), the proved tangent inequality dominates the full alias profile by c0=2 Catalan/pi-(3/4)log 2>0. The all-color core majorant, actual gate concavity and affine-wire cancellation are unchanged. This proves the same gap for every alias subset and the physical color complement, including the isolated s=4 endpoint. * Exact complex packet: its leaf finite functions and selected changed actions are unchanged. Strictness and the negative Hessian provide its fixed window. With H actual leaves the full primitive grid still has dimension 2H-3, with every D=N-1 offset retained. Its power is N^(3-H+(2H-3)/2)=N^(3/2); equal optimal seed labels do not reduce that dimension. The same nonzero odd amplitude and exponentially controlled interpolation residual apply. * Geometry: the seed is the literal stack of the same pyramids and prisms. The existing local convex gluing and FREE/CAP angle induction apply at each one of its gates. Strictness supplies all their required inequalities. Their ordered corner maps are the original stack maps, so the closed bowtie cut is unchanged. Every complete edge is a leaf bowtie edge, and the same pure/odd edge words and canonical rectangle decorations prove completeness. * Marked deformation: its rational white/prism/turn identities and actual signed shaded maps are local. The strict critical branch therefore assembles them with the same primitive peripheral paths, U=-2pi i chi and V=-2 partial_chi Phi. No new slope or phase convention is introduced by a larger seed. Consequently the quantum and geometric inputs of the [signed long-filling assembly](actual_odd_conway_long_filling_volume.md) hold for these enlarged classes. For every fixed signed coupon pattern and independently sufficiently long signed integral full-twist fillings of any selected auxiliary circles, the same original-source limit equals the actual filled hyperbolic volume. The source normalization, both level parities and the marked peripheral filling equation are exactly those of that assembly. ## 5. Constructive knot parity for every width Use the original endpoint pairings I,U,X. A pure leaf has U, an odd leaf X, and the only loop-creating stack choice is U times U. An odd-length seed can realize {U,X} without loops: use exactly one pure leaf or use all odd leaves. An even-length seed realizes {I,U} without loops by the same two choices. Thus every seed supplies at least two loop-free types. Turns permute I,U,X; the already checked set-product table preserves at least two choices under every product. Backtracking a root choice U or X gives one main component after the cylindrical closure. Full-twist fillings preserve that connectivity. Therefore filling all auxiliary circles produces a constructive knot subfamily for every allowed fixed expression, including isolated C(A_s) with s>=4. Partial fillings retain one main component together with the unfilled auxiliary components. This is still a specified diagram grammar, not a claim covering all arborescent or alternating knots. Audit: [seed recurrences, support and interval certificates](../experiments/audit_actual_conway_arbitrary_width_seeds.py). The proof for unbounded fixed seed widths is the induction and trigonometric argument above; a finite list of widths does not prove it. The claim concerns the stated recursive construction, not all k-bridge or alternating knots.

title: Boundary coefficient limits and the algebraic relation selected by the source
status: Full boundary limit and algebraic relation
text: # Boundary coefficient limits and the algebraic relation selected by the source 29 October 2026. Every coefficient of the actual positive Conway operator has a full-sequence volume profile, including coefficients approaching either endpoint at any rate. At every interior output the optimizer is unique and strictly positive. Its profile supplies one selected algebraic boundary relation and a relative Bloch boundary formula. The boundary coordinate here is the original Newton index. It has NOT been identified with the meridian eigenvalue of a knot, or with a literature quantum A-operator. This extends the closed-source theorem rather than replacing its normalization. In particular its endpoint b=1 is the original marked closure, while b=0 is the actual turned closure. ## 1. The full boundary profile For a fixed robust expression E write its ACTUAL full-normal operator E_N=sum_(r=0)^d e_(E,N,r) Bhat_r, d=N-1. Every coefficient is positive for N>=3. Use the wire polytope from [the Conway variational theorem](actual_positive_conway_variational_limit.md), but leave its final output free. Call this compact rational polytope P_E, its output coordinate b, and its sum of ideal-tetrahedron volumes V_E. Every slice P_E(b), 0<=b<=1, is nonempty. Indeed the constructive integer witnesses give every output r at every level d>=2; their normalized limits supply every real b. Define the boundary profile v_E(b)=max_(x in P_E(b)) V_E(x). (1) Then v_E is finite, continuous and concave on the CLOSED interval [0,1]. Concavity follows by taking convex combinations of maximizing states and using concavity of V_E. Compactness makes (1) upper semicontinuous. Interior continuity follows from finite concavity; at either endpoint concavity gives the reverse lower-limit inequality by interpolation with one fixed interior point. This proves endpoint continuity as well. **Boundary limit theorem.** For EVERY sequence of integers 0<=r_N<=N-1 such that r_N/(N-1)->b, lim_(N -> infinity) (2pi/N) log e_(E,N,r_N)=2v_E(b). (2) No parity restriction, fixed-denominator subsequence, interior saddle, or speed of convergence of r_N/(N-1) is required. ## 2. Exact-output integer approximation The existing uniform factorial estimate applies to every state before fixing its output: log(weight)= (N/pi) V_E(labels/d)+O_E(log N). (3) The number of states is polynomial in N. For the upper bound in (2), choose a largest state. Any convergent subsequence of its normalized labels has output b and lies in P_E(b), by compactness and the closed linear constraints. Equations (1),(3) prove the upper bound. The lower bound needs states with the EXACT prescribed output r_N. The additive semigroup property alone, without the following output correction, would not suffice. First let 0<b<1 and choose a maximizing x_* in P_E(b). Fix a small epsilon>0. Choose a rational point y in P_E sufficiently close to x_* that its output b_0 also satisfies (1-epsilon)b_0 < b < (1-epsilon)b_0+epsilon. (4) This is possible because at b_0=b both inequalities have strict margins. Let D y be integral and put k=floor((1-epsilon)d/D), l=d-kD, R=r_N-kD b_0. For all sufficiently large N, (4) gives 0<=R<=l and l>=2. The constructive full-support theorem gives an integer state a_l at level l with exactly output R. Consequently n_N=kD y+a_l is feasible at level d and has output EXACTLY r_N. Its normalized distance from y is at most (l/d) times the bounded diameter of P_E. Taking epsilon and the distance from y to x_* arbitrarily small, uniform continuity of V_E makes its value arbitrarily close to (1). That single positive state proves the required lower bound. For b=0 choose y rational in the rational face P_E(0), as close to x_* as desired, and let D y be integral. Choose the smallest l>=r_N+2 with l=d modulo D. Then l=o(d), l>=2, and the anchor of level l with output r_N gives the same construction with k=(d-l)/D. For b=1, choose y in P_E(1) and instead take the smallest l>=d-r_N+2 with l=d modulo D. Its required anchor output is l-(d-r_N), which lies in [0,l]. Again l=o(d). These constructions prove (2) at both endpoints, including sublinear but unbounded deviations from them. ## 3. The exact composition laws survive in the entire profile Let R denote the genuine physical turn and let m be the already proved Newton product action: m(x,y,z)=L(x+y)+L(z)-L(x)-L(y) -L(z-x)-L(z-y)-L(x+y-z), L(t)=integral_0^t log(2sin(pi u))du. The exact turn and multiplication of the original coefficients imply the following identities on the whole closed domains: v_(R E)(b)=v_E(1-b), v_(EF)(z)=max_[max(x,y)<=z<=x+y<=1] (v_E(x)+v_F(y)+pi m(x,y,z)). (5) They also follow directly from the source polytopes, keeping all internal variables and shared outputs. In particular v_(EF)(0)=v_E(0)+v_F(0), v_(EF)(1)=max_(0<=x<=1)(v_E(x)+v_F(1-x)). (6) The last product gate is flat in both cases. The first identity is the exact cap-sum decomposition; the second is the full cylindrical pairing and does not assert a connected-sum factorization. ## 4. Every robust interior profile has a unique strict optimizer Fix b in (0,1). There is a feasible state with EVERY leaf label in (0,1/2) and every product gate satisfying p,q,r,w>0, where p=z-x, q=z-y, r=x+y-z, w=1-x-y. Here is a constructive induction. For a product of two robust expressions choose their input labels x=y in (b/2,min(b,1/2)) and use the induction inside both children. A turn uses the child's output 1-b. For the seed h^3 choose a small positive c<min(b/2,(1-b)/2,1/4), put t=b-c/2, and choose a in (t/2,min(t,1/2)). Give its first two leaves label a, their product output t, and its last leaf label c. Both product gates are strict, all leaves are strict, and the final output is b. Now join a maximizing state to this strict state by a straight segment. An ideal atom with boundary angles (0,a,1-a), 0<a<1, has directional derivative +infinity toward the strict state: its zero-angle term is -epsilon c log epsilon+O(epsilon), c>0. At a simplex vertex (0,0,1), the epsilon log epsilon terms cancel, leaving a finite derivative. Positive atoms also have finite derivatives. Thus no nonvertex-flat atom can occur at a maximum. No wire can have value 0 or 1 there. A product output 0 forces both children to be 0. A product output 1 either has two interior children summing to 1, giving a nonvertex-flat first atom, or has an endpoint child. A turn interchanges the endpoints. Descending through endpoint children must reach a leaf: value 1 is infeasible there and value 0 gives its nonvertex-flat atom (0,1/2,1/2). A leaf value 1/2 gives the same obstruction with the angles exchanged. All wires are consequently interior. At a product, w=0 then makes the first atom (y,x,0) nonvertex-flat, and r=0 makes the third atom (z,0,1-z) nonvertex-flat. If p=0 and q>0, the second atom is (0,q,1-q); if p=q=0, the third is (0,x,1-x). The q=0 case is the same. Therefore every product is strict at the maximum. Finally the Hessian has no kernel in the affine wire space. A zero of its negative quadratic form leaves every positive atom angle unchanged. Leaf angles first fix their wire variations to zero; the product angle p=z-x then fixes the output variation, inductively through the tree. Turn variations follow their child. This proves negative definiteness, both with b fixed and with b varying. It follows that the optimizer is UNIQUE for every b in (0,1), and the implicit function theorem makes it real analytic throughout that interval. The Schur complement of the negative definite wire Hessian gives v_E''(b)<0. There is no maximizing-face change in the interior for this robust compiler. Endpoint degenerations are still allowed and are covered by the full limit theorem (2). ## 5. The algebraic boundary branch and its scope Choose a face F of P_E whose projection to b is nonconstant, and a point in its relative interior which is stationary in the internal directions at fixed b. Delete the atoms identically flat on F. Choose rational affine coordinates (y,b) on F and remove the rational kernel of the internal angle map. The remaining positive angles are alpha_jr=a_jr+sum_l B_jrl y_l+C_jr b. (7) All coefficients are rational; weights w_j are positive rational. The Conway case has w_j=1. The negative internal Hessian is positive definite by the [quotient-Hessian theorem](positive_source_algebraic_volume_period.md). Therefore the stationary point continues as a unique real analytic branch y(b), with positive atoms, for b in a small interval. It is the maximum on that face's fixed-b slice. It represents the FULL profile v_E only where this face remains globally maximizing; the argument does not assume away a change of maximizing face. For the robust Conway compiler, section 4 proves that F is the whole wire polytope and that the selected positive branch represents v_E throughout (0,1). Thus the following algebraic relation applies to its entire interior profile. Uniqueness and the nonsingular internal Jacobian continue the same selected component along that interval; there is no exchange of stationary branches on the positive place. Choose an integer Q clearing the denominators of B and C, and put U_l=exp(pi i y_l/Q), M=exp(pi i b/Q), t_jr=exp(pi i a_jr) product_l U_l^(Q B_jrl) M^(Q C_jr), s_jr=(t_jr-t_jr^-1)/i. The s_jr are Laurent polynomials over a cyclotomic number field, and are strictly positive at the selected real branch. For an integer H clearing the denominators of w_j B_jrl and w_j C_jr, internal stationarity is exactly product_jr s_jr^(H w_j B_jrl)=1, for every l. (8) Keep U,M and every s nonzero when clearing negative exponents. The internal Jacobian of these equations, in y, is -(H/pi) Hess_y V and hence invertible. It follows that the selected component is locally etale over M and its function field is finite algebraic over a number field's rational function field in M. This can also be seen from differentials: (8) expresses every dU_l in terms of dM; M is a local parameter, so the component has exactly one transcendence degree. This is a selected local branch statement, not a claim that every component or every point is unramified. Define the exact boundary multiplier P=product_jr s_jr^(H w_j C_jr). (9) It belongs to that algebraic function field. Thus there is a nonzero polynomial relation A_F(M,P)=0 over a number field, with a selected positive real place. On the real branch P>0, and the envelope identity gives the absolute differential normalization d v_F/db=-(pi/H) log P. (10) Internal derivatives disappear by (8); no unproved differentiation of a quantum asymptotic is used. If there are no internal variables, the same statements follow directly from (7),(9). The symbol A_F denotes THIS source boundary relation. It is not called the knot A-polynomial: M exponentiates the Newton output, and P is its variational conjugate. An actual peripheral interpretation is still required before identifying them with knot holonomy variables. Earlier geometric boundary constructions start with a marked gluing variety; here the original coefficient problem produces its own algebraic relation before that geometric comparison. The subsequent [actual Conway cell construction](actual_positive_conway_hyperbolic_volume.md) now supplies a geometric meaning throughout the robust interior: v_E(b) is the volume of an explicit convex ideal polyhedron with one quadrilateral port, and its ordered modulus is kappa_E(b)=exp(-v'_E(b)/pi), P=kappa_E(b)^H. Thus the boundary conjugate in (9) is an actual face modulus. The output phase M records its specified port-edge angle; this still does not identify M and P with a knot's peripheral eigenvalues. ## 6. The relative Bloch boundary fixes the period normalization Work in the selected algebraic function field, enlarged by the needed roots of unity, and tensor multiplicative groups with Q. For each positive atom define two algebraic shapes z_j=t_j1 s_j2/s_j3, z_j^dagger=t_j1^-1 s_j2/s_j3. On the real branch dagger is complex conjugation. For complex parameters it is the displayed algebraic companion; no unproved conjugation involution of the selected function field is assumed. The sine identity gives both 1-z_j=t_j2^-1 s_j1/s_j3 and 1-z_j^dagger=t_j2 s_j1/s_j3. Therefore the exact wedge calculation from [the source Bloch theorem](actual_positive_source_bloch_regulator.md) applies in the function field as well. With beta_F=(1/2)sum_j w_j([z_j]-[z_j^dagger]), it gives delta beta_F=(Q/H) M wedge P. (11) Indeed the internal phase wedges vanish by (8); the sole remaining row is Q M wedge sum_jr w_j C_jr s_jr, which is (Q/H)M wedge P by (9). This is a rational identity with the chosen exponent scaling visible. It makes no integral torsion or peripheral-framing claim. At any algebraic real specialization, the actual regulator is D(beta_F)=v_F(b). (12) Applying the regulator differential to (11), using |M|=1, arg M=pi b/Q and P>0, gives precisely (10). Thus the algebraic boundary relation, relative Bloch boundary and actual source-volume derivative have one consistent normalization. The closed-source theorem at b=1 remains valid even where a stationary branch degenerates. This note does not infer that it is obtained by unramified continuation of one interior branch. Nor does it identify the relative class with the marked geometric class of a complement. ## 7. An exact normalization check For the single positive angle family (y,b,1-y-b), with 0<b<1, the internal maximum has y=(1-b)/2. Here Q=H=1 and the equations are U^2 M=-1, P=2sin(pi b/2), P^2=2-M-M^-1, z=1-M^-1, z^dagger=1-M. (13) Thus both the algebraic boundary relation and its positive real place are explicit. Since P^2=-(1-M)^2/M, direct wedge expansion gives delta(([z]-[z^dagger])/2)=M wedge P, as required by (11). This is a check of the normalization, not an identification of this single-atom family with an actual knot source. The [audit](../experiments/audit_actual_conway_boundary_volume_relation.py) checks exact full-output anchors and prescribed-output semigroup corrections for robust expression trees, including sublinear endpoint sequences. It also checks (13) and its relative wedge identity exactly. The all-sequence and algebraic-branch conclusions are proved above; sampled large-level growth is not used to infer them. No identification with a knot-peripheral A-operator is asserted.

title: The actual closed Conway cut from its bowtie ribbon graph
status: Corrected closed cut and marked cusps
text: # The actual closed Conway cut from its bowtie ribbon graph 29 October 2026. This supplies a direct CLOSED-diagram identification for the complete Conway geometry. It also corrects an overstatement in the earlier explanation of the open cells: the quadrilateral port of a single leaf pyramid must not simply be called half of the physical four-punctured tangle boundary. The closed identification can and should be proved without that assertion. The proof below reconstructs the actual projection cut from literal main-wire connections and the original crossing disks. It compares EVERY colored face cycle and its ribbon order with the stationary polyhedron. Matching only component counts or volume is not used. ## 1. Why the open-port description needs qualification For a leaf pyramid the port is Q=(C0,C1,C2,C3), while its shaded faces are (O,C1,C2) and (O,C3,C0). Restoring the crossing disk pairs C1 with C0 and C2 with C3. In particular it identifies the two CAP edges of Q within each copy. The two FREE edges are joined across copies through the white faces. The two remaining quadrilateral faces consequently have four paired edges and TWO ideal vertex classes. Their compactification has Euler characteristic 2-4+2=0; it is not the usual two-quad cellulation of a four-punctured sphere, whose four punctures remain four distinct vertices. Thus an open metric port is useful auxiliary cut data. Its ordered cross ratio and its gluing identities are valid, but those facts do not identify it by itself with the physical four-punctured boundary or determine that boundary's full holonomy representation. In particular one cannot infer a deformed peripheral representation from port cross-ratio matching alone. This observation does NOT give a counterexample to the closed hyperbolic-volume theorem. The closed theorem has the following independent projection-cut proof, which avoids the open-port claim. ## 2. Compile the original main segments without using prisms Expand the robust expression into h leaves, actual turns and stacks. At leaf i label its four main half-segments C_i0 bottom-left, C_i1 bottom-right, C_i2 top-right, C_i3 top-left. These are the pieces from the leaf's crossing-disk punctures to its four physical ports. Its two original main arcs join 0 to 1 and 2 to 3, each crossing its own disk once. The half-segments on opposite sides of that puncture are kept DISTINCT in the projection polyhedron; the shaded face pairing will restore the main arc. An open expression has four exposed, still unpaired half-segments. The literal rules for these four labels are: * A turn replaces (C0,C1,C2,C3) by (C1,C2,C3,C0). * In a lower F, upper G stack, pair F2 with G1 and F3 with G0. The four exposed labels become (F0,F1,G2,G3). * The final cylindrical closure pairs C0 with C3 and C1 with C2. Each pairing joins exactly the two ends of one actual main segment between successive crossing disks. A structural induction shows that each exposed label is still unpaired, and every removed label is paired exactly once. Therefore a closed expression with H leaves has 2H such segment pairs, not an unspecified equivalence relation deduced from a quantum polynomial. Make one ideal vertex for each paired segment, and one further vertex O_i for each upper crossing-circle semicircle. At leaf i place the two SHADED triangles (O_i,C_i1,C_i2), (O_i,C_i3,C_i0). (1) Here each C now denotes its actual paired-segment vertex. These are the original two sides of that leaf's half crossing disk. Their six edges are the complete bowtie at that leaf. All pairings are the physical identity wires, with no auxiliary circle omitted. ## 3. Ribbon order determines all white faces Use the orientation of the original projection sphere. At O_i the cyclic neighbor order is (C_i0,C_i1,C_i2,C_i3). Both shaded triangles in (1) have their displayed positive cyclic order in the local projection chart. At an outer corner of a shaded triangle, list its outgoing next neighbor followed by its incoming previous neighbor. This ordered pair records the shaded sector; the complementary sector is white. When an actual identity segment joins two such corners, concatenate their two ordered shaded sectors. This is the cyclic order at the resulting four-valent vertex. It follows by taking a thin planar regular neighborhood of the actual joining arc: the two shaded sectors remain on its two sides and the white sectors connect through the two sides of that neighborhood. No strand crosses another during this contraction. Consequently the source's literal planar matching gives a complete oriented ribbon graph, including every shaded sector. A facial walk arriving along the dart (u,v) leaves v along the neighbor preceding u in that cyclic order. The walks (1) are exactly the shaded faces; all the remaining walks are WHITE faces. Thus all white polygons are fixed by the actual diagram, not guessed from face counts. The graph is embedded in the original projection sphere: quarter- turns rotate its charts, and products join the two matching ports by the two actual disjoint identity wires. This construction records nesting and cyclic order as well as abstract incidence. An unembedded graph or a linking matrix would not supply the same information. ## 4. This is the genuine cut of the closed link exterior Put the compiled untwisted main diagram in its projection sphere. Every auxiliary circle is the original small perpendicular circle with its recorded twice-punctured spanning disk. Those disks lie in disjoint leaf boxes, and remain disjoint under every actual turn and stack. In each projection ball, the upper or lower semicircle of an auxiliary component is boundary parallel by its literal half disk. Drill these disjoint semicircles and cut along those same half disks. This returns a ball: drilling one boundary-parallel arc introduces one handle, and opening its recorded bridge disk cancels that handle in the explicit collar of the arc. The collars are disjoint, so this cancellation can be performed for all arcs. The main segments lie on the projection boundary; removing their small neighborhoods makes ideal ends and does not add an interior handle to this cut ball. The ideal vertices of the cut ball are precisely the upper semicircles O_i and the main segments between disk punctures. Flattening each half disk exposes exactly its two triangles (1). At its punctures, the main-segment sides occur in the order of section 3. The remaining boundary pieces are the original planar projection regions, whose cycles are exactly the white facial walks of that ribbon graph. This gives a reversible cut with all faces labeled. The two balls glue across white faces by their projection labels. Within each ball, the two shaded faces of disk i are paired fixing O_i and matching C_i1 to C_i0 and C_i2 to C_i3. These restore the two original arcs through that disk. Reversing all cuts therefore recovers the ACTUAL original link exterior, with its retained auxiliary circles and component/mark paths. ## 5. The stationary polyhedron has exactly this ribbon boundary The geometric construction uses the same local shaded triangles (1). At a product its explicit prism maps are F:(C0,C1,C2,C3) -> (v0,v1,P,infinity), G:(C0,C1,C2,C3) -> (infinity,P,v2,v3). They make precisely the two segment pairings F2=G1 and F3=G0, and leave exposed corners (F0,F1,G2,G3). A turn cyclically rotates these exposed labels. The final face gluing j->3-j makes the remaining cylindrical pairings, exactly as in section 2. The right/flat angle table proves that every edge not belonging to a shaded leaf triangle is a flat WHITE/WHITE seam and is removed when those two white pieces are merged. No edge of a shaded triangle is removed. Hence the final nonflat boundary graph is precisely the union of the leaf bowties (1) under the actual segment pairings. The local orientation check in the displayed prism maps concatenates the shaded sectors exactly as in section 3; the maps are the left/right identity stack, not a reflection of one selected child or an unrecorded mutation. Flat white merging does not change any remaining cyclic order. Therefore the geometric polyhedron and the actual projection cut have the SAME oriented ribbon graph, the SAME two shaded triangles for every disk, and the SAME complete list of white face cycles. Their boundaries are labeled cellulations of a sphere. A map of the matched cells extends over the two balls by radial extension after choosing interior points. Together with the matched white and shaded gluing maps, this gives a homeomorphism of the assembled geometric manifold to the actual link exterior. This is the closed topological identification needed by the volume theorem. The independent audit below implements section 2--3 directly from the original wires, WITHOUT constructing any prism. It then compares every colored face cycle with the separately implemented stationary cell compiler. This is a stronger check than component counts or the numbers 3H,6H,3H+2; the proof itself is the local ribbon-order argument and reversible disk cut above. ## 6. Every actual crossing-circle cusp is explicitly marked The closed-cut identification also gives a general complete-cusp formula. The apex O_i retains the four original neighbors of its leaf pyramid, even after all white merges. In its original local upper-half-space coordinate they are C0=1, C1=E, C2=-1, C3=-E, E=exp(2pi i x_i), 0<x_i<1/2. On a horosphere at O_i=infinity these form a rectangle. Its FREE (white) sides have length W=2sin(pi x_i); its CAP (shaded) sides have length H=2cos(pi x_i). The complete cusp has TWO rectangles, one from each projection ball. Their original disk and projection pairings give the primitive lattice mu=E-1, lambda=-2(E+1), tau_geom=lambda/mu=2i cot(pi x_i). (2) One direct path check fixes the marking. The meridian is the inverse shaded map, fixing O and sending C3 to C2 and C0 to C1. Thus at completeness it is exactly z->z+(E-1). The longitude crosses the bottom white face to the other copy and returns through the top white face. Its translation is -2(E+1). This runs along the two sides of the original crossing disk, and is its disk-framed preferred longitude. It traverses those sides once, not twice. The parallelogram has area 2WH, the total area of the two rectangles, so these paths form a primitive peripheral basis. The sign convention agrees with a positive imaginary cusp shape. Equation (2) is a statement about ACTUAL crossing-circle meridians and longitudes. The Newton wire x_i is used to compute their shape; it is not itself renamed as a meridian logarithm. In the general source filling convention phi_titi(0)=2pi i tau_packet,i, the packet parameter is HALF this geometric ratio: tau_packet,i=i cot(pi x_i), dV_i/dU_i=2 tau_packet,i=tau_geom,i. Matching this Hessian is a useful necessary check, but a full deformed marked representation must still be supplied before the general quantum filling transfer can identify filled volumes. Audit: [literal bowtie ribbon faces and complete cusp paths](../experiments/audit_actual_conway_bowtie_projection_cut.py) and [results](../experiments/actual_conway_bowtie_projection_cut_results.json). This repairs the closed cut interpretation; it does not assert that the single open quadrilateral port is a physical four-punctured boundary, or that arbitrary deformed port matches already solve the full peripheral gluing equations. The audit additionally fixes one global sphere orientation and compares every oriented face cycle and every vertex cyclic order, rather than allowing independent reversal of faces. The closed disk cut, segment matching and oriented ribbon induction determine the cusp marking. The correction of the former open-face statement does not construct a deformed representation.

title: Exact cap-sum reduction of the source and its volume problem
text: # Exact cap-sum reduction of the source and its volume problem 29 October 2026. There is a general topological reduction of the actual positive Conway class, before any hyperbolic gluing problem is attempted. A cap closure of a stack is a componentwise connected sum of its cap closures. Its original full-normal quantum source factors exactly, and its entire angle polytope and volume functional factor with it. This does not turn a Conway four-punctured sphere into a rigid pair of pants. The separating surface used here is an explicitly different sphere: it crosses only the TWO wires between stacked boxes, after the outer cap closure has been made. The result applies to arbitrary boxes in the actual Conway algebra, not just to a pure run of circles. ## 1. Two closures and the exact source identity Use the physical boxes, genuine turn R, Newton basis Bhat_r, and original pointed functional phi of the [actual Conway compiler](actual_positive_complete_circle_conway_trees.md). Put d=N-1. For a box F write C_N(F)=phi(F), D_N(F)=phi(R F). The first is its ordinary two-strand cylindrical closure. Rotating the second diagram back to the original position of F identifies it with the cap closure: the two upper ports are joined to each other and the two lower ports are joined to each other. The same actual cups, caps, and single mark are retained. This is a description of a literal closed diagram, not of an extra functional invented for the proof. For F=sum f_r Bhat_r the established actual turn gives C_N(F)=f_d, D_N(F)=f_0. The full repeated-root multiplication rule has only ONE contribution at coordinate zero: i=j=k=0, with coefficient one. Therefore for ANY two actual boxes in this algebra, D_N(FG)=D_N(F)D_N(G). (1) There is no positivity hypothesis in (1); no root normal, auxiliary color, or framing scalar is removed. All factors are the raw sources of their recorded diagrams. Framing conversions, if desired, retain their separately recorded unit characters. This equality is proved in the actual full Newton algebra, not by citing a multiplicativity theorem for a different link invariant. For the robust positive class, D_N(F),D_N(G)>0 for N>=3. Iterating (1) gives an exact product for every finite cap-closed stack. The two turns also satisfy C_N(RF)=D_N(F) and D_N(RF)=C_N(F), because R reverses all Newton coordinates. At the level of unmarked closed diagrams, these last relations are realized by rotating the whole closed diagram; when a point is recorded, it must be transported with that rotation. The supplied source identities already specify their marks. They do not assert that arbitrary choices of a marked component of an arbitrary link have been proved equivalent. ## 2. The actual separating sphere and its component labels Put the lower box F and upper box G in disjoint balls, and connect their two interface ports by two short vertical arcs in an otherwise empty collar. Perform the cap closure outside the two boxes: the lower pair of F is capped, as is the upper pair of G. Every auxiliary component stays in its own box. Choose a horizontal disk through the middle of the interface collar. Closing that disk around the lower ball and its lower cap in the empty exterior gives a sphere S which meets the link in exactly the TWO interface arcs, once each, and no other component. Cut along S and cap its two punctures on each side by a trivial arc. The lower resulting link is exactly the cap closure of F: the newly inserted arc is its upper cap. The upper resulting link is exactly the cap closure of G: the inserted arc is its lower cap. This is a reversible construction, with the original ribbon framing inherited by each arc. Thus, as an actual unmarked link, cap(FG)=cap(F) #_(upper cap of F, lower cap of G) cap(G). (2) The subscript is essential. A general cap-closed box can have its upper and lower caps on DIFFERENT main components. Equation (2) does not silently choose an arbitrary distinguished component in either factor. Nor does the proof use a linking matrix to recognize the link: the empty collar and its two-punctured sphere exhibit the connected sum directly. If c(F) counts all components in cap(F), then c(FG)=c(F)+c(G)-1. (3) All components other than the two named cap components remain intact. For more than two factors, use parallel interface spheres, obtaining a tree of componentwise connected sums with the cap labels retained. The original marked point can be followed through this construction; (1) is independently the exact identity for the compiler's specified marked source, so no change-of-mark theorem is needed to infer it. This reduction is special to the cap closure. An ordinary cylindrical closure of FG has an outside return running across the same cut and does NOT give this two-punctured sphere. Its exact source is instead the full pairing sum_i f_i g_(d-i), which in general does not factor. ## 3. The entire variational problem splits, including its boundary For any fixed robust expression F, let P_F^0 be its wire polytope from the [whole-source variational theorem](actual_positive_conway_variational_limit.md), but with final output 0 instead of 1.
