The actual AC-cofactor angular theorem at phase difference \(\pi\) gives constants \(C_0,K,\gamma>0\) with \[ |P_N^0(-Cx,Y)|\le C_0N^Ke^{-\gamma N}P_N^+(L_Cx), \quad 1-\delta_0\le x\le1+\delta_0,\quad |Y_f|=L_f. \] The central formulas (11) retain every term at both parities; the ordinary AC variables are supported in one actual triangle. This bound is therefore uniform in every other face phase. Choose \(0<\delta<\delta_0\) and \(R>1+\delta\). Split the expectation in (23) into the lower, middle and upper ranges separated by \(1-\delta\) and \(1+\delta\). In the lower range, positivity of the endpoint product gives \( |R_N(x;Y)|\le P_N^+(L_C(1-\delta))\). In the upper range the TRUE total cap cutoff gives \[ |R_N(x;Y)|\le x^M P_N^+(L_C),\qquad \mathbb E\!\left[X_N^M\mathbf1_{X_N\ge1+\delta}ight] \le(1+\delta)^{-(d-M)}m_d. \] On the bounded middle range, use the finite identity \(R_N(x;Y)=P_N^0(-Cx,Y)-\sum_{j>M}p_{N,j}(Y)(-Cx)^j\). Its first term has the angular gap. The second has the finite Chernoff bound \((x/R)^{M+1}P_N^+(L_CR)\). The full product is evaluated only on this bounded interval: neither its higher powers nor its square is integrated against the moment law. Combining the three ranges gives \[  egin{aligned} \sup_{|Y_f|=L_f}|B_N(Y;2,0)|\le U_0 igg[&P_N^+(L_C(1-\delta))\ &+m_d(1+\delta)^{-(d-M)}P_N^+(L_C)\ &+C_0N^Ke^{-\gamma N}P_N^+(L_C(1+\delta))\ &+\left( rac{1+\delta}{R}ight)^{M+1}P_N^+(L_CR) igg]. \end{aligned}	ag{25} \] This is an explicit finite inequality for the actual positive star values; no individual neighbor A allocation is made. Let \(F_0=F(0)\). Choose \(t>0\) with \(F(t)-F_0<t/2\), set \(R=e^t\), and then take \(\delta>0\) small enough that all four deficits are positive: \[  egin{aligned} \eta_1&=F_0-F(\log(1-\delta)),\ \eta_2&=	frac12\log(1+\delta),\ \eta_3&=\gamma-F(\log(1+\delta))+F_0,\ \eta_4&=	frac12(t-\log(1+\delta))-F(t)+F_0. \end{aligned}	ag{26} \] The first uses \(F'(0)>0\); the fourth uses \(F'(0)<1/2\) with the radius \(t\) fixed first. Continuity gives the third. At even levels \(d-M=M+1=N/2\); at odd levels these quantities are \((N+1)/2\) and \((N-1)/2\). The bounded offsets, (24), and the endpoint weighted limit therefore turn (25) into a strict exponential gap relative to the actual \(P_N^+(L_C)\). This proof does not extend the positive moment sequence to a varying cap spectrum. Sections 2–7 provide that separate analytic extension. The fixed-spectrum argument also does not supply a coefficientwise comparison with the paired endpoint reference: it is the same weighted, phase-uniform star estimate as the main theorem. ## Inputs The original cap factors follow from the exact polynomial tail formula in the [all-demand source proof](research_cap_cross_all_demand_subexponential_contraction.md) and its [original-demand dictionary](research_two_port_main_cap_original_demand_convolution.md). The all-strip coefficientwise bound is the [original cofactor factorization](actual_cross_cofactor_factorization.md), section 8, equations (22)–(27). The [global cofactor angular theorem](actual_cross_cofactor_global_angular_gap.md), sections 1–4, supplies the fixed strip and the polynomial omitted-node cost. The [mixed CROSS/window note](research_mixed_cross_window_cycle_packing.md), sections 1–2, also records the exact central comparisons and support. The finite normal form is the [analytic switching theorem](research_analytic_switching_suppression.md), sections 1–3; its forward version is proved explicitly in (15)–(17). The endpoint action comes from the [even closed half-block theorem](actual_fejer_half_block_entropy.md), section 5, and the [odd raw factorization and coefficient theorem](actual_fejer_odd_regularized_full_numerator.md), sections 1–3. The stationary interpretation uses the [full-fiber common-weight classification](research_full_fiber_sharp_stationary_classification.md). The [incidence and assembly note](research_cap_cross_incidence_and_disjoint_assembly.md) explains why the present whole-star operation is different from attaching a two-port estimate to an exterior carrying A. All divisions in the antidifference argument are confined to the bulk, where both g_(j+1) and a_N-1 are nonzero. The proof retains both window endpoints and both contour-joining currents. The endpoint moment argument in Section 9 uses only the finite d-th moment. The full product is evaluated on the bounded central interval, not integrated beyond the available moment range.

title: The original cap/CROSS contraction on a complex two-spectrum neighborhood
text: # The original cap/CROSS contraction on a complex two-spectrum neighborhood 31 October 2026. Both polynomial spectral parameters, both projectors, and the odd central transition are retained. The statement is restricted to the scope below. ## 1. The original coefficient and the claim Keep the exact two-port incidence \[ E=(A,0,C,Z),\qquad F=(0,A,0,C). \] with A incident only to these ports and its unchanged target A^d, d=N−1. Write \[ \begin{aligned} \theta&=\pi/N,& c_j&=2\cos((2j+1)\theta),&s_j&=2\sin(j\theta),\\ a_j&=2+c_j,&\gamma_j&=2-c_j,&B_j&=\prod_{r=1}^j s_r^2,\\ M&=\lfloor N/2\rfloor-1,& H&=\lfloor d/2\rfloor,\\ J_n&=[\max(0,n-H),\min(M,n)]\cap\mathbb Z. \end{aligned} \] The cap parameter is sigma, near +2; the E parameter is tau, near −2. Define the genuine polynomial cap weights \[ \begin{aligned} g_j(\sigma)&=\sigma-c_j,\\ b_j(\sigma)&=B_j\prod_{r=j+1}^{d}g_r(\sigma),\\ \chi_N(\sigma)&=\prod_{r=0}^{d}g_r(\sigma). \end{aligned} \] Let C_(j,h)(tau) be (−1)^d times the coefficient of A^j C^h Z^(d−j−h) in the full original H_(V_N(tau))(A,0,C,Z). Thus C_(j,h)(−2)=C_(j,h) is the old nonnegative raw endpoint coefficient. Apply the actual CROSS cutoff h<=H and RIGHT cutoff j<=M only in the final sum \[ T_n(\sigma,\tau)=\sum_{j\in J_n}(-1)^j b_j(\sigma)C_{j,n-j}(\tau), \qquad 0\le n\le N-2.\tag{1} \] The remaining original degrees are C^n Z^(d−n). The common raw sign (−1)^d does not affect its modulus and has not been changed. Let D_n^ref be the same fixed positive comparator in the [all-demand theorem](research_cap_cross_all_demand_subexponential_contraction.md): even raw positive endpoint at both ports; odd actual regularizer V_N(−2)−N^(−2)V_N'(−2) at both reference ports. The numerator (1) is always RAW. **Theorem.** There are epsilon_0>0 and omega(epsilon)->0 such that, for 0<epsilon<=epsilon_0, \[ \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log \max_{0\le n\le N-2} \sup_{\substack{|\sigma-2|\le\varepsilon\\|\tau+2|\le\varepsilon}} \frac{|T_n(\sigma,\tau)|}{D_n^{\mathrm{ref}}} \le\omega(\varepsilon).\tag{2} \] Both disks are complex. Every spectral root is included, and the level runs through both parities. In particular any two shrinking radii tending to zero give a uniform subexponential comparison: fix epsilon first, use eventual inclusion in its polydisk, then let epsilon decrease to zero in (2). This is a statement for the exact internal A^d contraction, not for a larger star or a whole invariant. No polynomial factor or spectral estimate for arbitrary incidence is asserted. ## 2. Polynomial source identities, including the odd transition The general-coupon physical identity in sections 2–3 of the durable [Newton source proof](research_cap_cross_low_demand_newton_contraction.md) gives BEFORE projection \[ \begin{aligned} C_{j,h}(\tau)&=v(\tau)^T\widehat B_j(Z_N)e_{d-j-h},\\ v_r(\tau)&=(-1)^{d+r}B_r\prod_{l=r+1}^{d}(\tau-c_l). \end{aligned} \] For clarity, its literal physical-index identity is \[ Z(E,F,G)=\phi\bigl(G\mathscr R(F\mathscr R(E))\bigr) =\alpha_E^T F(Z_N)P_{\mathrm{rev}}\alpha_G. \] for arbitrary polynomial coupons, before endpoint specialization. Choose E=V_N(tau), F=Bhat_j, G=g_n=product_(r<n)(z−c_r), n=j+h. The actual protected-face monomials are \[ \begin{aligned} H_{\widehat B_j}(0,A,0,C)&=A^{d-j}C^j,\\ H_{g_n}(0,C,0,Z)&=(-1)^n B_n C^{d-n}Z^n. \end{aligned} \] The unchanged three face targets therefore give the raw scalar (−1)^(d+n)B_n C_(j,h)(tau). On the Newton side it equals (−1)^n B_n alpha_(V_N(tau))^T Bhat_j(Z_N)e_(d−n). Cancelling B_n, with alpha_(V_N(tau),r)=(−1)^r B_r product_(l>r)(tau−c_l), proves the displayed v(tau) formula with exactly its (−1)^d sign. No extra N occurs. This is a general physical polynomial identity, not endpoint interpolation. The Newton relations (c_j−Z)Bhat_j=s_(j+1)^2 Bhat_(j+1), Z_Ne_k=c_ke_k−s_(k+1)^2e_(k+1), and the literal row reflection c_(d−n)=c_n, s_(d−n+1)=s_n then give for both spectra \[ \begin{aligned} g_n t_j(n)+s_n^2t_j(n-1)&=g_jt_j(n)-g_{j+1}t_{j+1}(n),\\ t_j(n)&=(-1)^j b_j(\sigma)C_{j,n-j}(\tau). \end{aligned}\tag{3} \] These are polynomial identities, including when g_j or chi_N vanishes. For n<=M the original cutoffs are redundant, so \[ \begin{aligned} g_nT_n+s_n^2T_{n-1}&=\chi_N(\sigma)C_{0,n}(\tau),&T_{-1}&=0,\\ C_{0,n}(\tau)&=\frac{N^2}{B_n}\prod_{r=0}^{n-1}(c_r-\tau). \end{aligned}\tag{4} \] For n>H set L=n−H. Summing (3) over the actual moving range J_n=[L,M] and retaining the adjacent-projector difference yields \[ g_nT_n+s_n^2T_{n-1} =(g_{L-1}-g_n)t_{L-1}(n)-g_{M+1}t_{M+1}(n).\tag{5} \] At even N=2m these currents contain C_(n−m,m)(tau) and C_(m,n−m)(tau). At odd N=2m+1 they contain C_(n−m−1,m+1)(tau) and C_(m,n−m)(tau). The first odd current DOES NOT generally vanish when tau differs from −2. There is one transition not covered by either n<=M or n>H: at odd level n=H=m, J_n=J_(n−1)=[0,M]. Summing (3) there gives \[ g_mT_m+s_m^2T_{m-1} =\chi_N(\sigma)C_{0,m}(\tau) +(-1)^M s_m^2 b_M(\sigma)C_{m,0}(\tau).\tag{6} \] Equations (4), (5), and (6) cover EVERY transition. No central zero, lower-current term, or top coefficient is omitted. ## 3. Existing coefficientwise majorants at the fixed original root Let kappa=arcosh(1+epsilon/2). The literal cap product gives \[ |b_j(\sigma)|\le U_j e^{N\kappa},\qquad |\chi_N(\sigma)|\le4e^{N\kappa},\qquad U_j=b_j(2).\tag{7} \] uniformly in its complex disk. For j<=M+1, U_j<=C N^2, including the single current index above the cap cutoff. All divisions used to prove (7) are by fixed gamma_r>0, never by varying g_r. For E, use the EXISTING source-proved coefficientwise comparison in [odd regularization](actual_fejer_odd_regularized_full_numerator.md), section 4, equations (13)–(15), and its even comparison in section 5. Denote the positive full reference coefficients by C_(j,h)^ref: they are C_(j,h) at even level, and Cbar_(j,h) from the fixed-root regularizer at odd level, including outside the CROSS cutoff. Then for |tau+2|<=epsilon, \[ |C_{j,h}(\tau)|\le Q_N(\varepsilon)C_{j,h}^{\mathrm{ref}},\qquad Q_N(\varepsilon)\le(1+N^2\varepsilon)e^{N\kappa}.\tag{8} \] Here is why this comparison is root-safe. Each path has distinct unused spectral factors. At even level all a_r>0, and the product of their possible ratios is at most product_r(1+epsilon/a_r)<=exp(N kappa). At odd level a_m=0 is the sole central zero. A path retaining it is bounded by epsilon times the product of its noncentral factors, which is paid by N^2 epsilon times its positive derivative-reference term. Paths without it are paid by the raw reference term. The noncentral product is \[ \prod_{r\ne m}\left(1+\frac{\varepsilon}{a_r}\right) =\left[\frac{\sinh(N\kappa/2)}{N\sinh(\kappa/2)}\right]^2 \le e^{(N-1)\kappa}. \] This proves (8), and shows explicitly why no vanished a_m is divided out. The comparison applies coefficientwise to the full source, hence to either original projected part and both currents. The same source results give uniform CLOSED coefficient entropy for C^ref. On CROSS degrees it is the two-triangle maximum; on the adjacent one-sided seam it is the same continuous full endpoint entropy. These are actual coefficient upper/lower theorems, not merely weighted capacities. Two corner consequences will be used. Let q_L=(0,0,0,1) and q_R=(1/2,0,1/2,0), in degree order (A,input middle,C,Z). Their reference entropies are zero. There are nonnegative e_L(eta),e_R(eta)->0 such that the original coefficients in eta-neighborhoods of these corners obey the uniform upper rates e_L(eta), e_R(eta). The precise fixed multiplicative enlargement of the neighborhoods is immaterial and is included in these definitions. ## 4. A complete comparator-rate lemma, including the high corner The all-demand proof used the rate \[ \begin{aligned} J(u)&=f(u-\tfrac12)+\max_{u-1/2\le a\le1/2} \{3f(a)+f(a-u+\tfrac12)\},\\ f(t)&=-\int_0^t\log\tan(\pi s)\,ds. \end{aligned}\tag{9} \] We need the same actual coefficient estimate beyond its former middle interval. In fact, uniformly for M<n<=N−2, \[ \frac1N\log D_n^{\mathrm{ref}}=J(n/d)+o(1).\tag{10} \] and n=M has rate J(1/2)+o(1). This includes sequences tending to n/d=1. Here is the finite-support lower check for that extension. The existing positive convolution gives the continuous objective \[ E(a,v;u)=2f(a)+f(v-a)+f(u-v)+f(u-a)-2f(v), \qquad u-\tfrac12\le a\le v\le\tfrac12.\tag{11} \] Its derivative in v in the interior is \[ \log\frac{\tan(\pi(u-v))\tan^2(\pi v)}{\tan(\pi(v-a))}\ge0. \] because u>=1/2, so tan(pi(u−v))>=cot(pi v), while tan(pi(v−a))<=tan(pi v). Thus its closed maximum is v=1/2 and equals (9). All actual allocations have limiting data in this compact domain. The closed coefficient upper, polynomial number of terms, and continuity give a uniform upper for (10), including its endpoints. A subsequence compactness argument avoids imposing an interior-optimizer assumption at u=1. For the LOWER, choose the actual cap index j=M, whose reference weight is polynomial: V_M=N at even level and V_M^o=1/[4cos^2(theta/2)] at odd level. At even level use the exact lower block \[ 4(A+Z)R_M^*(0)R_M^*(C)\le P_{E,\mathrm{CROSS}}. \] with its genuine modified path numerators and original scalar normalization, as in [the closed half-block theorem](actual_fejer_half_block_entropy.md), section 5. If one rewrites R_M^* using that theorem's determinant D_M, its scalar C_front=N/[2sin(pi/N)] must multiply EACH factor; it has not been removed here. Choose the forced Z unit. The actual first-triangle A-degree then ranges over \[ n-M\le k\le M\qquad(N\text{ even}).\tag{12} \] The two remaining triangle degrees are exactly M. At odd level the true positive D_m convolution gives instead \[ n-m\le k\le M\qquad(N\text{ odd}).\tag{13} \] with both triangle degrees m=N/2−1/2. The raw-to-regularized CROSS comparison is by uniform positive factors. These are the original integer intervals, not enlarged supports. After dividing by d, the intervals (12), (13) are within O(1/d) of [u−1/2,1/2] at both endpoints and are nonempty for every n<=N−2. Clamp a maximizing a in (9) to the actual interval, then round to an integer. The total change is O(1/d), even when the interval is a singleton near n=N−2. The uniform CLOSED triangle lower theorem and continuity therefore give the matching lower rate J(u). The forced Z and the true R_M^* scalar have remained in this lower estimate throughout. This proves (10). As already proved for (9), J is continuous on [1/2,1], strictly concave in the interior, with a unique peak u_* in (1/2,3/4). It is increasing before the peak and decreasing afterwards. Also, choosing a=u−1/2 gives \[ J(u)\ge4f(u-\tfrac12)\ge0,\qquad J(1)=0.\tag{14} \] These properties and (10) do not depend on either varying spectrum. ## 5. Three row scales and the exact initial block Fix small eta>0 and require epsilon<=c_0 eta^2, with c_0 a small absolute constant. Set \[ k=\lceil\eta N\rceil,\qquad b=\lfloor(\tfrac12-\eta)N\rfloor, \qquad n_R=\lfloor(1-\eta)N\rfloor,\qquad a=k/N. \] For sufficiently large N, k<b<M<n_R<=N−2. Parameters epsilon and eta remain fixed while N grows. The four relevant regions are: the short initial block n<=k; the contour range k<=n<=b; the central low strip b<n<=M; and the projected middle up to n_R. The high corner n>=n_R is bounded directly. For n<=k, every E reference coefficient in (1) approaches q_L. Equations (7), (8), U_j<=CN^2, and the polynomial number of terms give \[ |T_n(\sigma,\tau)|\le\exp\{N[2\kappa+e_L(\eta)+o(1)]\}.\tag{15} \] uniformly on both disks and that initial range. Let C_(0,n)^0=C_(0,n)(−2)>0. Its exact product implies, uniformly through the full low range n<=M at both parities, \[ \log C_{0,n}^{0}=2Nf(n/N)+O(\log N),\qquad D_n^{\mathrm{ref}}\ge C_{0,n}^{0}/4,\qquad C_{0,n}^{0}\ge N^{-C}.\tag{16} \] For n<=b, no varying a-factor is close to a zero. Writing zeta=tau+2, \[ \frac{C_{0,n}(\tau)}{C_{0,n}^{0}}=\prod_{r=0}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{\zeta}{a_r}\right). \] The factors have |zeta/a_r|<=1/2. Since sum_(r<n) a_r^(−1)<=CN/eta for n<=b, their logarithms give the TWO-SIDED estimate \[ e^{-CN\varepsilon/\eta}\le \left|\frac{C_{0,n}(\tau)}{C_{0,n}^{0}}\right| \le e^{CN\varepsilon/\eta}.\tag{17} \] This elementary lower is used only before b. No such nonvanishing claim is made through the central rows. ## 6. Two exact Gamma products on the root-free contour range For k<=n<=b both g_n(sigma) and c_n−tau stay uniformly away from zero by c eta^2. Define \[ Y_n=\frac{g_n(\sigma)T_n(\sigma,\tau)}{C_{0,n}(\tau)},\qquad t_r(\sigma,\tau)=\frac{s_r^4}{(c_{r-1}-\tau)(\sigma-c_{r-1})}. \] Only n>k is solved in this normalization. The polynomial identity (4) and its exact C_0 ratio yield \[ Y_n=\chi_N(\sigma)-t_n(\sigma,\tau)Y_{n-1}.\tag{18} \] Put P_(k,n)=product_(r=k+1)^n t_r, A_(k,j)=P_(k,j)^(−1). The solution retains the original starting source: \[ Y_n=(-1)^{n-k}P_{k,n}Y_k +\chi_N(\sigma)(-1)^nP_{k,n}\sum_{j=k+1}^{n}(-1)^jA_{k,j}.\tag{19} \] There is no reciprocal chi_N. Choose small complex delta,beta with \[ \sigma=2\cos(2\pi\delta),\qquad \tau=-2\cos(2\pi\beta), \qquad |\delta|,|\beta|\le\eta/8. \] The choice of signs does not matter because every expression is even in each parameter. For t_r=(r−1/2)/N in the next display (this local notation denotes a mesh point, not the recurrence coefficient), the exact product ratio is \[ \frac{A_{k,j}(\sigma,\tau)}{A_{k,j}(2,-2)} =\prod_{r=k+1}^{j} \frac{\sin(\pi(t_r+\delta))\sin(\pi(t_r-\delta))}{\sin^2(\pi t_r)} \frac{\cos(\pi(t_r+\beta))\cos(\pi(t_r-\beta))}{\cos^2(\pi t_r)}. \tag{20} \] Let s(t)=sin(pi t)/(pi t) and L_delta(t)=log s(t+delta)+log s(t−delta)−2log s(t), with the fixed analytic sinc logarithm. Define m=N/2, not necessarily an integer. The two exact Gamma multipliers are \[ \begin{aligned} G_\delta(z,k)&= \frac{\Gamma(z+\frac12+N\delta)\Gamma(z+\frac12-N\delta)\Gamma(k+\frac12)^2} {\Gamma(k+\frac12+N\delta)\Gamma(k+\frac12-N\delta)\Gamma(z+\frac12)^2},\\ H_\beta(z,k)&= \frac{\Gamma(m-k+\frac12+N\beta)\Gamma(m-k+\frac12-N\beta)\Gamma(m-z+\frac12)^2} {\Gamma(m-z+\frac12+N\beta)\Gamma(m-z+\frac12-N\beta)\Gamma(m-k+\frac12)^2}. \end{aligned}\tag{21} \] Equation (20) is exactly G_delta(j,k)H_beta(j,k) times the exponential of the midpoint sum of \[ L(t)=L_\delta(t)+L_\beta(\tfrac12-t). \] Both nearby endpoint zero pairs have therefore been removed from the Euler–Maclaurin input and placed in EXACT Gamma factors. Let Acal_N(z) be the explicit Gamma/smooth-product interpolant in sections 2–3 of the durable [endpoint contour proof](research_cap_cross_full_low_demand_subexponential_contraction.md), with m=N/2 and the literal half-integer extension in [the odd theorem](research_cap_cross_odd_low_demand_subexponential_extension.md). For an analytic L, the midpoint expression used here is explicitly \[ \mathcal E_{1/2,N}(L;u)=N\int_0^u L(t)\,dt +\sum_{l=1}^{p-1}\frac{B_{2l}(1/2)}{(2l)!N^{2l-1}} \bigl[L^{(2l-1)}(u)-L^{(2l-1)}(0)\bigr]. \] with the analytic primitive and Bernoulli polynomials, radius rho=1/5, and optimal truncation p=floor(pi rho N). Define \[ I(z)=\frac{\mathcal A_N(z)}{\mathcal A_N(k)}G_\delta(z,k)H_\beta(z,k) \exp\{\mathcal E_{1/2,N}(L;z/N)-\mathcal E_{1/2,N}(L;a)\}. \tag{22} \] For each fixed contour height Y this is analytic and nonzero on \[ k-\tfrac14\le\Re z\le b+\tfrac14,\qquad |\Im z|\le NY. \] Every shifted Gamma argument has real part >=eta N/2 for N large, uniformly in both spectral disks. The sinc logarithms in L have a common fixed-width zero-free neighborhood of radius rho around the scaled rectangles, independently of eta sufficiently small. Thus the same Bernoulli remainder estimate as in the cap-only proof gives \[ I(j)=A_{k,j}e^{e_{N,j}},\qquad |e_{N,j}|\le e^{-6N/5},\qquad k\le j\le b.\tag{23} \] The constants may depend on each fixed Y; they are uniform in both spectral parameters. Adding the second smooth logarithm only changes a finite prefactor, absorbed by 2pi/5>6/5. ## 7. The calibrated action and the contour estimate The leading logarithm of G_delta is the difference of \[ N\bigl[(u+\delta)\operatorname{Log}(u+\delta)+(u-\delta)\operatorname{Log}(u-\delta)-2u\operatorname{Log}u\bigr] \] between u=z/N and a. The leading logarithm of H_beta is the NEGATIVE difference of the same expression with u replaced by 1/2−u and delta by beta. The exact normalization makes both differences vanish at a. Stirling errors are O_(eta,Y)(log N), uniformly in both disks; all arguments remain in the right half-plane. The smooth midpoint terms have the corresponding integrals with O_Y(N^(−1)) corrections. Differentiating these leading expressions and adding the smooth terms gives exactly \[ \Psi'(u)=\operatorname{Log}\left(1+\frac{\sigma-2}{4\sin^2(\pi u)}\right) +\operatorname{Log}\left(1-\frac{\tau+2}{4\cos^2(\pi u)}\right), \qquad\Psi(a)=0.\tag{24} \] The small logarithms are the branches zero at the base spectra. Exponentiating verifies the sine/cosine identities in (20), and analytic continuation in the small delta,beta disks fixes the branches. Normalization at a fixes the integration constant. There is no unrecorded branch-dependent scalar. For eta/2<=x<=1/2−eta/2, use \[ \begin{aligned} |\sin(\pi(x+iy))|^2&=\sin^2(\pi x)+\sinh^2(\pi y),\\ |\cos(\pi(x+iy))|^2&=\cos^2(\pi x)+\sinh^2(\pi y). \end{aligned} \] Integrating first horizontally from a to x and then vertically, the elementary integrals of 1/(x^2+y^2) and 1/((1/2−x)^2+y^2) prove \[ |\Psi(x+iy)|\le C\varepsilon/\eta=:B.\tag{25} \] for ALL heights y. This bound is independent of the fixed Y used in the interpolation. It applies on the full enlarged rectangle for sufficiently large N. The calibrated growth formula is consequently \[ \begin{aligned} \log|I(z)|&=N\Re[2f(z/N)-2f(a)+\Psi(z/N)]+O_{\eta,Y}(\log N),\\ \log|P_{k,n}|&=-2N[f(n/N)-f(a)]-N\Re\Psi(n/N)+O_\eta(\log N). \end{aligned}\tag{26} \] Apply the exact alternating residue argument to (22). Enclose the integers k,...,n by real sides k−1/4,n+1/4 and imaginary sides ±NY, integrate pi I(z)csc(pi z), then subtract the exact first term I(k)=1. After multiplication by P_(k,n), the leading exponent is \[ N[h(x,y)-2f(n/N)+2B],\qquad h(x,y)=\Re[2f(x+iy)]-\pi|y|.\tag{27} \] The endpoint estimates give h(x,y)<=2f(x), and on the horizontal sides \[ |h(x,Y)|\le\varepsilon_Y=\frac{2e^{-2\pi Y}}{\pi(1-e^{-4\pi Y})}\longrightarrow0. \] The left side costs at most 2Nf(a)+2NB; the right side costs 2NB+O_eta(1); the horizontal sides cost N(epsilon_Y+2B). Contour lengths and all Gamma corrections are only polynomial in N for fixed eta,Y. The error (23) remains negligible AFTER propagation and forcing: \[ |\chi_NP_{k,n}|\sum_{j=k}^{n}|I(j)-A_{k,j}| \le\exp\{N[2\max f-6/5+2B+\kappa]+O_\eta(\log N)\}. \tag{28} \] Choose eta_0,c_0 small so that 2B+kappa<1/10. Since 2max f<1, this is exponentially small. The parameter bounds in (17), needed to convert back to the fixed comparator, add at most C epsilon/eta to a rate; the same smallness choice leaves a strict error margin after that conversion as well. The initial value in (19), by (15), (17), and bounded g_k, has rate at most 2kappa+e_L(eta)+C epsilon/eta. Its homogeneous propagator in (26) costs at most 2f(a)+B. The forcing term is bounded by the contour estimate just described. Fix epsilon,eta,Y, let N grow, and only then let Y grow. Equations (17), (19), and (26)–(28) prove the STRONG core estimate \[ \begin{aligned} \limsup_N\frac1N\log\max_{k\le n\le b}\sup_{\mathrm{disks}} \frac{|T_n(\sigma,\tau)|}{C_{0,n}^{0}}&\le\Omega_{\mathrm{core}},\\ \Omega_{\mathrm{core}}&=2\kappa+e_L(\eta)+2f(\eta)+C\varepsilon/\eta. \end{aligned}\tag{29} \] The stronger denominator C_(0,n)^0 is retained deliberately: using only D_n^ref here would lose the small absolute boundary rate needed for the next strip. No normalization is continued past b. ## 8. Raw propagation across the central low strip For b<n<=M use the polynomial recurrence (4) itself. The factor g_n(sigma) stays uniformly close to 4. The old low ratio s_n^2/gamma_n is at most one, and replacing gamma_n by g_n changes its modulus by at most exp(C epsilon). Hence every raw forward propagator across this strip costs at most exp(CN epsilon). There is no division by c_(n−1)−tau or C_(0,n)(tau), which may vanish on these rows. For this step use the EXACT PREFIX PRODUCT in (4), not a replacement of the raw C_0 coefficient by an unspecified reference coefficient. For n<=M every a_r in that prefix is positive; at odd level the central a_m=0 is outside it. Consequently \[ |C_{0,n}(\tau)|\le C_{0,n}^{0}\prod_{r=0}^{n-1}\left(1+\frac{\varepsilon}{a_r}\right) \le e^{N\kappa}C_{0,n}^{0}.\tag{29a} \] The last inequality uses the full positive product at even level, and the noncentral product displayed in section 3 at odd level. Thus it compares to the RAW C_(0,n)^0 exactly, with no need to identify it with the odd regularized coefficient. For b<=n<=M, equation (16) and f(1/2−v)=f(v) imply log C_(0,n)^0<=2N f(eta)+o(N). Thus the forcing in (4) has rate at most 2kappa+2f(eta). At the starting row b, the stronger estimate (29) has absolute rate at most Omega_core+2f(eta). Summing the O(N) raw recurrence terms yields \[ |T_n(\sigma,\tau)| \le\exp\{N[2\kappa+e_L(\eta)+4f(\eta)+C\varepsilon/\eta+o(1)]\}, \qquad b<n\le M. \] The fixed comparator has D_n^ref>=C_(0,n)^0/4>=N^(−C). Combining this strip with (15), (16), and (29) gives the full-low comparison \[ \begin{aligned} \limsup_N\frac1N\log\max_{n\le M}\sup_{\mathrm{disks}} \frac{|T_n|}{D_n^{\mathrm{ref}}}&\le\Omega_{\mathrm{low}},\\ \Omega_{\mathrm{low}}&=2\kappa+e_L(\eta)+4f(\eta)+C\varepsilon/\eta. \end{aligned}\tag{30} \] This is precisely where a raw recurrence is necessary: the nearby tau roots in the central rows have NOT been divided out. ## 9. The high corner is bounded directly For n>=n_R, the original range J_n forces BOTH j/d and (n−j)/d to lie within O(eta)+O(1/N) of 1/2, while (d−n)/d is O(eta). Thus every E reference degree approaches q_R. Equations (7), (8), the polynomial bound for U_j, and the definition of e_R give \[ \max_{n\ge n_R}\sup_{\mathrm{disks}}|T_n|\le\exp\{N[2\kappa+e_R(\eta)+o(1)]\}.\tag{31} \] This is an absolute coefficient bound ONLY in this shrinking corner. It does not discard cancellation in an interior region. By the genuine comparator lower (10) and J>=0, D_n^ref>=exp(−o(N)) uniformly here. Consequently \[ \limsup_N\frac1N\log\max_{n\ge n_R}\sup_{\mathrm{disks}}\frac{|T_n|}{D_n^{\mathrm{ref}}}\le2\kappa+e_R(\eta).\tag{32} \] No high-demand monotonicity for the varying E coefficients is assumed; it would generally be unavailable. ## 10. Both projected currents on the remaining middle For M<n<n_R use (5), except for the odd transition (6). The cap current index is M+1, so its reference E coefficient tends to the CROSS data with A-load 1/2. Its closed reference rate is J(n/d), exactly as in the endpoint all-demand proof. The lower current has h=H+1 at BOTH parities. Its normalized data approach the original one-sided seam \[ (q_x,q_b,q_c,q_y)=(t,0,\tfrac12,\tfrac12-t),\qquad t=n/d-\tfrac12. \] The full reference closed entropy there is 2f(t), and 2f(t)<=J(n/d) by (14). At odd level this uses the actual positive derivative-reference coefficient for a path whose raw central zero no longer vanishes; it does not reuse the former odd zero simplification. Equations (7), (8) thus bound BOTH currents by \[ \exp\{N[J(n/d)+2\kappa+o(1)]\}.\tag{33} \] At the odd transition n=m, the extra coefficient C_(0,m)(tau) in (6) has reference corner rate zero, while chi_N has rate at most kappa. Its total rate is at most 2kappa; the other transition current has rate J(1/2)+2kappa. Thus (33) also bounds the complete transition forcing. No missing odd index is hidden in the generic moving-range formula. On the interval M<=n<=n_R, the fixed s_n^2 and gamma_n have lower bounds c eta^2. The endpoint raw forward and backward products are bounded by a constant depending on eta: each logarithmic step is O(1/(N eta)), so a product of at most N steps has logarithm O(1/eta), not O(N). Perturbing gamma_n to g_n(sigma) changes a logarithmic modulus by at most C epsilon/eta^2 per step. Therefore EVERY raw propagator over this interval is bounded by \[ C_\eta\exp(CN\varepsilon/\eta^2).\tag{34} \] in either direction. Forcing denominators g_n or s_n^2 cost only fixed eta-dependent constants. No tau factor is divided out during this projected propagation. The comparator J increases to its unique peak and decreases after it. For eta small, n_R/d lies to the right of that peak. Propagate from M up to the peak using (30), and backward from n_R down to the peak using (32). Each encountered boundary or forcing term has comparator rate no greater than the target J in the chosen direction. There are O(N) such terms. Equations (10), (33), and (34) prove the remaining ratio bound with exponent at most \[ \max\{\Omega_{\mathrm{low}},2\kappa+e_R(\eta)\}+C\varepsilon/\eta^2. \] For example all demands are bounded at rate \[ \Omega(\varepsilon,\eta)=2\kappa+e_L(\eta)+e_R(\eta)+4f(\eta)+C\varepsilon/\eta^2.\tag{35} \] Integer rounding near the peak, b, or n_R costs o(1) by the closed continuity already used in (10) and (16). Choose eta=epsilon^(1/4) for sufficiently small epsilon. Then epsilon<=c_0 eta^2, and every term of (35) tends to zero: \[ \omega(\varepsilon)=2\operatorname{arcosh}(1+\varepsilon/2) +e_L(\varepsilon^{1/4})+e_R(\varepsilon^{1/4}) +4f(\varepsilon^{1/4})+C\sqrt\varepsilon.\tag{36} \] This proves (2). A monotone upper envelope may be used if desired. ## Scope The proof uses the original general-coupon polynomial contiguity, the already proved coefficientwise tau-neighborhood majorant, two exact Gamma products on a root-free interior interval, raw propagation through the central roots, BOTH original projected currents, and a genuine high-corner coefficient bound. The actual odd central transition (6) is explicit. All fixed spectral zeros and Hermite data are retained; no quantum root is varied. No whole-source, larger-star, filled-period, or general volume assertion is made. The private cap-only derivation is historical background, not an additional proof dependency of this standalone theorem.

title: Actual continuant recurrences and an explicit positive cap tensor metric
text: # Actual continuant recurrences and an explicit positive cap tensor metric 31 October 2026. **, unpublished analytical continuation** of the [original-demand convolution](research_two_port_main_cap_original_demand_convolution.md). All statements below retain its even-level restriction and original summation cutoff. The polynomial comparison (8) in that note remains open. This note derives recurrences and a positive Jacobi metric; it does not identify that metric with the separately derived cap-moment metric. ## 1. Normalization of the actual continuant Use the notation of the source note: N=2m, d=N-1, M=m-1, theta=pi/N, q=exp(i theta), Q=q^2, s_r=2 sin(r theta), a_r=2+2 cos((2r+1)theta), K_0=1, K_1=s_1^2(A+Z), K_r=s_r^2(A+Z)K_(r-1) +s_r s_(r-1) a_(r-1) AZ K_(r-2). Write S_r=product_(a=1)^r s_a and L_r=K_r/S_r. Direct division gives L_r=s_r(A+Z)L_(r-1)+a_(r-1)AZ L_(r-2). (1) There is no small-eigenvalue inverse in (1). With the exact scalar normalization L_r=i^r q^(-r(r+1)/2) R_r, the recurrence is R_0=1, R_1=(1-Q)(A+Z), R_r=(1-Q^r)(A+Z) R_(r-1) -(1+q Q^(r-1))^2 AZ R_(r-2). (2) Indeed s_r=i q^(-r)(1-Q^r), and a_(r-1)=q^(-(2r-1))(1+q^(2r-1))^2. These two identities prove every factor and sign in (2), including r=2. All denominators (Q;Q)_r are nonzero for r<=d. Dividing by this product recovers the positive normalized source recurrence with dimer coefficient beta_r=a_(r-1)/(s_r s_(r-1)) =cos^2((r-1/2)theta) /[sin(r theta) sin((r-1)theta)] > 0, 2<=r<=d. (3) The strict positivity here uses EVEN N: the half-integer angle never equals pi/2. No odd-level Jacobi assertion is made. ## 2. An actual positive Jacobi metric and its CD identity Let p_0(z)=1, p_1(z)=z and p_r(z)=z p_(r-1)(z)-beta_r p_(r-2)(z). (4) For t>0, exact substitution in the source recurrence gives K_r(-t,1)=S_r^2 t^(r/2) p_r((1-t)/sqrt(t)). (5) This is a polynomial identity after canceling the powers of sqrt(t), so its endpoint values are obtained without a new limiting assumption. Take the d-by-d real symmetric Jacobi matrix J with zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries sqrt(beta_2),...,sqrt(beta_d). Its spectral measure at the first coordinate is a positive probability measure nu_N. The off-diagonal entries are nonzero, so its d eigenvalues are distinct and each has positive first-coordinate mass. Recurrence (4), or direct induction on the coordinate vectors p_r(J)e_1, gives integral p_r(z)p_s(z) dnu_N(z) =delta_(r,s) h_r, 0<=r,s<=d-1, h_0=1, h_r=product_(a=2)^(r+1) beta_a. (6) The indexing in (6) matters: p_r has norm beta_2 ... beta_(r+1), not beta_2 ... beta_r. For example p_1=z has norm beta_2. The polynomial p_d is the characteristic polynomial and vanishes on the support; no positive norm for degree d is asserted. For 0<=r<=d-2 the exact Christoffel-Darboux identity is sum_(a=0)^r p_a(z)p_a(w)/h_a =[p_(r+1)(z)p_r(w)-p_r(z)p_(r+1)(w)] /[h_r(z-w)]. (7) The same formula holds for r=d-1 with the right side divided by h_(d-1); it is a polynomial identity, obtained by telescoping the recurrences, with p_d retained as the endpoint polynomial. Diagonal z=w is interpreted by differentiation. In particular the right side at w=z is nonnegative on the real line. This is an exact positive orthogonality statement for the actual continuant after its negative-outer substitution. It does not follow from a conjectured quantum-group unitarity or an imported q-Hahn identification. ## 3. The coefficient recurrence keeps an undetermined endpoint Extend the notation C_(j,h) from the source note temporarily to 0<=h<=d by its literal formula C_(j,h)=[A^j Z^(d-h-j)]K_(d-h) product_(r=d-h+1)^d a_r. It is zero outside 0<=j<=d-h. For 0<=n<=d define f_n(j)=C_(j,n-j) for 0<=j<=n. Reflection of the original recurrence, using a_(d-h)=a_h and s_(d-h)=s_(h+1), gives, for h=n-j, a_h f_n(j) =s_(h+1)^2 f_n(j-1) +s_(h+1)^2 f_(n+1)(j) +s_(h+1)s_(h+2) f_(n+1)(j-1), (8) for 0<=n<=d-1 and 0<=j<=n, with missing negative-index terms zero. To check the last term, its source unused product contains both a_(d-h) and a_(d-h-1); the latter cancels the actual dimer factor. This leaves precisely the product of the two displayed s factors. Equation (8) supplies n+1 relations for the n+2 coefficients of f_(n+1). Its new top coefficient f_(n+1)(n+1)=C_(n+1,0) is not determined by these equations. Formally extending the recurrence to j=n+1 gives s_0=0 and only 0=0. This coefficient is fixed instead by the original K_d. Omitting it would delete a genuine source boundary. ## 4. Why these identities do not yet settle the original sum The original signed coefficient is (-1)^d sum_(j=max(0,n-M))^(min(M,n)) (-1)^j U_j C_(j,n-j). (9) The [positive cap moment construction](research_flat_cap_positive_moment_form.md) gives U_j/U_0=E X_N^j for every 0<=j<=d, with X_N>0, non-atomic and unbounded. Thus (9) is exactly (-1)^d U_0 E F_(N,n)(-X_N), with F_(N,n)(t)=sum_(j in J_n) C_(j,n-j)t^j. Moments through 2M=d-1 supply a positive Gram form on this original cutoff space. That cap-moment form and (6) are different constructions. No equality of their measures, and no isometry between their polynomial spaces, has been derived. In particular, CROSS restricts the tail degree r=d-h to m<=r<=d, whereas RIGHT restricts the A-coefficient index j<=M. The latter is not the Jacobi row index. Formula (7) does not by itself turn the projected sum (9) into an orthogonal projection. At n<=M, J_n is the full interval 0..n. At n>M, both endpoints n-M and M must remain. A complete-polynomial summation identity at the same n would need explicit correction terms at BOTH boundaries before it could estimate (9). The exact missing estimate remains a polynomial comparison of (9) with sum_(j in J_n) V_j C_(j,n-j), uniformly in N and n. Positive moments, positive Jacobi orthogonality, and the scalar recurrence separately do not establish that comparison. The actual typed unprojected two-port patch uses overlapping pair Casimirs on three heads, rather than two functions of one Casimir; its RIGHT/CROSS projections must also be retained in any future Racah identity. No numerical growth test or general source bound is part of this continuation. ## 5. A finite operator identity and the exact cutoff commutator This appendix uses the full coefficient slice only as an algebraic auxiliary. Define, for 0<=n<=d, H_n(t)=sum_(j=0)^n (-1)^j C_(j,n-j)t^j, D=t partial_t, A_n(D)=a_(n-D), B_n(D)=s_(n+1-D)^2, E_n(D)=s_(n+1-D)s_(n+2-D). All functions of D are finite diagonal operators on monomials. Thus s_(n-D) on t^j means the real number 2 sin((n-j)theta), including negative indices. Equation (8), with its sign (-1)^j, is equivalent to [A_n(D)+t B_(n-1)(D)] H_n =[B_n(D)-t E_(n-1)(D)] H_(n+1), 0<=n<=d-1. (10) The operator order is literal: t B(D) first applies B(D), then multiplies by t. This avoids an implicit D-versus-t commutation error. The nominal highest coefficients on both sides vanish: B_(n-1)(n)=0, B_n(n+1)=0, and E_(n-1)(n)=E_(n-1)(n+1)=0. Thus (10) retains, rather than determines or deletes, the top coefficient discussed in section 3. For 0<=l<=u, let Pi_[l,u] select polynomial degrees l through u. For any diagonal G(D) and polynomial p(t)=sum p_j t^j, direct coefficient extraction gives the exact commutator [Pi_[l,u], t G(D)]p =G(l-1)p_(l-1)t^l-G(u)p_u t^(u+1). (11) Negative coefficients are zero. The original demand slice is Pi_[max(0,n-M),min(M,n)] H_n. Its range changes with n; in particular (10) cannot simply be asserted for these projected slices. Formula (11), together with the difference between the adjacent projectors, specifies the exact two boundary terms to retain. Empty ranges are zero projectors and can be handled directly. This statement does not replace an original projected sector by a full sum. There is a compatible exact relation for the root's cap functional L_N(p)=sum_j U_j p_j. Its moment proof gives L_N[t sin^2(theta(D+3/2))p] =L_N[sin^2(theta(D+1))p], deg p<=d-1. (12) Put J(D)=sin^2(theta(D+1/2)) and T(D)=sin^2(theta(D+1)). Multiplying (10) on the left by J(D), using J(D)t=t J(D+1), then (12), yields L_N[(J A_n+T B_(n-1))H_n] =L_N[(J B_n-T E_(n-1))H_(n+1)]. (13) This is valid throughout 0<=n<=d-1 without requiring a divergent moment: B_(n-1)H_n has degree at most n-1, and E_(n-1)H_(n+1) has degree at most n-1. The other highest terms are annihilated by B_n. For n=0 these products are zero. In particular no extension of (12) to degree d has occurred. The diagonal operators in (13) are Laurent polynomials in Q^D of degree at most two. The resulting relation is not closed on L_N(H_n) alone. It must not be read as a scalar recurrence for the original cutoff sum. Any use on that sum first requires the projector terms (11), as well as the adjacent-projector difference, before applying the degree-restricted functional identity. ## 6. An explicit orthogonal basis for one beta factor, and the cap tensor metric There is a further exact positive construction, distinct from the source-continuant Jacobi matrix. Keep only one of the two independent copies in the cap moment proof. It gives a positive random variable Y_N with w_j=E Y_N^j=sqrt(U_j/U_0), 0<=j<=d, w_j/w_(j-1)=sin(j theta)/sin((j+1/2)theta). (14) The square root is positive. The single-copy convergence and moment proof is the same beta-product proof with no squaring. Its distribution is non-atomic and positive; moments through d are finite. Thus ell_N(p)=E p(Y_N) is a positive definite polynomial inner product on V_M, the space of degrees at most M, by ell_N(p conjugate(q)). On V_M define the degree-preserving real operator T=t^(-1)[cos(2theta D)-1] -cos(theta(2D+1/2)). (15) The first factor annihilates the constant, so (15) is a polynomial operator, not division of a nonzero constant by t. Write A_j=cos(2j theta)-1 and B_j=-cos((2j+1/2)theta). Then T(t^j)=A_j t^(j-1)+B_j t^j. This operator is symmetric for ell_N. On a pair of monomials t^i,t^j, with s=i+j>=1, the difference of the two matrix elements is (A_i-A_j)w_(s-1)+(B_i-B_j)w_s =2sin((i-j)theta) [-sin(s theta)w_(s-1)+sin((s+1/2)theta)w_s]=0. (16) For i=j=0 both first coefficients vanish and the assertion is immediate. All used moments have degree at most 2M<=d. Real coefficients then give the Hermitian statement for complex polynomials. The triangular eigenvalues B_n, 0<=n<=M, are distinct: their angles (2n+1/2)theta lie strictly between zero and pi. There is therefore a unique eigenpolynomial P_n of degree n normalized by P_n(0)=1. Its coefficients c_j satisfy the explicit finite recurrence c_0=1, c_(j+1)/c_j =- sin((n+j+1/2)theta) sin((n-j)theta) /sin^2((j+1)theta), 0<=j<n. (17) This follows directly by equating the t^j coefficient of T P_n=B_n P_n. All factors in (17) are nonzero in the indicated range, so the normalization and degree are valid. Symmetry and distinct eigenvalues prove that P_0,...,P_M are mutually orthogonal for the positive single-factor metric. Their norms are strictly positive and finite. No external q-polynomial identity or representation-theoretic unitarity is used in this derivation. Let Y_N' be an independent copy. The cap moment variable can be taken as X_N=Y_N Y_N'. For F of degree at most M define the monomial-diagonal embedding I F(t,u)=F(tu) in V_M tensor V_M. Then its exact tensor norm is ||I F||_(ell tensor ell)^2 =sum_(i,j) F_i conjugate(F_j) w_(i+j)^2 =U_0^(-1) ||F||_cap^2. (18) Equivalently the cap Gram matrix divided by U_0 is the entrywise square of the single-factor Gram matrix. Its original signed functional is L_N(F(-t))=U_0 < I(F(-t)), 1 tensor 1 >. (19) Thus the explicit orthogonal product basis P_a(t)P_b(u) is a genuine positive tensor metric for the original cutoff polynomial. Both J_n boundaries remain in F=F_(N,n); no unrestricted degree is introduced. The monomial-diagonal subspace is NOT automatically invariant under T acting on either factor. Indeed for 1<=j<=M, A_j is nonzero and (T tensor I)(t^j u^j) =A_j t^(j-1)u^j+B_j t^j u^j has a nonzero off-diagonal monomial. The positive tensor metric alone therefore supplies no source continuant identity, projected Racah operator, or endpoint norm comparison. Deriving such an identity with the actual coefficient projections is still required for the original uniform polynomial convolution bound. ## 7. Exact norms of the single-factor eigenpolynomials The explicit coefficients also give their norms without an imported orthogonality formula. In this section write sigma_r=sin(r theta), tau_r=sin((r+1/2)theta), kappa_n=[t^n]P_n(t). Multiplying (17) gives kappa_n=(-1)^n product_(r=n)^(2n-1) tau_r /product_(r=1)^n sigma_r, [t^(n-1)]P_n/kappa_n =-sigma_n^2/(sigma_1 tau_(2n-1))=:r_n, r_0=0. (20) The coefficient formula (17) is also meaningful for n=M+1=m. This one additional polynomial is an eigenpolynomial whose eigenvalue is distinct from all those at 0,...,M: its angle is (N+1/2)theta, and no angle (2j+1/2)theta for j<=M has the same cosine. Applying (16) to its pairings with degrees<=M uses only moments through 2M+1=d. It is therefore orthogonal to V_M in this cross-moment sense. Its squared norm is NOT used or asserted finite; it diverges. Indeed the single-copy Y_N contains an independent inverse Beta(N-1/2,1/2) factor, so E Y_N^N is infinite; the nonzero leading term of the degree-N/2 polynomial forces its squared integral to diverge. Orthogonality gives the multiplication recurrence, including n=M, t P_n=Acal_n P_(n+1)+Bcal_n P_n+Ccal_n P_(n-1), Acal_n=-sigma_(n+1)tau_n/[tau_(2n)tau_(2n+1)], Bcal_n=r_n-r_(n+1), Ccal_n=-sigma_n tau_(n-1)/[tau_(2n-1)tau_(2n)]. (21) For n=0 the last term is zero. To prove the absence of lower terms, pair tP_n with P_j, j<=n-2, move multiplication to tP_j, and use its degree<n; the P_(n+1) cross pairings also vanish. The leading and next coefficients give Acal_n=kappa_n/kappa_(n+1) and Bcal_n as displayed. Finally P_j(0)=1 implies Ccal_n=-Acal_n-Bcal_n. The last formula in (21) follows from the following exact sine addition identity, which records the only simplification required: sigma_(n+1)^2 tau_(2n-1)tau_(2n) -sigma_n^2 tau_(2n)tau_(2n+1) =sigma_1 [sigma_(n+1)tau_n tau_(2n-1) +sigma_n tau_(n-1)tau_(2n+1)]. (22) It follows by substituting sin(a+b) and sin(a-b), or by writing each sine as its two exponentials and canceling. All denominators in (20)--(21) that are used are nonzero at the stated even levels. Write g_n=ell_N(P_n^2)>0 for 0<=n<=M; these are not the source-Jacobi norms h_r in (6). Pair (21) with P_(n-1), then move t to the other factor. This yields g_n/g_(n-1)=Ccal_n/Acal_(n-1) =tau_(2n-2)/tau_(2n). Since g_0=1, telescoping proves the exact closed formula g_n=sin(theta/2)/sin((2n+1/2)theta), 0<=n<=M. (23) This is positive throughout the original finite Hilbert degree. The product basis in section 6 therefore has explicit norm g_a g_b. In fact 1/N<=sin(theta/2)<=g_n<=1, so these product norms lie between N^(-2) and 1. This is a polynomial normalization of the displayed orthogonal basis, NOT a condition-number bound for its change of basis from the original monomials. The original cap norm remains the restriction to the monomial-diagonal embedding, and that subspace still fails the invariance test following (19). Formula (23) does not identify the source continuant or prove its required endpoint comparison. ## 8. The actual slices are not a scalar orthogonal family This exact finite obstruction rules out one possible identification; it does not rule out the tensor construction or the original convolution bound. Normalize the auxiliary signed slices of section 5 by Hhat_n(t)=H_n(t)/C_(0,n). At N=12, M=5, so n=0,1,2,3 all have their original genuine range J_n=0,...,n. Direct exact arithmetic from the source recurrence and every unused suffix factor gives Hhat_0=1, Hhat_1=1-2t, Hhat_2=1-(2+sqrt(3)+sqrt(2)+sqrt(6)/2)t +(7+sqrt(2)+sqrt(3)+sqrt(6))t^2/2, Hhat_3=1-(8+5sqrt(2))t +(15+10sqrt(2)+3sqrt(3)+2sqrt(6))t^2 -(14+8sqrt(2))t^3. (24) All coefficients belong to Q(sqrt(2),sqrt(3)). Write Hhat_2=1+a t+b t^2 and Hhat_3=1+c t+e t^2+f t^3. Comparing powers of t in t Hhat_2=A_3 Hhat_3+A_2 Hhat_2+A_1 Hhat_1+A_0 Hhat_0 gives A_3=b/f, A_2=(a-A_3 e)/b, A_1=(1-A_3 c-A_2 a)/(-2), and A_0=-A_3-A_2-A_1. Hence A_0=(5341-5789sqrt(2)+1110sqrt(3)+665sqrt(6))/13906 !=0. (25) The nonzero assertion is exact because 1,sqrt(2),sqrt(3),sqrt(6) are linearly independent over Q. Its sign and decimal approximation are unnecessary. Were these four actual slices an orthogonal family for a nonzero positive scalar measure with finite squared norms, symmetry of multiplication would give <t Hhat_2,Hhat_0>=<Hhat_2,t Hhat_0>=0, because t Hhat_0 lies in span(Hhat_0,Hhat_1). But (25) makes the left side A_0 ||Hhat_0||^2 nonzero. Rescaling the individual slices does not remove this obstruction. They therefore cannot simply be one positive scalar orthogonal-polynomial family. No tensor or block identification is refuted, and no source-growth conclusion follows. The [focused exact verifier](../experiments/research_audit_cap_demand_scalar_orthogonality.py) rebuilds the original K_r and all unused tails, checks the ten coefficients in (24), and verifies the full triangular expansion and (25) in the exact field. Its [recorded result](../experiments/research_cap_demand_scalar_orthogonality_results.json) contains only exact field arithmetic. It concerns this finite scalar-identification obstruction only; it is not an audit of the analytical metric theorems or an asymptotic numerical experiment. ## scope and exact remaining question The portable finite audit checks the displayed identities. It does not establish an asymptotic norm comparison. The two positive metrics must remain distinct: the source continuant has the Jacobi measure of section 2, while the original cap has the [positive moment and finite quadrature form](research_flat_cap_positive_moment_form.md) and the tensor realization in sections 6--7. The still-open statement is the uniform polynomial comparison in the [original-demand convolution](research_two_port_main_cap_original_demand_convolution.md), with both endpoints of J_n and every unused source factor retained. No source-volume or full-invariant bound is obtained here.

title: An exponential obstruction to the bare cap-moment Cauchy estimate
text: # An exponential obstruction to the bare cap-moment Cauchy estimate This obstruction keeps the original even-level demand. It disproves the proposed strengthening by a positive Cauchy norm, not the signed convolution, a shared source estimate, or a volume-conjecture limit. ## 1. The original coefficient and the particular proposed norm bound Use the exact source in [original-demand cap/CROSS convolution](research_two_port_main_cap_original_demand_convolution.md): the adjacent ordered quartets are \[ E=(A,0,C,Z),\qquad F=(0,A,0,C), \] with the two original protected faces specialized to zero. The ordinary face \(A\) occurs only at these two ports, so its degree \(d=N-1\) is extracted first. The CROSS coupon at \(E\) is evaluated at \(-2\) and the RIGHT coupon at \(F\) at \(+2\). Keep \[ N=2m,\quad M=m-1,\quad \theta=\pi/N,\quad s_r=2\sin(r\theta),\quad a_r=4\cos^2((r+\tfrac12)\theta). \] The original positive endpoint continuant and its unused factors are \[ \begin{split} K_0&=1,\qquad K_1=s_1^2(A+Z),\\ K_r&=s_r^2(A+Z)K_{r-1} +s_rs_{r-1}a_{r-1}AZK_{r-2},\\ C_{j,h}&=[A^jZ^{d-h-j}]K_{d-h} \prod_{r=d-h+1}^{d}a_r. \end{split} \tag{1} \] For \(0\le n\le d-1\), the actual remaining coefficient is, up to the common raw sign \((-1)^d\), \[ S_{N,n}=\sum_{j\in J_n}(-1)^jU_jC_{j,n-j},\qquad D_{N,n}=\sum_{j\in J_n}V_jC_{j,n-j}>0, \quad J_n=[\max(0,n-M),\min(M,n)]\cap\mathbb Z, \tag{2} \] where the endpoint comparator is \(D_{N,n}\), and \[ \begin{split} U_j&=\csc^2(\theta/2) \prod_{r=1}^{j}\frac{\sin^2(r\theta)} {\sin^2((r+\tfrac12)\theta)},\\ V_j&=\sec^2(\theta/2) \prod_{r=1}^{j}\frac{\sin^2(r\theta)} {\cos^2((r+\tfrac12)\theta)}. \end{split} \tag{3} \] The degree \(A^d\), both remaining degrees \(C^nZ^{d-n}\), every unused row in (1), and the genuine RIGHT/CROSS cutoffs are unchanged. The positive moment theorem [positive cap-moment theorem](research_flat_cap_positive_moment_form.md) constructs a positive random variable \(X_N\) with \(U_0\mathbb E X_N^j=U_j\) through degree \(d\). Set \[ F_{N,n}(t)=\sum_{j\in J_n}C_{j,n-j}t^j,\qquad \mathcal L_N(p)=U_0\mathbb E p(X_N). \] Thus \(S_{N,n}=\mathcal L_N(F_{N,n}(-t))\). The bare moment-Cauchy upper bound is \[ |S_{N,n}|\le \mathcal N_{N,n},\qquad \mathcal N_{N,n} :=\sqrt{U_0\mathcal L_N(F_{N,n}(-t)^2)} =U_0\sqrt{\mathbb E F_{N,n}(-X_N)^2}. \tag{4} \] Its square is finite because \(\deg F_{N,n}\le M\) and \(2M=d-1\). The proposed strengthening \(\mathcal N_{N,n}\le C N^kD_{N,n}\), uniformly in \(N,n\), is false. More precisely, with \[ f(t)=-\int_0^t\log\tan(\pi s)\,ds =\frac{\Lambda(\pi t)+\Lambda(\pi/2-\pi t)}{\pi}, \quad 0\le t\le\tfrac12, \] for every fixed \(u\in(0,1/4]\) and every sequence of even levels and original degrees satisfying \(N\to\infty\) and \(n/N\to u\), we prove \[ \boxed{ \liminf_{N\to\infty} \frac1N\log\frac{\mathcal N_{N,n}}{D_{N,n}} \ \ge\ \chi(u):=4f(u/2)-2f(u)-k(u)>0,\qquad k(u)=2\int_0^u\log(2\cos(\pi t))\,dt.} \tag{5} \] This is an obstruction with the original face demand already imposed. The open comparison \(|S_{N,n}|\le C N^kD_{N,n}\) is not contradicted: the signed expectation in (4) can be much smaller than its norm. ## 2. A single exact orthogonal projection The beta-product construction can be split into two independent copies: \(X_N=Y_NY_N'\), where \[ w_j=\mathbb E Y_N^j=\sqrt{U_j/U_0},\qquad \frac{w_j}{w_{j-1}} =\frac{\sin(j\theta)}{\sin((j+\tfrac12)\theta)}. \tag{6} \] All moments used below have degree at most \(d\). Let \(\ell_N(p)=\mathbb E p(Y_N)\). For completeness, the exact orthogonal polynomials used here follow directly from these moments. On polynomials of degree at most \(M\), with \(D=t\partial_t\), set \[ T=t^{-1}(\cos(2\theta D)-1) -\cos(\theta(2D+\tfrac12)). \] The first numerator annihilates constants. Writing \(A_j=\cos(2j\theta)-1\), \(B_j=-\cos((2j+\tfrac12)\theta)\), its monomial action is \(Tt^j=A_jt^{j-1}+B_jt^j\). The exact sine ratio (6) gives \[ (A_i-A_j)w_{i+j-1}+(B_i-B_j)w_{i+j}=0. \] Thus \(T\) is symmetric for \(\ell_N\). The eigenvalues \(B_0,\ldots,B_M\) are distinct, and its eigenpolynomials \(P_r\), normalized by \(P_r(0)=1\), are orthogonal. Coefficient comparison gives \[ \frac{[t^{j+1}]P_r}{[t^j]P_r} =-\frac{\sin((r+j+\tfrac12)\theta)\sin((r-j)\theta)} {\sin^2((j+1)\theta)}. \] Consequently their leading coefficients and squared norms are \[ \kappa_r=[t^r]P_r =(-1)^r\frac{\prod_{a=r}^{2r-1}\sin((a+\tfrac12)\theta)} {\prod_{a=1}^{r}\sin(a\theta)},\qquad g_r=\ell_N(P_r^2) =\frac{\sin(\theta/2)}{\sin((2r+\tfrac12)\theta)}. \tag{7} \] Here empty products give \(\kappa_0=g_0=1\). One direct verification of the norm formula is the multiplication recurrence \(tP_r=\mathcal A_rP_{r+1}+\mathcal B_rP_r+ \mathcal C_rP_{r-1}\), whose leading coefficients and value at zero give \[ \mathcal A_r=-\frac{\sin((r+1)\theta)\sin((r+\tfrac12)\theta)} {\sin((2r+\tfrac12)\theta) \sin((2r+\tfrac32)\theta)},\qquad \mathcal C_r=-\frac{\sin(r\theta)\sin((r-\tfrac12)\theta)} {\sin((2r-\tfrac12)\theta) \sin((2r+\tfrac12)\theta)}. \] Symmetry then gives \(g_r/g_{r-1}=\mathcal C_r/\mathcal A_{r-1} =\sin((2r-\tfrac32)\theta)/\sin((2r+\tfrac12)\theta)\), which telescopes to (7). For the indices needed below, eventually \(r\le n<M\), since \(n/N\to u\le1/4\). Thus no polynomial beyond the finite Hilbert degree is needed. These are the single-factor polynomials, not the different Jacobi polynomials of the source continuant. Now take any sequence specified in (5), at sufficiently large \(N\). Then \(n<M\), so the original range is exactly \(J_n=\{0,\ldots,n\}\), not a replacement cutoff. In the positive tensor metric \(\ell_N\otimes\ell_N\), project \(F_{N,n}(-tu)\) onto \(P_n(t)\otimes1\). Orthogonality removes every \(j<n\), while \(\ell_N(t^nP_n)=g_n/\kappa_n\). Therefore \[ \langle F_{N,n}(-tu),P_n(t)\otimes1\rangle =(-1)^n C_{n,0}w_n\frac{g_n}{\kappa_n}, \] and a single orthogonal projection gives the exact bound \[ \boxed{\mathcal N_{N,n} \ge U_0 C_{n,0}\frac{w_n\sqrt{g_n}}{|\kappa_n|}.} \tag{8} \] This projection is unaffected by any cancellation among the other tensor components. It uses no condition-number estimate for the monomial-to-orthogonal basis change. The remaining factors in (8), apart from \(C_{n,0}\) and \(\kappa_n\), have zero exponential rate. The literal sine product gives, for \(j\le M\), \[ 4\cos^2(\theta/2)\le U_j\le\csc^2(\theta/2)\le N^2, \qquad N^{-1}\le g_j\le1. \tag{9} \] For the lower bound on \(U_j\), compare each denominator sine to \(\sin((r+1)\theta)\) and telescope; all the angles are at most \(\pi/2\). In particular \(w_n\ge\sqrt3/N\), and none of these factors can hide an exponential loss. ## 3. The exact endpoint comparator rate The uniform closed endpoint coefficient theorem in [uniform half-block and triangle coefficient theorem](actual_fejer_half_block_entropy.md) and [continuous full-kernel coefficient theorem](actual_fejer_full_kernel_entropy_identity_reduction.md) applies to the actual coefficients (1). On a triangle of total load \(1/2\), its entropy is the sum of \(f\) at the three corner loads. The CROSS rate is the maximum of the sum over its two genuine triangles, with one shared outer split. Finite forced degree shifts and polynomial scalar factors are already covered by that uniform closed theorem. For \(n/N\to\rho\le1/4\), \(j/N\to v\), the endpoint cap has \(N^{-1}\log V_j\to-2f(v)\). The CROSS coefficient in (1) has limiting loads \((v,0,\rho-v,1-\rho)\). Write the first outer split as \(a\). The two triangle entropies give the combined rate \[ E_\rho(a,v)=2f(a)+f(v-a)+f(\rho-v)+f(\rho-a)-2f(v), \qquad 0\le a\le v\le\rho. \tag{10} \] The uniform closed coefficient theorem and the polynomial number of terms in (2) imply that the rate of \(D_{N,n}\) is the maximum in (10), along any such sequence. The \(d=N-1\) versus \(N\) normalization changes the arguments by \(O(1/N)\); continuity handles it. At limiting \(\rho=1/4\), one does not need the finite ratio \(n/d\) to be at most \(1/4\). We prove the elementary maximum identity \[ \max_{0\le a\le v\le\rho}E_\rho(a,v)=2f(\rho), \qquad 0<\rho\le\tfrac14. \tag{11} \] On this interval \(f\) is nonnegative, increasing and concave. The three boundary edges satisfy \[ \begin{array}{ll} a=0:&E=f(\rho-v)+f(\rho)-f(v)\le2f(\rho),\\ a=v:&E=2f(\rho-v)\le2f(\rho),\\ v=\rho:&E=2[f(a)+f(\rho-a)-f(\rho)] \le4f(\rho/2)-2f(\rho)\le2f(\rho). \end{array} \] Equality occurs at \(a=v=0\). There is no critical point in the open triangle. Indeed put \(z=\tan(\pi v)\), \(p=\tan(\pi\rho)\), \(u=\tan(\pi a)\). The two critical equations are \[ u^2=\frac{(z-u)(p-u)}{(1+zu)(1+pu)},\qquad \frac{z-u}{1+zu}=z^2\frac{p-z}{1+pz}. \] Let \(r=p-z\), so \(0<r<1\). The second equation forces \(u=z/(1+rz)\). Substituting into the first forces \[ 1+2rz+z^2=r^2(1+rz)^2. \] But the left side minus the right side is \[ (1-r^2)\bigl[1+2rz+(1+r^2)z^2\bigr]>0. \] This contradiction proves (11), since every interior maximum of the smooth function would be critical. Compactness and the displayed boundary checks include all corners. It follows, along the sequences in (5), that \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log D_{N,n}=2f(u). \tag{12} \] The lower bound can also be seen without a coefficient limit: the original \(j=0\) term has \[ C_{0,n}=N^2\prod_{h=0}^{n-1} \frac{\cos^2((h+\tfrac12)\theta)}{\sin^2((h+1)\theta)}, \] whose logarithmic rate is \(2f(\rho)\), while \(V_0\) has zero rate. Thus the maximizing boundary term is genuinely present in the original finite sum. For the numerator projection, \(C_{n,0}\) has both middle loads zero and total outer load \(n/d\to u\). Its two endpoint triangles maximize \(2f(a)+2f(u-a)\) at \(a=u/2\). Hence \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log C_{n,0}=4f(u/2). \tag{13} \] The lower bound here is specifically the positive endpoint coefficient lower theorem, not the later sharp spectral limsup majorant. To see its application directly, the original coefficientwise comparison (15) of [uniform half-block and triangle coefficient theorem](actual_fejer_half_block_entropy.md) specializes at both middle variables zero to \[ 4(A+Z)D_0(A,Z)^2\ \le\ K_d(A,Z) \ <\ 12(A+Z)D_0(A,Z)^2. \] The actual \(D_0\) coefficients have the uniform closed triangle rate \(2f(a)\), including this protected-middle face. Choose a genuine integer split of the desired outer degree within a bounded distance of \(n/2\), and retain either forced outer term \(A\) or \(Z\). The positive convolution supplies the lower rate in (13); concavity and its polynomial number of terms supply the matching upper rate. The forced outer unit and each degree \(M=N/2-1\) cause only bounded degree offsets, covered by the closed coefficient theorem. Thus (13) uses the original continuant coefficient, not an auxiliary unconditioned face polynomial or an unproved spectral lower estimate. ## 4. A strictly positive excess and its precise limitation The explicit product (7) yields \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log|\kappa_n| =\int_u^{2u}\log\sin(\pi t)\,dt -\int_0^u\log\sin(\pi t)\,dt =k(u). \tag{14} \] For the last equality, rewrite the difference as \(\int_0^{2u}\log\sin(\pi t)\,dt -2\int_0^u\log\sin(\pi t)\,dt\), then use sine doubling. The endpoint logarithm is integrable; upper and lower sums on the two monotonicity intervals, with its first cell integrated directly, justify these shifted Riemann sums. The error from the finite products to the same integrals with endpoint \(n/N\) is \(O(\log N/N)\); continuity then handles arbitrary \(n/N\to u\), including integer floors. Combining (8), (9), and (12)--(14) proves the lower bound in (5). The excess is strictly positive by a direct derivative identity. It is continuous at zero with \(\chi(0)=0\), and \[ \begin{split} \chi'(u) &=2f'(u/2)-2f'(u)-2\log(2\cos(\pi u))\\ &=2\log\frac{1+\cos(\pi u)}{2\cos^2(\pi u)}>0 \qquad(0<u\le1/4). \end{split} \tag{15} \] Indeed if \(c=\cos(\pi u)\), then \(1+c-2c^2=(1-c)(2c+1)>0\). At \(u=1/4\), reflection in (14) also gives \(k(1/4)=f(1/4)\), recovering the special value \(\chi(1/4)=4f(1/8)-3f(1/4)>0\). No rational or numerical evaluation of special values is required. On each compact subinterval of \((0,1/4]\), (15) gives a positive lower bound for this excess; no uniform positive bound as \(u\downarrow0\) is asserted. The constant-tensor component \(\langle F(-tu),1\otimes1\rangle\) is the signed coefficient divided by \(U_0\). The large component used in (8) lies instead in the orthogonal direction \(P_n\otimes1\). Its growth cannot be removed from the positive norm, but it contributes zero to that constant-tensor expectation. More explicitly, if \(F_{N,n}(-tu)=\sum_{a,b}d_{a,b}P_a(t)P_b(u)\), then \[ d_{n,0}=(-1)^n C_{n,0}w_n/\kappa_n,\qquad d_{0,0}=S_{N,n}/U_0. \] Since \(g_n\) has zero exponential rate, the same proof gives \(\liminf N^{-1}\log(U_0|d_{n,0}|/D_{N,n})\ge\chi(u)>0\). Thus even a single coefficient defeats a polynomial comparison with the absolute coefficient sum or Euclidean coefficient norm in this fixed explicit basis. This is not a claim about every possible basis, and supplies no lower bound for the distinct coefficient \(d_{0,0}\). Consequently this proof explains precisely why a bare Cauchy step can lose exponential information. It leaves open a cancellation-aware operator identity or estimate for the original signed expectation. It does not show that any actual shared coefficient exceeds its endpoint rate, nor does it change the original source or its cutoffs. ## Proof inputs and validation scope The single-factor tensor construction and norms (6)--(7) are also derived in [actual continuant and cap tensor metric](research_cap_demand_continuant_jacobi_interface.md), §§6--7; the algebra needed here is stated explicitly above. The new inputs are the single-component lower bound (8), the elementary maximization (11), and their consequence (5). No finite numerical sampling is used to prove the asymptotic obstruction.

title: The classical boundary-pressure germ determines the cap root loss
text: # The classical boundary-pressure germ determines the cap root loss 31 October 2026. **analytical research reduction.** Unpublished. This concerns the original ONE-cap coefficient at cap spectrum +2 and all other CROSS spectra -2, at ODD levels. It strengthens the effective-response criterion without assuming a global continuation of a saddle. It does not prove the required comparison for every diagram. ## 1. Keep the same polynomial and the same classical pressure Use the original globally extracted binary polynomial and its genuine real-root factorization from [the negative-axis reduction](research_global_cap_negative_axis_and_mahler_bound.md): \[ P_N(A,C)=P_N(1,1)\prod_{r=1}^{N-1} [(1-\lambda_{N,r})C+\lambda_{N,r}A], \qquad 0\le\lambda_{N,r}\le1. \tag{1} \] Assume the strict finite positive one-cap stationary exterior in [the effective-response theorem](research_global_cap_effective_response_criterion.md). That theorem gives a fixed complex neighborhood of zero on which \[ N^{-1}\log P_N(e^z,1)\longrightarrow F(z),\qquad F(0)=M_{\mathrm{cap}},\quad F'(0)=\nu,\quad F''(0)=\kappa_D>0. \tag{2} \] Convergence is locally uniform and the logarithm continues from real positive weights. Here F is obtained from the original finite exterior potential by eliminating precisely the extracted ordinary log weights. It is not an assumed asymptotic of a modified signed coefficient. Put \[ \mu_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=1}^{N-1}\delta_{\lambda_{N,r}},\qquad G(x)=F(\log(1+x))-F(0). \tag{3} \] Only a fixed small disk about x=0 is used. The logarithms log(1+px), with p in [0,1], have a common analytic branch there. ## 2. A unique compact root measure is determined by the local germ There is a unique probability measure mu_D on [0,1] such that mu_N converges weakly to mu_D along the odd levels and \[ \begin{aligned} G(x)&=\int_0^1\log(1+px)\,d\mu_D(p),\\ m_0&=1,\qquad m_j:=\int_0^1p^j\,d\mu_D(p) =\frac{(-1)^{j+1}}{(j-1)!}G^{(j)}(0),\qquad j\ge1. \end{aligned} \tag{4} \] Proof. Equation (1) gives the first integral exactly with G replaced by its finite-N version and mu_D by mu_N. Locally uniform convergence in (2), composed with log(1+x), permits Cauchy differentiation at zero. Thus every moment converges to the displayed value; the total masses (N-1)/N tend to one. Measures of bounded mass on compact [0,1] have weakly convergent subsequences, and each limit has these moments. Two such limits agree on polynomials. For any continuous function h, its Bernstein polynomials converge uniformly to h: uniform continuity controls |h(j/n)-h(p)| when |j/n-p| is small, and the remaining binomial mass tends uniformly to zero by its variance bound 1/(4n). Consequently the two limits agree on every continuous function and are the same measure. Every subsequence therefore has the same limit, which proves convergence of the full odd sequence. This argument uses the local pressure germ only. There is no global real or complex fugacity saddle hypothesis and no attempt to evaluate the saddle directly across the negative real axis. ## 3. Exact limiting Mahler loss and a finite hierarchy of tests The continuous function \[ h(p)=-\log\max(p,1-p),\qquad 0\le p\le1 \tag{5} \] is Lipschitz with constant 2, including its corner at p=1/2. Therefore \[ \frac{L_N}{N}=\int h\,d\mu_N\longrightarrow \ell_D:=\int h\,d\mu_D,\qquad \frac1N\log\operatorname{Mahler}(P_N) \longrightarrow M_{\mathrm{cap}}-\ell_D. \tag{6} \] All original degree demands remain inside P_N. The original cap bound, including its strictly smaller omitted tail, now gives \[ \limsup_{\substack{N\to\infty\\N\ \mathrm{odd}}} \frac1N\log|S_N| \le\max\{M_{\mathrm{cap}}-\ell_D,\Phi_D-\gamma_D/2\}. \tag{7} \] In particular ell_D > M_cap-Phi_D is sufficient for a strict absolute cap-sector gap at these fixed spectra. This is a sufficient Mahler criterion, not a necessary criterion for cancellation of S_N. It has finite certificates involving only derivatives of the classical pressure. For n>=1 let \[ \begin{aligned} H_n(p)&=\sum_{j=0}^n h(j/n)\binom nj p^j(1-p)^{n-j},\\ b_n&=\sum_{j=0}^n h(j/n)\binom nj \sum_{a=0}^{n-j}(-1)^a\binom{n-j}{a}m_{j+a}. \end{aligned} \tag{8} \] The binomial variance and the Lipschitz bound imply \[ \|H_n-h\|_\infty\le n^{-1/2},\qquad b_n-n^{-1/2}\le\ell_D\le b_n+n^{-1/2}. \tag{9} \] Thus any single verified inequality \[ b_n-n^{-1/2}>M_{\mathrm{cap}}-\Phi_D. \tag{10} \] certifies the strict fixed-spectrum odd cap gap. Conversely, if the strict Mahler criterion holds, some finite n satisfies (10). These are exact mathematical certificates; floating-point evaluations without error bounds do not certify (10). The lower bounds need not be monotone; the running maximum of them is a monotone hierarchy with limit ell_D. All m_j in a fixed test come from finitely many derivatives of the finite classical gluing potential at its genuine stationary weights. ## 4. A sharper test using only the effective conductance There is also an improvement using only the already computed response. Define, for 0<=v<=1/4, \[ \psi(v)=-\log\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-4v}}2\right). \tag{11} \] Then h(p)=psi(p(1-p)). On 0<=v<1/4, \[ \psi'(v)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-4v}(1+\sqrt{1-4v})}. \tag{12} \] This derivative is increasing, so psi is convex, including its continuous endpoint value psi(1/4)=log 2. Equations (2)-(4) give \[ \int p(1-p)\,d\mu_D=m_1-m_2=\kappa_D,\qquad \ell_D\ge\psi(\kappa_D)>\kappa_D. \tag{13} \] The last inequality uses kappa_D>0, psi(0)=0 and psi'(v)>1 for v>0. Jensen's inequality proves the first bound. Hence the finite classical condition psi(kappa_D)>M_cap-Phi_D suffices and is stronger than the previous condition kappa_D>M_cap-Phi_D. It is still not automatic. In particular positivity of conductance alone does not compare it with the original geometric volume deficit. ## 5. A local response integral and a fourth-derivative improvement The same original pressure gives stronger low-order tests. Put v=p(1-p) and use its distribution under mu_D. The elementary series \[ \psi(v)=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\binom{2r}{r}}{2r}v^r, \qquad \psi''(v)\ge3 \quad(0\le v<1/4) \tag{14} \] follows by expanding (12). Thus psi is 3-strongly convex, with continuous extension at 1/4. Choose t>0 inside the certified local real gluing neighborhood and set \[ \begin{aligned} s&=4\sinh^2(t/2),\\ D(t)&=F(t)+F(-t)-2F(0) =\int_{-t}^t(t-|u|)F''(u)\,du,\\ \delta(t)&=\log(1+s\kappa_D)-D(t). \end{aligned} \tag{15} \] Multiplying the two original linear factors at exp(t) and exp(-t) gives (1-p+pe^t)(1-p+pe^{-t})=1+s v. Hence D(t) is exactly integral log(1+s v) dmu_D. Jensen gives delta(t)>=0. The curvature bound for log(1+s v) gives delta(t)<=s^2 Var(v)/2; strong convexity of psi gives ell_D>=psi(kappa_D)+3 Var(v)/2. Consequently \[ \ell_D\ge\psi(\kappa_D)+\frac{3\delta(t)}{s^2}. \tag{16} \] Every F''(u) here is the original Schur-complement response at the nearby positive gluing weights. The cap itself need not be stationary at nonzero u. No global real-fugacity saddle is assumed. The added term is positive unless v is constant almost everywhere. At a mean v equal to an endpoint, v is constant and the inequalities hold directly without differentiating psi at its singular endpoint. The fourth derivative of the Bernoulli logarithm in (1) gives F''''(0)=integral v(1-6v) dmu_D. Thus the limit t tending to zero of (16) is the explicit finite-germ bound \[ \ell_D\ge\psi(\kappa_D) +\frac{\kappa_D-F^{(4)}(0)-6\kappa_D^2}{4}. \tag{17} \] The numerator is 6 Var(v), hence is nonnegative. The full moment hierarchy can improve these low-order tests further. ## 6. The exact negative-axis supremum rates also come from the germ The Mahler bound can lose information by maximizing each root factor separately. Keep the common real variable instead. Define \[ \begin{aligned} U^-(t)&=\int\log|1-(1+t)p|\,d\mu_D(p),\\ U^+(t)&=\int\log|t-(1+t)p|\,d\mu_D(p),\\ m^\pm&=\max_{0\le t\le1}U^\pm(t),\qquad \chi_D=-\max(m^-,m^+). \end{aligned} \tag{18} \] The maxima are finite and attained, although individual values may be minus infinity. The exact original suprema satisfy \[ \begin{aligned} \lim_{\substack{N\to\infty\\N\ \mathrm{odd}}} \frac1N\log B_N^\pm&=M_{\mathrm{cap}}+m^\pm,\\ \chi_D&\ge\ell_D\ge\psi(\kappa_D)>\kappa_D. \end{aligned} \tag{19} \] Here B_N^- is sup |P_N(-t,1)| and B_N^+ is sup |P_N(-1,t)| on 0<=t<=1, exactly as in the original cap reduction. We prove the continuity of these supremum rates, rather than assuming pointwise logarithmic-potential convergence at polynomial zeros. For a finite positive measure mu on [0,1], put U_mu(t)=integral log|1-(1+t)p| dmu(p). For a nondegenerate interval I=[a,b] in [0,1], the averaged kernel is \[ A_I(p)=\frac{H(1-(1+a)p)-H(1-(1+b)p)}{p(b-a)},\qquad H(x)=x\log|x|-x,\quad H(0)=0. \tag{20} \] It is continuous for p>0, including a zero at an integration endpoint. At p=0 it extends continuously by A_I(0)=0, since the original kernel tends uniformly to zero. Thus A_I is bounded and continuous on the whole root interval. Tonelli applied to the nonnegative negative kernel justifies averaging; the finite integral of A_I then proves finiteness of every such interval average. The truncated kernels max(log|1-(1+t)p|,-R) are continuous and decrease to the logarithmic kernel. Their integrals show U_mu is upper semicontinuous. Its full-interval average is finite, so it is finite somewhere and has a finite attained maximum on [0,1]. For a shrinking-interval estimate, take a point t0 with U_mu(t0) finite. Use I_epsilon=[t0,t0+epsilon] if t0<1 and the left interval if t0=1. For p>0, put r=p^{-1}-1. Apart from the single singular root value, cancel log p and rescale. The difference between the averaged and point kernels is \[ \begin{aligned} \omega(v)&=\int_0^1\log|u-v|\,du-\log|v|\\ &=(1-v)\log\left|\frac{1-v}{v}\right|-1,\qquad v=(r-t_0)/\varepsilon. \end{aligned} \tag{21} \] At v=1 the continuous value is -1. The left interval uses omega(-v). For nonzero real v, omega(v)>=-2 and omega(v) tends to zero as |v| tends to infinity. For 0<v<=1/2 the logarithm in (21) is nonnegative; for 1/2<v<1 use (1-v)log(1-v)>=-1/e. For v>=1, rewrite it as (v-1)log(1+1/(v-1))-1>=-1. For v<0 use log(1+x)>=x/(1+x), giving omega(v)>=0. At p=0 the difference is exactly zero. Finiteness of U_mu(t0) excludes an atom at its singular root and makes the point kernel integrable. The differences tend to zero almost everywhere and are bounded below by -2. Fatou gives that the lower limit of shrinking averages is at least U_mu(t0). Upper semicontinuity gives the opposite upper limit. Thus these averages converge to every finite point value, including endpoints. Now let mu_j converge weakly to mu, with bounded finite masses. Choose maximizing t_j and a subsequence converging to t. Each continuous truncated kernel gives limsup U_mu_j(t_j)<=integral max(log|1-(1+t)p|,-R) dmu(p). Let R tend to infinity to obtain the upper bound by max U_mu. For the lower bound, average on a fixed short interval adjacent to a finite maximizing point of U_mu. Equation (20) permits passage through weak convergence; then shrink the interval using (21). Therefore max U_mu_j converges to max U_mu. Apply this lemma to the actual mu_N of mass (N-1)/N. Factorization (1) proves the first line of (19). The plus kernel is the minus kernel with p replaced by 1-p, so the same proof applies. Both affine factors have absolute value at most max(p,1-p); integrating and maximizing proves chi_D>=ell_D. The original finite cap identity and its strict omitted-tail estimate therefore give the stronger bound \[ \limsup_{\substack{N\to\infty\\N\ \mathrm{odd}}} \frac1N\log|S_N| \le\max\{M_{\mathrm{cap}}-\chi_D,\Phi_D-\gamma_D/2\}. \tag{22} \] The condition chi_D>M_cap-Phi_D suffices for strict absolute cap suppression at these fixed spectra. There is no signed-S lower bound: the expectation defining S_N can have additional cancellation. ## 7. Finite certificates for the stronger common-variable criterion Even the criterion using chi_D can be detected by finite gluing derivatives. This needs an approximation argument because the logarithmic kernel is unbounded below. For R>0 set \[ \begin{aligned} K_R^-(t,p)&=\log\max\{|1-(1+t)p|,e^{-R}\},\\ K_R^+(t,p)&=K_R^-(t,1-p). \end{aligned} \tag{23} \] These kernels are Lipschitz with constants e^R in t and 2e^R in p. Let B_n be the Bernstein polynomial operator of degree n in p, as in (8), and let m>=1 be an integer grid size. Define \[ C_{R,n,m}^{\pm} =\max_{0\le j\le m}\int B_n[K_R^\pm(j/m,\cdot)](p)\,d\mu_D(p) +e^R\bigl(n^{-1/2}+m^{-1}\bigr). \tag{24} \] The Bernstein error is at most e^R/sqrt(n), and the grid error is at most e^R/m. Thus m^pm<=C^pm. Each integral in (24) is the finite moment expression in (8), with h(a/n) replaced by K_R^pm(j/m,a/n). It uses only m_0 through m_n, hence finitely many derivatives of the original pressure. For fixed R, letting n,m tend to infinity makes (24) converge to the maximum of integral K_R^pm(t,p) dmu_D(p). These maxima decrease to m^pm as R tends to infinity. Indeed choose maximizers along a diverging R sequence, pass to a convergent t subsequence, and bound by each fixed smaller truncation level before letting that level tend to infinity. The reverse inequality holds because every truncated kernel dominates the original one. Consequently any verified finite test \[ M_{\mathrm{cap}}+\max(C_{R,n,m}^-,C_{R,n,m}^+)<\Phi_D. \tag{25} \] proves the strict fixed-spectrum odd cap gap. Conversely every strict instance of chi_D>M_cap-Phi_D is detected by some finite R,n,m. Finite enclosures must include all approximation and evaluation errors; no sample of growing quantum polynomials is part of the test. ## 8. What this closes and what remains The normalized Mahler loss and both exact negative-axis supremum rates are now determined by the SAME local classical gluing germ that computes the boundary response. A growing collection of quantum roots need not be computed separately. Finite derivative certificates can detect every strict instance of the stronger common-variable criterion. This does not claim that the germ or the measure is encoded by the ordinary knot A-polynomial alone; the original exterior, degree demands, and selected pressure branch are part of the data. No argument here proves that all eligible fixed plat diagrams pass the criterion. The two-cap case also needs its actual joint extraction: a projection onto a selected total degree is not in general stability preserving. For example, the stable polynomial (A+B)(C+D), projected to total degree one in A,C, becomes AD+BC. This vanishes at A=D=exp(i*pi/4), B=C=exp(3*i*pi/4), all in the upper half-plane. This is a closure counterexample, not an actual two-cap source counterexample. Even levels, spectral neighborhoods, the original Green truncations and the full filled-knot assembly retain their stated requirements. The general prescribed long-twist conjecture remains open.

title: Cap-star cuts and exact CROSS stellar elimination
text:
# Cap-star cuts and exact CROSS stellar elimination 31 October 2026. **analytical research theorem.** Unpublished. Original unit face demands and the original protected MAIN edge are retained throughout. Sections 1–2 are source-flow statements at the stationary classification; sections 3–5 are exact classical entropy surgery. No finite signed coupon identity, universal cap exclusion, or volume theorem is asserted. ## 1. A matching edge opposite a cap forces an outgoing overload Let T be a simple triangulated sphere whose triangle pairs are the original ports and whose unpaired edges form the simple MAIN quadrangulation Q. Fix protected adjacent vertices u,v. Name a residual cap \[  egin{gathered} F=(u,A,v,C),\qquad (u,A,C),\ (u,v,C),\qquad 	ext{matching edge }uC,\ q_{F,A}=1-
u,\quad q_{F,C}=
u,\quad 0<
u<	frac12,\quad L_A=L_C>0. \end{gathered}	ag{1} \] All ordinary demands are one and all ordinary incidences are positive. Assume the classification into complete CROSS, strict Green, and residual marked caps. We do not assume that the other A ports are CROSS. Suppose the opposite edge Av EXISTS in T. Bipartiteness of Q implies that it is MATCHING: A and v have the same color, whereas uA and uv are MAIN. The simple cycle uAv bounds two disks. Let D be the closed side not containing C and let r be its number of interior vertices. They are all ordinary. Euler gives exactly 2r+1 triangles in D. The only paired edge on its boundary is Av. Thus D contains r WHOLE ports and one triangle from a unique crossing port E. Write Z for E's middle on the D side and W for its middle on the other side; its outer vertices are A,v. Z is interior unless D is the single face uAv, when Z=u. W is outside D. Let a_D be the sum of the original A loads of the r whole ports in D. Every whole port supplies one, irrespective of its CROSS/Green/cap type. Their total interior contribution is r-a_D, because u,v have zero load and A is the only other boundary vertex. The only further interior contribution is q_(E,Z). The original r interior demands therefore give \[ a_D=q_{E,Z}.	ag{2} \] This includes r=0, where both sides are zero.
